少女をとめ革命かくめいウテナ 鳳雛子 作

An alternate history in twenty-one parts

Utena, 1885: the Meiji serial and the world it made

What if all thirty-nine episodes of Revolutionary Girl Utena had first appeared as a pseudonymous illustrated serial in a Tokyo newspaper in 1885, four years before Japan wrote its constitution and thirteen before it wrote its family law? This is the history of that serial, from its first installment to 2026.

Written October 2026. Real history is marked documented; what follows from it, inference; where I picked one outcome among several, choice.

I

The premise and the rules of the game

What appears, where, and what is held fixed

On Thursday, 2 April 1885, Jiyū no Tomoshibi (自由燈, "The Lamp of Liberty"), a Tokyo "small newspaper" of the kind that printed its kanji with readings beside them so that shop clerks and their wives could follow, carried the first installment of a new serial novel. Its heading read 少女をとめ革命かくめいウテナ, Otome Kakumei Utena, and under it, where an author's name would go, stood three characters nobody recognised: 鳳雛子.

Over the next two years, in four parts and thirty-nine chapters, interrupted twice by the police and finished in book form, that serial told the whole story of the 1997 television series Revolutionary Girl Utena: Utena Tenjō in her boy's jacket, Anthy Himemiya and the duels for the Rose Bride, the Student Council and its creed of the chick and the egg, the Black Rose, Akio Ōtori and the night rides, the Rose Gate, and Anthy walking out of the academy at the end. This document works out what follows. Where the record allows, it uses documented history. Where the record runs out, it reasons from the nearest documented case and says so.

The idea comes from a forum thread that asked what the classical world would have made of Tolkien's legendarium if it had been found in antiquity, and from an earlier companion piece that sent the first Magic: The Gathering cards back to 1593. That piece transported the cards unchanged. A television series cannot travel that way. Thirty-nine half-hours of animation, with their sports car and planetarium and electric lift, would be magic in any century before the twentieth, and magic is the wrong genre for this story. So the first rule here is different.

The rules of the thought experiment

A novel, not a relic. What appears in 1885 is a work of fiction written in 1885, by someone living then, in the language, print technology and visual conventions of a Tokyo newspaper of that year. Nothing comes from the future, and nobody in this history ever learns that the story existed anywhere else. The premise is simply that this book was written. The question of where its author got the story does not arise, any more than it arises for Genji.

The story intact. Every episode has a chapter, in order. The events, the people, their names and their relations are the series'; so is everything the series refuses to explain (what Akio shows his passengers, who lit the fire at Nemuro Memorial Hall, what happens to Utena). What changes is the furniture. Where the anime uses a machine or a custom 1885 did not have, the serial uses the nearest thing an 1885 reader could picture, and one that carries the same charge where possible: Akio's sports car becomes a light carriage he drives himself, the planetarium becomes an orrery and a magic lantern, blood types become the family register. Part IV gives all thirty-nine chapters beside the episodes, with how each was received as it came out.

An author nobody can name. The byline is a pen name and stays one. I do not decide who wrote the serial. Part XVII sets out what the scholars of this timeline argue, and leaves it there.

Everything else is real. Laws, prices, people, newspapers, wars and institutions behave as the record says they behaved until the serial gives them a reason to behave otherwise. When I say that something happened differently, I say why, and what in the record makes it plausible.

Real people. Real people appear in this history, because a story that mattered in Meiji Japan would have mattered to them. What they do differently is labelled, and kept to things their own records make likely. Some of them make different things: a writer writes another book, an artist draws another series. When that happens I describe the work and label it, and I do not quote it. I never put invented words in a real person's mouth, or in a real newspaper's.

Invented critics. What real critics would have thought of a book that never existed cannot be documented. So the critics, reviewers, columnists and correspondents who speak in this document, in Parts IV, XIII and XIX above all, are invented, and the published ideas of real critics appear only as the frames inside which this timeline's critics argue.

Other people's versions. The book was staged, continued, parodied and rewritten from its first year, and from 1919 it belonged to everyone. Those versions change endings, characters and whole chapters, and Part XIV follows them. When a version settles something the book leaves open, that is the version's answer, not the book's.

Impact is allowed. A cultural object cannot rewrite a constitution by itself. It can tip decisions that were already close, give a movement a vocabulary, a set of symbols and an audience, and change what a generation takes for granted. When it does, I follow the consequences forward, through law and money as well as literature, and do not stop at listing what might have changed.

How to read the labels

Three labels run through the whole document. documented marks real history, sourced in Part XXI. inference marks what follows from documented conditions once the serial exists: a prediction, argued, that a reader could dispute. choice marks a place where several outcomes were plausible and I picked one; those are the places to push back. A sentence with no label is either the serial's own content (which is the anime's) or connective tissue. The buttons in the contents rail highlight any one kind.

What this document is not

It is not a novel, and it is not a summary of the anime. It is a systematic working-out of one premise: the serial itself (Parts III and IV); how its first readers read it (V); a chronicle from 1885 to 2026 in five parts (VI to XI), with a detour abroad (VIII); its economy (XII); its critics (XIII); the versions made of it (XIV); the culture it made (XV); what it did not change (XVI); the authorship question (XVII); its texts and editions (XVIII); a set of period documents (XIX); and the two timelines side by side (XX).

The short version

For readers who want the outcome before the argument, these are the largest differences between this timeline and ours, each argued in the Part named:

  • A newspaper enriched and a word coined. The serial swells the sale of a hounded Liberal paper until the Asahi buys it, gives schoolgirls words for their attachments a generation early, and makes the rose the flower of love between women (Parts V, VI, VII, XII).
  • The throne closed a little more firmly. The imperial household's draft allowing female-line succession is killed in 1886 as in our history, with one more argument against it (Part VI).
  • Women on the stage sooner. An all-woman Utena at the Misaki-za in 1893; a Takarazuka Utena in 1919; a film actress in 1918 (Parts VII, IX).
  • Four thousand versions. From its first autumn the book is continued, parodied, staged, sung and filmed by other hands, with reunions, witches, a kamishibai superhero and a national-policy ending; the 1997 anime is the first faithful screen version (Part XIV).
  • A different girls' culture. New words, genres and stock figures; no Princess Knight, no Oscar, and the boys' love comics of the 1970s as a flight from a classroom classic (Part XV).
  • The vote that passed. The House of Peers passes women's local suffrage in 1931 and frees wives from legal incapacity sixteen years early (Part IX).
  • A classic in every classroom. From 1952 every senior high school student reads its first and last chapters (Part X).
  • Two roads abroad. A French Fiancée des roses read in the Paris salons, and a Chinese 少女革命 read by the women students of Tokyo (Part VIII).
  • Today. More women in the Diet, a partnership law for same-sex couples, the same first woman prime minister, and the same revised house law, which still keeps women off the throne (Part XI).

And much does not change at all: the wars, the empire, the mills, the governing party, and all of the household law of 1898 but the wife's incapacity (Part XVI).

A note on names. Japanese names are given family name first when they are real people of the period (Kishida Toshiko, Tsubouchi Shōyō) and in the anime's familiar Western order when they are the serial's characters (Utena Tenjō, Akio Ōtori), as English writing about both usually does. Long vowels are marked (Ōtori, Tōga) in running prose; the anime's English spellings ("Ohtori", "Touga") appear only where they are the series' own.

II

Why 1885

The earliest year the story can be told whole, and the last in which it can still change the laws

1885 is the first year in which every piece of Utena's furniture exists in Japan or in Japanese print, and the year before the state began, law by law, to fix the shape of the modern Japanese family. A story about breaking the shell of the world lands while the shell is still being made.

Japanese names and a Japanese setting were a preference of the request, and they rule out most of the world. Within Japan I weighed six moments. The table compares them on four of the things the premise needs: a medium that can carry thirty-nine episodes with pictures; a world that can hold the series' Western furniture without magic; a censor strong enough to make the book dangerous but not strong enough to erase it; and decisions still ahead of it that a book could tip.

MomentMediumThe Western furnitureThe censorWhat lies ahead
Heian court, c. 1010A monogatari in 39 chapters, hand-copied, perhaps an illustrated scroll (the scroll has been called "twelfth-century animation")None: no school, no sword duels between girls and boys, no castles in the Western senseNone needed; circulation is a few hundred court readersA thousand years, too much to follow honestly
Genroku Osaka, c. 1700Illustrated prose fiction or a puppet playOnly as the exotic of the Dutch trading postLight, sporadicToo far from the modern questions the story asks
Tenpō Edo, 1830A gōkan, the illustrated serial books issued every New Year, with a picture on every pageHardly: no Western school, roses only as Chinese garden plants, the prince and the witch foreign conceptsSevere: the Tenpō Reforms of 1841–43 suppressed the best-selling serial of the dayThe fall of the shogunate, 38 years on
Meiji Tokyo, 1885A daily illustrated newspaper serial, reissued as books and adapted for the stageAll of it, present or described in printSuspensions, seizures, an ordinance in 1887; no erasureThe constitution, the imperial house law, the family law, girls' schooling, women's political rights
Meiji Tokyo, 1905A girls' magazine serialAll of it, and a motor carModerateThe law is already written; the story joins a girls' culture instead of founding one

An earlier sketch of this premise set the story in Tenpō Edo, as a gōkan. The medium fits beautifully: the gōkan was a serial form led by its pictures, illustrated on every page, with characters often drawn in the likeness of kabuki actors. documented It was the nearest thing pre-modern Japan had to an animated cast. inference But the story's furniture is Western, and the Edo telling would have had to invent a European academy, a European prince, a European witch and a rose garden out of nothing. In Meiji Japan those things were arriving by the shipload, and the Edo version would have spent its energy explaining what 1885 could simply show. inference

The medium threshold

By 1885 Tokyo had two kinds of newspaper. The "large papers" (ōshinbun) were written in dense literary Japanese for officials and political men. The "small papers" (koshinbun) printed every character with its reading beside it, ran crime, scandal and theatre news, and from the late 1870s carried tsuzukimono, serial stories in daily installments, each with a woodblock illustration. documented The small papers were read aloud in households and to groups of listeners, so their audience was larger than their circulation and included many people, women above all, who could not read a large paper. documented (Part XXI)

A daily installment with one picture is the closest thing to an animated episode that 1885 possessed. On most mornings a reader got a scene, a cut and a cliffhanger. Serials were then reissued as illustrated volumes and, if they were popular, staged. documented In Utena a chapter, usually of five to seven installments, took one to two weeks to appear, sometimes three, close to the rhythm of a weekly television episode (Part III). choice A girl who reads Utena in 1885 hears it read aloud at breakfast, buys the picture of the duel as a single sheet, sees the women's troupe play it at a Yokohama theatre, and reads it again in a book. That is the life of a television series, rebuilt from what 1885 actually had. inference

The Western threshold

Every piece of the anime's furniture has an 1885 equivalent that a reader had seen or read about:

  • The academy: the mission schools on Yokohama's Bluff, Ferris above all, founded in 1870 and on the Bluff since 1875, with Western buildings, dormitories, pianos and English teachers; the Peeresses' School opened in Tokyo in 1885. documented
  • The ball: the Rokumeikan, the government's hall for Western-style balls, open since November 1883. documented
  • The duels: Western fencing taught to army officers; Japanese swordsmanship in police training and public exhibitions after the 1876 ban on wearing swords, a ban on wearing them, not on owning them; young women with halberds fought in the first public sword shows of 1873, and in the 1880s, by the usual account, the dormitory mistress of the peers' daughters was Chiba Sana, a licensed swordswoman. documented
  • The car: the private carriages of ministers and peers, a conspicuous luxury in Tokyo; there were some 1,800 passenger carriages in the whole country in 1885. documented
  • The lift, the phonograph, the telephone: a freight hoist at a Tokyo paper mill since 1875, and a mine-shaft cage in the Iwakura Mission's published record; a phonograph demonstrated in Tokyo in 1878 and shown to the public in 1879; about two hundred telephones in government offices and none in private hands. documented
  • The planetarium: the orrery, which is what English called a "planetarium" until the projector was invented in the 1920s, and the magic lantern, which the Ministry of Education had supplied to normal schools, with sets of astronomical slides, from 1880 until its money ran out in 1883, and which one of its photographers had been showing free in Tokyo since 1883. documented
  • The roses, the prince, the witch, Lucifer: Western roses in Yokohama gardens; Aesop in a new Meiji translation in the 1870s (the Jesuits had printed one in 1593) and the Arabian Nights in Japanese since 1875, the first books of Grimm from 1887; the New Testament complete in Japanese in 1880. documented

None of this was ordinary. All of it was known, which is what a fantasy needs: the reader must be able to picture the conservatory, the carriage and the lift without ever having been inside one. inference

The legal hinge

Between 1884 and 1900 Japan wrote down who a woman was in law. In 1884 it created a modern peerage, with princes. In 1889 the Imperial House Law restricted the throne to men, the first such rule in Japanese history, which had had eight reigning empresses. In 1890 a law on assemblies barred women from political meetings and associations, and the Imperial Rescript on Education set out the family morality every school would recite. A fight over the Civil Code from 1889 to 1892 ended with the liberal draft shelved, and the code of 1898 made the household head the master of the family and the wife a legal incompetent. In 1899 the state organised girls' secondary schools around the ideal of the "good wife and wise mother", and in 1900 it reaffirmed the ban on women in politics. documented (dates in Parts VI and VII)

A serial that began in 1885 and finished in 1887 reached its readers before every one of these decisions but the first. A girl of fourteen who cried at chapter 39 in 1887 was twenty-five when the family law of 1898 came into force. That is the leverage the premise needs. Earlier, the furniture is missing; later, the law is written. inference

The censor

The press law of the 1880s let the Home Ministry suspend a newspaper or seize an issue for disturbing public order or public morals, and it did so constantly; editors went to prison by the dozen. Books had to be submitted before publication. In December 1887 a new ordinance expelled some 570 activists from the capital within three days. documented (Part XXI) That is enough to make Utena dangerous, to cut it and to stop its serialization, and not enough to destroy it. Meiji Japan banned many books; it did not have the means or the will to pulp a best-seller that had already been printed in tens of thousands of copies. inference

The reach

The 1880s and 1890s were the high point of Western Japonisme. Japanese prints filled Paris, Japanese plays toured Europe and America by 1900, and a Japanese book with pictures could cross into French or English within a decade. From the 1880s Korean and from 1896 Chinese students came to Tokyo to study modern ideas, men first and women in the 1900s and 1910s, and they read what Tokyo read. documented A serial of 1885 has both routes open, and Part VIII follows them.

What 1885 costs the scenario

Honesty requires the downsides. In 1885 about a third of Japanese girls of school age were enrolled in elementary school, and the Ministry of Education counted nine girls' secondary schools in the whole country, with 616 pupils; the new Peeresses' School had 133. documented There was no "girls' market" for publishers to sell to; Utena has to build one. The small newspapers' buyers were mostly men, and the serial's first audience is a household's, read aloud by a father or an elder brother. The paper that runs it is a party organ without a party, in political trouble from the start. The story's third part, with a grown man's courtship of a schoolgirl and an incestuous brother, is more dangerous in 1886 than in 1997, not less. Each of these is a friction, and each, worked through, produces history rather than preventing it.

III

The serial

What appeared, where, when, in what form, and under what name

Otome Kakumei Utena ran in a Liberal party paper that changed its name while the serial was in it, was suspended by the police two chapters before the end of its third part and given up when that part ended, and was finished as a book. The newspaper it began in became, in 1888, the Tokyo Asahi.

The paper

Jiyū no Tomoshibi, "The Lamp of Liberty", was founded on 11 May 1884 by Hoshi Tōru as the popular organ of the Liberal Party, the Jiyūtō: a small newspaper, in the small papers' style, meant to carry the party's ideas to readers who would never open its serious daily. documented Five months later the party dissolved itself, on 29 October 1884, under police pressure and the shame of the risings its radicals had led. documented The paper survived it. On 14 January 1886 it renamed itself Tomoshibi Shinbun, on 1 April 1887 Mezamashi Shinbun ("Wake Up!"), and on 10 July 1888, bought by the Osaka publisher of the Asahi, it reappeared as the Tokyo Asahi Shinbun, the paper that would later employ Natsume Sōseki, become one company with its Osaka parent in 1908 and, in 1940, share with it the single title Asahi Shinbun. documented

It was not a struggling paper. For a time in 1884–86 it had the largest sale in Tokyo, and it was one of the main venues for political fiction. documented From December 1884 it had been serialising Miyazaki Muryū's Kishūshū (鬼啾啾, "Ghosts Wailing"), a history of the Russian nihilists whose heroines were Vera Zasulich, who shot the governor of St Petersburg, and Sophia Perovskaya, hanged for the assassination of Alexander II, who in Muryū's telling gives up the man she loves for "ten million compatriots". The serial ended on 3 April 1885; its book edition, published in October, was banned, and Muryū was convicted. documented Political fiction had been allegorising Japan's politics as a woman courted by rival suitors since 1880, when the first political novel cast the people's rights as a geisha named O-Ken ("Rights") wooed by "People" and "Government". documented The paper's readers were therefore primed for exactly what arrived in its mailbox in February 1885: a story with "revolution" in its title, a girl who fights in a man's coat, and a bride whom rival suitors win by force. inference It also needed a successor to Kishūshū. inference

The first installment

It appeared on Thursday 2 April 1885, the day before the last installment of Kishūshū, under a two-line heading beside the day's woodblock cut. choice The opening is the anime's fairy-tale prologue, told in the voice of an Edo storyteller, with the narrator's doubt at the end turned into the kind of aside a gesaku author made to the reader. The mock-up below sets the opening in vertical columns read from right to left, as the paper would have printed it, with two simplifications: it gives readings only beside the harder characters, where the paper glossed every one, and it leaves out the heavier ruled frame in which the paper boxed the fairy tale (Part IV). The Japanese is new writing for this document, in the literary style of 1885, and is not a translation of the anime's script.

The shape of the serial

The newspaper printed about 210 installments in a year and a half, and the unserialised Part Four was the length of about forty more. A chapter took between three installments (the "story so far" chapters) and nine (chapter 22, the fire at Nemuro Memorial Hall), usually five to seven; since the serial did not run in every issue, a chapter usually took one to two weeks to appear, close to the rhythm of a weekly episode, and three or a little more during the paper's suspension of December 1885, over the New Year holiday of 1885–86 and in the last months of 1886, when the paper, warned in July and suspended in August, ran the serial less often. Each installment had one cut. Each chapter but the last ended with a notice naming the next chapter's heading and the same unexplained tag, 絶対運命黙示録. choice for the counts.

The pictures

The cuts were signed 芳年: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, the greatest print artist of the day, who had begun a series called One Hundred Aspects of the Moon that very year and who had got into trouble in 1884 with another Liberal paper for supplying pictures to Jiyū no Tomoshibi. documented for Yoshitoshi's Moon series, his 1884 work for the paper and his newspaper illustration in general; choice that he drew this serial. The plates of the 1887 book were by his pupil Mizuno Toshikata. choice Each newspaper cut was a small woodblock, cut by a professional carver from the artist's drawing and printed with the text: line only, no tone, no colour. documented for the method. Within those limits the illustrator invented most of what later generations thought of as the look of Utena, because the text describes very little: Utena's long hair loose under a boy's cap, which she never wears in the series and always wears in the cuts; Anthy's spectacles as two blank white circles; the duelling garden as a flat ellipse seen from an angle, with the upside-down castle cut off by the top of the frame; the silhouetted girls of the shadow plays against a wall of rose lattice. The single-sheet colour prints that publishers made from the most popular scenes added the colours readers argued about for decades: a pink that 1880s aniline dyes made almost violet for Utena's hair, a deep red-brown for Anthy's skin, black for Akio's carriage. choice

The language

The narrative is in the mixed literary style of 1885, Edo storyteller's rhythms over a frame of Sino-Japanese, with a narrator who steps forward now and then to address the reader. The dialogue is in the spoken Tokyo Japanese of its speakers, which is how the small papers already wrote dialogue and how the serial gets most of its effects. documented for the convention. Each character's speech places them in 1885 society as exactly as their clothes:

  • Utena says 僕 (boku) for "I" and 君 (kimi) for "you", the pronouns of male students. In the anime she uses the same boku; in 1885, from a girl, it is a social act, and the first thing readers imitated. inference
  • Anthy speaks the soft, deferential language of a maid in a great house, calls Utena ウテナ様, and changes the form of address with each new owner, exactly as in the anime. To readers who had been in service, that was the most frightening thing in the book.
  • Nanami and the Kiryū household speak the new Yamanote dialect of rich Tokyo families, with its -asobase and its onii-sama; Saionji the clipped orders of a swordsman; Akio the easy, self-mocking courtesy of a man educated abroad.
  • The narrator calls himself, or herself, "the author" (作者) and never says which.

The readings beside the words

Small papers printed the reading of every character, and the serial uses the space beside the text to play. Its most famous glosses became part of the language:

少女 → をとめ
The title's "girl", read otome, the older word for a maiden (Part XVIII).
決闘者 → デユエリスト
"Duellist", glossed with the English word in katakana, as political novels glossed liberty. The duel itself was news: 決闘 in the sense of a formal, pre-arranged fight is first recorded in a debate of 1881, where it is glossed with the native word for a samurai's settled combat. documented
世界の果て
"End of the World", left unglossed throughout, so that readers could not be sure even how to say it. choice It is the serial's central mystery, and Part V lists the guesses.
牛鈴 → カウベル
"Cowbell", in chapter 16: a cow's bell, glossed as an English brand-name might be.
鳳学園 → おほとりがくゑん
"Ōtori Academy". Schools of 1885 were 学校, 女学校, 学舎 or 塾, and mission schools began to call themselves 学院 only in 1886; the compound 学園, "school-garden", has no dictionary example in our history before 1906. documented In this timeline the serial coins it, for a school that is mostly a garden, and it is the word every private school founded after 1890 wants in its name. choice
総代会 → そうだいくわい
"The Council". There were no student councils in Japanese schools before the Occupation, and the word 生徒会 is a post-war one. documented The serial uses 総代, the word for the pupil chosen to speak for a class at a ceremony, and makes a council of them. choice The nearest real thing was at the Meiji Girls' School, founded in the autumn of 1885, whose pupils came to sit on its governing council and to run their own dormitory. documented The chairman of the board is the 校主, the proprietor, as private schools then called their owners, and Akio is his 代理; "chairman of the board of directors" would not be Japanese for another twelve years. documented for the dates of the words.
王子 → わうじ
"Prince". Meiji Japanese had no settled word for the prince of a fairy tale: a crown prince was 皇太子, an emperor's grandson 皇孫, and 王子 was the son of a foreign king. When Tsubouchi Shōyō retold Cinderella for a school reader in 1900, her prince became a 若殿, a young lord. documented To a Tokyo reader Ōji was also a village north of the city, with a famous fox shrine and the paper mill whose freight hoist, installed in 1875, was Japan's first lift. documented The serial's prince is therefore foreign by definition, and a little bit of a fox.
男装 → だんさう
"Men's dress", of a woman, in chapter 1. The dictionary's earliest example of the word is from a novel of 1889. documented Here it is four years older, and it is the serial's word for Utena's whole manner, not only her clothes. choice
永遠 → えいゑん
"Eternity". A new word: the philosophers' dictionary of 1881 had fixed it as the translation of the English eternity. Ordinary people said 永久 or とこしへ. documented The castle that holds "eternity" therefore sounds, in 1885, like something out of a lecture on Western philosophy, which is exactly the effect. inference
魔女 → ウヰツチ
"Witch", in chapter 34. Read in the ordinary way, the characters meant manyo, a she-demon of Buddhist scripture; the European witch did not yet have a Japanese word. documented The serial glosses it with the English word, so that the Rose Bride is accused in a foreign language. choice
彼の女 → かのをんな
"She", in the heading of chapter 31, in the older spelling; the newer 彼女, read かのぢよ, glossed in a school reader as early as 1876, was just entering fiction.

The book editions

The paper reissued each part as soon as it finished, in three illustrated paper-covered volumes per part with colour-printed covers, in the format the old Edo picture-serials had used and that Meiji publishers still used for newspaper fiction. documented for the practice. Part Four appeared first as a typeset book in April 1887, published by Shun'yōdō, the house founded in 1878 that would later publish most of Ozaki Kōyō and Natsume Sōseki, and that had reissued a Liberal newspaper serial, Sakazaki Shiran's life of Sakamoto Ryōma, as a book in 1885 (documented for the firm; choice that it published this book), and all thirty-nine chapters were collected in four volumes in 1888. The textual history of those editions, which is more interesting than it sounds, is in Part XVIII.

IV

The thirty-nine chapters

Each episode of 1997 beside the chapter of 1885–87 that tells the same story, and how each chapter was received as it came out

Every episode of the television series has a chapter in the serial, in the same order, with the same events, the same people under the same names, and the same things left unexplained. The serial's author changed the furniture and nothing else.

Each entry below gives the chapter's heading as it stood in the newspaper or the 1887 book, in the serial's literary Japanese, with a reading and a translation, and the episode it matches with that episode's official English title. Under The chapter comes what the 1885 telling does with the episode; under As it came out, how it was received in the days and weeks it appeared. Two habits run through the chapters. Where the anime used a machine that 1885 did not have, the serial substitutes the nearest thing an 1885 Tokyo reader could picture and, if possible, one that carries the same charge: an adult's carriage for an adult's sports car, a magic lantern for a planetarium projector, a family register for a blood-type chart. And where the anime's Japanese title rests on a pun, the serial finds a Meiji pun to put in its place. choice All headings are my compositions, and so is everything the entries say about the serial's reception: the dates of each chapter's run, the letters, the prints, the columns, the censor's marks. Where an entry sets a chapter beside a real event of the same week, the event is real and labelled. choice The headings' spelling follows the mixed habits of the 1880s press, with historical kana in the readings.

The part titles (第一編 to 第四編) are the serial's own: the first three as the newspaper printed them, the fourth as the book did. The names in brackets are the ones readers gave them, and which stuck: the third part has been "the Carriage Book" since 1886, much as the anime's staff called their third arc the sports-car arc.

Part One 第一編 [the Council Book, 総代会の巻] · chapters 1–13 · Jiyū no Tomoshibi, April–August 1885

Eighty-four installments, one woodblock cut each, in a four-page paper sold for a sen a copy. choice The serial began as one entertainment among several, after the nihilists and beside the court news and the price of rice, and for its first fortnight the only people who wrote about it were its readers. Small papers printed readers' letters in a column of their own, often under pen names, and answered them in print. documented Such columns had been liveliest in 1876, when the Yomiuri, the Tokyo Eiri and the Kanayomi sometimes printed more than three hundred letters a month between them; by about 1880, as the historian of the small papers Tsuchiya Reiko puts it, the days when the letters column was a lively liberated zone were over. documented The serial is what filled this one again. choice The reception notes below draw on four sources of this timeline: that column; the Monday column in which a rival paper's critic, who signed himself Suimutei, reviewed other papers' serials; the memoir the serial editor published in 1909; and the letters and diaries of readers, a few of which were printed in the 1930s, when the first generation of readers began to die. choice

1
薔薇の花嫁Bara no hanayomeThe Rose Bride

Episode 1: The Rose Bride · 2–10 April 1885

The chapter

Opens on a boxed "Western tale" printed in a ruled frame like a page of an imported picture book: an orphaned princess, a travelling prince on a white horse, a ring, and the narrator's gesaku aside that resolving to become a prince herself may not have been wise. Ōtori Academy stands on a bluff above a harbour in Kanagawa; its woman teacher objects to Utena's boys' high-collared jacket and red knee breeches, and Utena answers that no rule forbids them. She beats the boys' baseball nine single-handed and explains the jacket: she means to be a prince who saves princesses. The birdcage conservatory is iron and glass, like the palm houses in imported prints; from a window Utena sees Saionji strike Anthy there. A love letter that Utena's friend Wakaba wrote to Saionji, and that he threw where others would find it, is pinned on the notice board; Utena challenges him in the kenjutsu hall; the gate in the forbidden wood opens when water falls on her ring; the stone stair climbs to the duelling garden under a castle hanging upside down, which Saionji calls a mirage (蜃気楼). Anthy, in a red gown, pins a green rose on him and a white one on Utena, and he knocks her down for wishing Utena luck. He draws the sword from Anthy's breast; Utena fights with a bamboo shinai cut short, remembers the prince's words, and wins with the stub. Tōga has watched it all through opera glasses. Anthy is waiting at the gate: she belongs to Utena now.

As it came out

Almost nobody noticed. The paper's readers were finishing the nihilists, who had one more day to run, and the first installment drew a single letter, from a reader in Honjo who took the boxed fairy tale for a translation and asked which Western picture book it came from; the paper did not answer. choice The first sign of anything more came from Yokohama, where the paper's agent, who sold it at the station and in the Japanese shops near the foreign settlement, ordered ten more copies for the second week and thirty more for the third (Part VI). choice The orders came from the Bluff, where pupils of the mission schools had noticed that an academy on a hill above a harbour, with Western buildings and a woman teacher who disapproved of everything, looked very like their own. inference Utena's answer to that teacher, that no rule forbids her jacket, was the first sentence of the serial to be repeated in a classroom, and the first to be punished there. choice

2
誰が為に薔薇は微笑むTa ga tame ni bara wa hohoemuFor Whom the Rose Smiles

Episode 2: For Whom the Rose Smiles · 11–19 April 1885

The chapter

The council rides a hydraulic lift up the tower. No reader had ridden one: Japan's first lift, a freight hoist installed at the paper mill at Ōji in 1875, carried goods, not passengers, and the nearest thing in print was Kume Kunitake's account of the Iwakura Mission, whose envoys were hauled up a mine shaft near Newcastle in an iron cage and felt "as if rising from the underworld to heaven". On the way up the council recites the creed of the chick and the egg, printed in the clipped Sino-Japanese of a proclamation. At the top it discusses the rose-sealed letters by which it is governed, signed 世界の果て, End of the World, to which nobody can reply. The empty east dormitory, which Anthy is already cleaning; Anthy's tea; Chu-Chu, "a small beast of the southern seas, neither mouse nor monkey". Saionji's exchange diary becomes an exchange notebook of letters, his proof that Anthy must obey him. When she refuses him he strikes her to the ground, and Utena accepts a rematch, meaning to lose. In the garden it is Utena, champion now, who draws the sword from Anthy; Saionji fights with his own, which since the edict of 1876 a civilian might keep but not wear in the street. Utena shields her rose by reflex, and a young man in white with a red-lined cape dives from the castle into her; her next stroke cuts through his steel and his rose. Tōga, at his opera glasses, wonders whether that was the Power of Dios.

As it came out

The creed made the second chapter. Printed in the clipped Sino-Japanese of a proclamation and attributed to nobody, it read like the handbills of the People's Rights men, and Kanda's boarding-house students, who already read political fiction aloud to one another, copied it into their notebooks and chanted it. choice Reading aloud in company was still the usual way to take in a popular novel in the 1880s, as the critic Maeda Ai argued in his essay "From Reading Aloud to Reading in Silence", collected in 1973 in The Formation of the Modern Reader. documented Among the students who read it aloud were the founders of the Ken'yūsha, the literary club that Ozaki Kōyō, Yamada Bimyō and two friends at the University Preparatory School had started that year, whose hand-copied magazine Garakuta bunko began in May. documented for the club and the magazine. In this timeline they read the serial aloud at their meetings, and nothing any of them published ever mentioned it. choice The cut of the dive, the young man in white plunging from the inverted castle, was reprinted as a single-sheet print within the month, the first of hundreds. choice And on the Monday after the chapter ended, the critic of a rival small paper in Kyōbashi, who signed his weekly column on other papers' serials 酔夢亭, Suimutei, "the Pavilion of Drunken Dreams", noticed it for the first time: "A gesaku in a schoolgirl's hand, with a sermon pinned to it. The best-drawn character is the lift." choice He wrote about it nearly every Monday while it ran in the paper and, except twice, never stopped saying he disliked it. choice

3
舞踏会の夜Butōkai no yoruThe Night of the Ball

Episode 3: On the Night of the Ball · 20–28 April 1885

The chapter

Utena wakes turning over her ring and breakfasts with Anthy alone in a hall of empty chairs. Tōga introduces himself, lifts a lock of her hair, has his hand knocked away, and shows Utena a ring like hers, worn, he says, so that he might meet her; she wonders whether he could be the prince. Three girls corner Anthy over Saionji's disgrace, and Nanami Kiryū, Tōga's sister, drives them off and sweetly invites Anthy to the ball as a candidate for its queen. It is held at a mansion the chapter does not name, in the manner of the Rokumeikan, which had opened some seventeen months earlier: bustled gowns, a naval band, dance cards. Tōga sends Utena a pink gown with a card bearing the chapter's heading in his hand, and Nanami sends one to Anthy. Anthy admits that crowds frighten her, because the faces all begin to look alike, and at the ball the cuts draw the guests as empty outlines. A "waiter" ruins Anthy's gown with champagne, and the three tormentors prove to be Nanami's own attendants. Utena comes down the stair in her own jacket, crosses the buffet, makes a gown of a tablecloth and dances with Anthy, and Chu-Chu cues the band. In the last cut the guests have faces, and Anthy looks up at Utena, startled into a smile.

As it came out

The first chapter to be read as satire of the Rokumeikan, the hall for Western balls that the foreign minister, Inoue Kaoru, had opened in November 1883 to show the treaty powers a Japan fit for equal treaties. documented for the Rokumeikan; choice for the reading. The serial never names the mansion, and readers named it at once. choice Inoue's partner in that policy, Itō Hirobumi, who had signed a convention with Li Hongzhang at Tianjin on 18 April, landed back in Japan on 28 April, the day the chapter ended. documented The cut that drew the guests as blank outlines was the joke of the season; the last cut, in which they have faces again, was the one readers kept. choice Nanami's three attendants drew their first letters, nearly all from girls who said they knew the type. choice On the Bluff, girls began to call a tablecloth worn as a skirt an "Utena gown" and to dance in pairs in the dormitory after prayers, which the teachers allowed until they learned where it came from. choice

4
光さす庭　序の曲Hikari sasu niwa: jo no kyokuThe Sunlit Garden: Prelude

Episode 4: The Sunlit Garden: Prelude · 29 April – 6 May 1885

The chapter

The chapter opens on a duel not yet fought: a cut of Miki saluting Utena in the duelling garden and saying he needs the Bride to win back "that music". Nanami fawns on Miki Kaoru, piano prodigy, and finds a carte-de-visite photograph of Anthy in his score; he plays one piece only, on an instrument most readers had never heard, hoping that "she" will hear it. When the three girls corner Anthy again Miki steps in, and each time she thanks him the text breaks for a bar of handwritten music before he blushes. He tutors Anthy, and swears to Utena that he will never duel for the Bride. Tōga asks whether he has found his "shining thing" (輝くもの), and the memory of two children at a garden piano is drawn with their faces left blank. Nanami's three "Operations" (snail, snake, octopus) are each undone by what Anthy keeps in her pencil box, drawer and cupboard; the snake meets a mongoose, a creature most readers knew only from Indian travel books. Anthy serves sweetened ice for dinner, crushed with a mallet in the manner of the ice-water shop Yokohama had had since 1869. Then she slips downstairs to the piano, and Miki hears in her playing the sound he lost as a child, his sister's. The last cut closes the remembered garden round Anthy.

As it came out

Few readers had ever heard a piano, and fewer could read the bars of music the chapter prints, in the Western notation that the government's Music Investigation Committee, set up in 1879, was teaching to the first trained music teachers; Uryū Shigeko, back from Vassar and often called Japan's first pianist, had been teaching there since 1882. inference for the readers; documented for the committee and Uryū. Two music teachers wrote in. One wrote out how the bars would sound and found them the opening of something unfinished; the other said they could not be played by one person. choice Nanami's three Operations drew the first letters about her, nearly all hostile, and a cut of the mongoose meeting the snake was pasted up in a Kanda lending library. choice A careful reader in Shiba noticed that in the remembered garden the two children's faces were left blank, and asked whether the illustrator had run out of time. It is the first record of anyone asking why the faces were missing. choice

5
光さす庭　終の曲Hikari sasu niwa: tsui no kyokuThe Sunlit Garden: Finale

Episode 5: The Sunlit Garden: Finale · 7–15 May 1885

The chapter

Miki at last beats Juri at fencing, and she tells him his blade is not made for battle. Anthy plays, and Miki tells the twins' story: they wrote the piece together, and on the day Miki had measles his sister went on stage alone and never played again. The cut draws every face in the memory as a blank. Measles was no metaphor to the 1885 reader; nearly every family had nursed a child through it, and many had buried one. When Utena says she cannot forgive a system that takes away Anthy's freedom, Miki moves to dissolve the council; Juri puts it down to love, Tōga to youth, and an apple on a chair, whole when the meeting begins, lies in six wedges at its end though nobody has touched it. Kozue leaves the music room straightening her dress; Tōga is inside, shirt open, and tells Miki that precious things are taken unless defended, and that only the Bride's betrothed can make her keep playing. Anthy agrees brightly that she would stop if Utena told her to. Miki hands Utena a white rose in class. He duels with his own fencing foil, evenly, until Anthy calls out for Utena; his face goes blank, his pale blue rose is cut, and the picture of the garden cracks. Afterwards Kozue tells a friend she never had any talent: her brother covered for her.

As it came out

Measles was the surprise. Miki's illness on the day of the recital was no metaphor to the families who read it, and most of the week's letters came from parents; a mother in Ushigome who had lost a daughter to it wrote that she had read the chapter twice. choice The first complaint about morals came the same week, from "a father in Hongō", who wished to know what Tōga had been doing in the music room with his shirt open, and was answered by another reader, who wrote that a father who did not know should not ask. choice Suimutei called the apple that falls into six wedges with nobody touching it "the only honest member of the council". choice On 13 May, while the chapter ran, the Yomiuri printed a reader's letter on reforming Japanese poetry, signed with a pen name, which also announced the treatise on the novel that its writer, the young Tsubouchi Shōyō, would start publishing in September. documented In this timeline nothing Shōyō published ever mentioned the serial (Part V). choice

6
七実様御用心Nanami-sama goyōjinTake Care, Miss Nanami

Episode 6: Take Care, Miss Nanami! · 16–22 May 1885

The chapter

The first comic chapter, in the old gesaku manner. Nanami, alone at night, runs as if followed; a figure stands under a gas lamp, and the chapter never explains it. A stray baseball of Utena's knocks her flat. Overhearing Tōga and Anthy plan a killing in the conservatory, she pictures them as lovers plotting her death; the victims are the ticks on the roses. Runaway horse, the boy Tsuwabuki and his embroidered handkerchief: her rescuer is a pupil of the elementary division, and she claims him on the spot as her sweetheart, then uses him as servant and bodyguard. Miki's diagnosis uses words 1885 had: she cannot see past her brother, and every other boy is tsuma, the garnish beside the sashimi, where the anime has parsley. Then Tsuwabuki confesses: as a small child he watched Tōga stop a runaway bull and carry Nanami off, and he staged the accidents so that he could save her as her brother once did. Nanami records his confession on a phonograph (the 蘇言機, "machine that brings words back to life", first demonstrated in Tokyo in 1878), and the chapter's climax is a boxing kangaroo escaped from a travelling circus, felled by Tōga in Western boxing drawers after Nanami has carried the boy to safety. Nanami dismisses her suitor, and he asks to be her little brother instead.

As it came out

The first comic chapter split the readers. Liberal subscribers who had been reading a political novel wrote that the author had lost his nerve, or had been got at; the women who read the paper, by the editor's later account, wrote to say they had laughed aloud. choice Suimutei was delighted: the serial had "found its true reader at last, which is a kangaroo". choice The print-sellers could not keep up with Tōga in Western boxing drawers, a cut the paper had thought daring, and learned what they would sell from the serial for the next ten years: Tōga, half dressed. choice Readers who had heard the phonograph at its public demonstrations in Tokyo in 1879, at the Chamber of Commerce in Tsukiji or at a restaurant in Asakusa, wrote to say that it could not have recorded a confession made across a garden, and the paper replied that it could at Ōtori Academy. documented for the demonstrations; choice for the rest. About the figure under the gas lamp, nobody wrote at all, which the editor thought the strangest thing about the week. choice

7
見果てぬ樹璃Mihatenu JuriJuri Unfulfilled

Episode 7: Unfulfilled Jury · 23–31 May 1885

The chapter

Juri Arisugawa, captain of the academy's French fencing, duels to prove that miracles do not happen. The chapter opens on a hand laid over the young Juri's eyes. In the present she beats every fencer who faces her and agrees with Utena that duelling for the Bride is foolish; when Anthy offers her an orange rose, she knocks her to the floor. Shiori and the stolen boy are told in tableaux; the string telephone is a children's toy of the day, its line running past Juri, and Shiori covers Juri's eyes while the boy kisses Shiori. By a pond at night Utena tells the prince story; Juri strokes her hair, then tries to wrench the ring from her finger and, in tears, demands proof of the miracle by the sword. The shadow girls play a girl who says she is glad a cold kept her from the class outing to the animal garden at Ueno, opened three years before, and who really wanted to go. In the duel Juri calls Utena "prince" only to sneer; the castle flares with no figure in it, and Juri disarms her anyway. The sword falls from the air and spears Juri's orange rose; Utena never touches it. The locket holds a carte-de-visite photograph cut from a class picture, and the chapter's last cut shows whose face it is; no line of the text says so.

As it came out

The chapter that made the serial notorious. Within days of the locket opening, while the serial was silent, the letters column, which usually printed three or four letters a week, printed eleven in a single issue, most of them from women, and the editor opened a second column of letters for the first time in the paper's history (Part VI). choice Some letters were outraged and more were grateful; one, signed "a woman of Kōjimachi, aged forty", said only that she had once had a friend like Shiori. choice Suimutei called the chapter indecent, and then gave the whole of his next column to it, which his readers noticed. choice Photographers in Yokohama found girls asking them to cut a friend's carte-de-visite down to fit a locket, and a Ginza clockmaker advertised lockets "that open, in the Western manner" the following month. choice The first letters about Juri herself came from girls who wanted to know whether she would be punished, and from more who hoped she would not. choice The silence lasted two weeks.

8
華麗なる天竺道中Karei naru Tenjiku dōchūThe Splendid Road to India

Episode 8: Curried High Trip · 15–24 June 1885

The chapter

The anime's pun on 華麗 (splendid) and curry survives, because one Meiji spelling of curry was カレイ: the heading's ruby gives both, and its 道中 is the road-journey word of Jippensha Ikku's comic travel novels. Nanami's girls say they have doctored Anthy's curry with the wrong tin of spice; the cooking-class curry explodes and swaps Utena's and Anthy's minds. The council meets in emergency, and the anime's telephone call reaches it through a speaking tube. The cuts tell the reader who is who by posture alone: "Anthy" slaps back at the bullies and hits the ball out of the grounds, while "Utena" waters roses. Nanami confesses, pleading dry-eyed on her brother's chest, and is packed off to India by mail steamer for the spice; every glimpse of India ends in elephants. The shadow girls lecture on four-character sayings, ending on an outlaw hit by her own bullet: 因果応報, deeds repaid in kind. Saionji drags "Anthy" to the gymnastics store and hands over their exchange notebook, and Utena, reading his insults about herself, writes a one-phrase reply in red, the colour of a teacher's corrections. Nanami comes back sunburnt with the spice. Chu-Chu's banana skin sends her sprawling and the spice is lost; the first tin turns up unopened, and the explosion was simply Anthy's cooking. A second curry puts the girls back and swaps Saionji with Chu-Chu.

As it came out

The fortnight's silence filled the town with rumours, and Suimutei collected them in one column: the author was ill, was in prison, was dead, was a woman whose husband had found the manuscript, was three people. choice (The scholars of this timeline now think the last came nearest the truth: Part XVII.) Readers who had waited two weeks to learn what Juri would do next were given curry. The letters were furious and delighted in equal parts, and the delighted won: within the month Western restaurants in Tsukiji and Ueno served a rice curry under the chapter's heading. choice Curry had been on Tokyo's Western menus since the 1870s, and Seiyō ryōri shinan, one of the two cookery books of 1872 that first explained it to the Japanese, listed a red frog among the meats to put in it. documented On 19 June, in the middle of the chapter, the paper printed a letter signed "a schoolgirl of Yokohama", pointing out that the byline could be read as a girl's name (Part XIX, document 2). choice Fukuzawa Yukichi's editorials on Japanese women had appeared in his own paper in the fortnight of the pause (Part VI). documented

9
永遠ありといふ城Eien ari to iu shiroThe Castle Said to Hold Eternity

Episode 9: The Castle Said to Hold Eternity · 25 June – 5 July 1885

The chapter

Beaten again by Tōga at kenjutsu, Saionji tells Utena he wants the Bride only so as not to lose to him: with her he will possess eternity. His memory: the two boys share a hired tricycle in the rain, the toy every Tokyo boy wanted in the early 1880s, and enter a church with three coffins laid flat in the Western way, which to a reader used to seated barrel coffins was itself uncanny. In the one Tōga opens, a girl whose face the cut never shows lies among roses and wants to be left there: her parents are in the other two, she says, and nothing is eternal. Next day she walks in the funeral, and Saionji supposes Tōga showed her something eternal. A rose-sealed letter tells Saionji the castle will fall tonight, and an unseen voice tells Utena that Anthy has been taken. The serial uses the anime's own word, kamikakushi, spirited away, which in 1885 still described something that happened to children. Saionji drags Anthy to the gate while she protests that the rules forbid it; Utena finds him senseless there and Anthy in a coffin inside a giant rose on the duelling garden, and the chapter shows nobody felling him or laying her in it. The castle falls, Utena pulls Anthy out, and everything stands again. Saionji cuts at her with a live blade, and Tōga takes the cut meant for Utena's back, asking her whether her prince was not a man like him. In bed that night, not alone, Tōga writes to someone the chapter never names: he sent Saionji's letter himself, in that person's name, and Saionji will be expelled. Whoever believes in friendship, he adds, is a fool.

As it came out

Coffins sold papers. The three Western coffins laid flat in a church were what readers talked about, and the word kamikakushi, which mothers still used of children who vanished, made the chapter frightening in a way the fencing had never been. inference Two questions filled the letters column for the rest of the summer: who was the girl in the coffin, and to whom does Tōga write in bed? Every candidate was proposed, Anthy, Nanami, Juri and Utena herself among them, and the paper answered nobody. choice Readers waited until 1887 to hear whom Saionji would name, and have argued ever since about whether to believe him. choice Among the Kanda students the chapter made two parties, Tōga's and Saionji's, who lodged in the same boarding houses and fell out over the cut in which Tōga takes the blow meant for Utena: generous, said one party; staged, said the other. choice Suimutei sided with Saionji, "the only character in the book who is exactly as stupid as he looks". choice On the night of 2 July, in the middle of the chapter, the Sumida rose in Tokyo's worst flood since 1846 and carried away the Senju bridge, which had stood since the Edo period, and the Azuma bridge below it. documented The cut of the falling castle was pinned up in a Honjo bathhouse beside the flood notices. choice

10
七実の大切なるものNanami no taisetsu naru monoNanami's Precious Thing

Episode 10: Nanami's Precious Thing · 6–15 July 1885

The chapter

Saionji is expelled. He leaves his exchange notebook with Tōga, whose arm is in a sling and who calls them best friends; the next cut shows it burning. Anthy brings the moping Utena a kitten, and Nanami dreams of the birthday when she gave her brother a kitten and was kissed for it. Tōga's birthday party follows, a Western custom then practised only by the most Westernized families, since everyone else grew a year older at New Year; the sling is gone. Nanami knocks Utena's flowers away and slaps Anthy, whose present is the kitten, and remembers that her brother preferred the first kitten to her. A rose lands at Utena's feet, and only then does Tōga slide a ring onto his sister's finger, speaking as if she had worn one all along. Utena knocks Nanami's curved sabre into the air and cuts her pale-yellow rose; Nanami fights on with a dagger, cuts Utena's rose in turn, and stops only at her brother's shout, as her sabre snaps against the wall beside Utena's head. Then the memory she has kept from herself: a box sealed with pasted paper at the edge of a sluice, then in the current, with no kitten shown inside. Tōga holds her, thinking about the Power of Dios.

As it came out

The box at the sluice is the cut readers of 1885 remembered longest. Readers who had heard Kishida Toshiko speak in 1883 on "daughters in boxes" made the connection at once, and one of them wrote to say so, signing himself a former Liberal of Ōtsu, the town where she had been arrested for the speech. documented for the speech and arrest; choice for the letter. The paper's older subscribers had read her in its own columns: in May and June 1884, in its first weeks, it had printed her essay to her "sisters" (同胞姉妹に告ぐ) in ten installments, a plea for the equality of men and women (Part XVII). documented The serial does not say what was in the box, and the letters column filled with readers who were sure. choice Nanami became loved in this chapter. Until it she had been the villain of the comic chapters; after it most of the letters about her came from girls with elder brothers, and the first print of her alone, in the gown she wore to her brother's birthday party, with his ring, sold out in Ginza. choice The Western birthday party puzzled readers who counted their ages from New Year, and the paper printed a short note on the custom. choice

11
優雅にして冷酷　其の花を摘む者Yūga ni shite reikoku: sono hana wo tsumu monoGraceful and Cruel: The One Who Plucks That Flower

Episode 11: Gracefully Cruel: The One Who Picks That Flower · 16–27 July 1885

The chapter

A picnic, with Chu-Chu in Anthy's three-tiered lacquer box. Tōga watches through opera glasses and sees a lonely princess; Utena sees him against the light, like the figure in her memory. In the birdcage conservatory, which Tōga calls Anthy's domain, Utena has Anthy say she hates being the Rose Bride, and Anthy says it in the words Utena hands her. Tōga claims to be Utena's prince, takes her ringed hand and leans in to kiss her, his hair hiding whether he does, then challenges her in the same voice. Utena resolves to keep Anthy even from her prince. Tōga fights with his own sword and leads the bout. The figure from the castle, drawn whole for the second and last time in Part One, dives into Utena; then Tōga lowers his sword and stands open, she sees him again asking whether her prince was not a man like him, and she falters. Her white rose scatters and the Sword of Dios melts in her hand. Anthy, smiling, says she is happy as the Rose Bride, and Tōga explains that she only ever followed the victor's wishes. Told by Tōga to say goodbye, Anthy calls Utena "Miss Tenjō", 天上さん where it had been ウテナ様: a surname and a plain san, for someone outside the house. Then she leaves on his arm. Utena kneels, repeating that it is not true.

As it came out

Tōga won, and Anthy went with him. The serial's readers had now watched a woman pass from one owner to a third, and the letters column filled. choice Most of the letters said one thing in different words, "give her back", and the editor, who could not print forty letters saying the same, printed the angriest of them with a note that the author had been told. choice Anthy's change of address, from ウテナ様 to 天上さん, was the sentence most often quoted, and girls on the Bluff began to call one another "Miss Tenjō" when they meant that a friendship was over. choice The mission schools broke up for the summer that week, and the serial went home with their pupils into households that had never taken the paper; the Yokohama agent's July orders, swollen by girls buying up the back numbers to take home with them, were the largest of the year. choice On 20 July, in the middle of the chapter, the first number of Jogaku zasshi, the "Magazine of Women's Learning", appeared in Tokyo. documented It never named the serial (Part VI). choice

12
或は友情の為にAruiwa yūjō no tame niPerhaps for Friendship

Episode 12: For Friendship, Perhaps · 28 July – 9 August 1885

The chapter

Utena stays in bed; Wakaba, visiting, finds her jacket slashed, and Utena says she caught it on something. Next day she comes to school in the girls' uniform, which in 1885 means a Western day-dress of the kind the girls' normal schools were about to adopt, and calls it ordinary. At Ōtori Academy it is; in Tokyo such a dress was still mostly seen at the Rokumeikan. Anthy, Tōga's bride now, greets her as Miss Tenjō, and in the council room stands at his shoulder. At lunch Tōga propositions her. Wakaba, up on the table, throws a glass of water that lands on Anthy; when Wakaba blames Anthy, Utena slaps Wakaba and hands Anthy a handkerchief, which Anthy, left at Tōga's table, sits looking at. Then Wakaba, in tears, shames Utena into taking herself back. Utena challenges Tōga, and Juri lends her a foil for "the last scene". Tōga draws the Sword of Dios from Anthy and orders his Bride to give up her body and guard the sword; she kisses the blade, and it becomes a shaft of light that breaks Juri's foil and shreds the dress. Utena fights on with the stub. Anthy, watching with something like pity, thinks that she has seen this before; the light drains from Tōga's sword, a tear stands in her eye, and Utena cuts his rose with the broken blade, still in her red stockings. At night Anthy waits with her bag and begins the speech of chapter 1. Utena cuts her short: "Let's just go home."

As it came out

Utena in a dress drew the largest postbag of the summer, and for once the letters agreed: the jacket must come back. Girls who had begun to wear a boy's jacket over their kimono wrote that they felt betrayed; their mothers wrote that the chapter was the first sensible thing in the serial. choice Wakaba, slapped, found her first defenders, and the red stockings went into the prints. choice The chapter's last line, "Let's just go home", became schoolgirls' slang for ending a quarrel, and has stayed so; in 2026 a girl who says it to a friend is quoting chapter 12, whether or not she knows it. choice Suimutei, who had promised his readers after Tōga's victory that he would stop reading, reported that he had not. choice

13
描かるる軌跡Egakaruru kisekiA Locus Traced

Episode 13: Tracing a Path · 12–21 August 1885

The chapter

The serial's first "story so far", a chapter that re-tells Part One so that new subscribers could start. It opens on the boxed Western tale, and the shadow girls report that the meddlesome hero has won again and may be called back to battle. A phonograph cylinder repeats the creed in an empty room, and a girl drawn like Nanami looks in. A tall man whose face is never drawn stands at the gate of the duelling garden; then, in darkness, he speaks to a prince in white who sits hunched and still on a sphere, and asks whether he has still not woken. Each duel is announced by a sand-glass and a stained-glass plaque bearing a French word (アミチエ, amitié, with a kanji gloss), the language of Meiji law and the army, and told again beside cuts reprinted from the earlier chapters' blocks: friendship, choice, reason, love, adoration; conviction gets only its plaque, and self a single line. The seal on the Power of Dios has begun to break, the man says; she may reach the duel named revolution, and both of them will profit. He drops a pink rose among dark ones. In the dormitory Anthy comes in late and does not answer when Utena asks where she has been. Last images, without a word: a glowing jar, a pinned butterfly, a black rose, a black ring, a crowd of boys.

As it came out

The first "story so far" did what it was written for: readers who had heard about the serial all summer could start it, and the paper ran it under a notice inviting them to. choice Old readers wrote to ask about the tall man at the gate whose face the cuts never draw, and about the hunched prince on the sphere he speaks to; they guessed that the tall man was the prince grown old, or the chairman of the academy, whom the serial had not yet shown, and one reader guessed the author. choice On 21 August the paper announced a second part for the autumn and the first three volumes of the book. choice Its daily sale was by then half as large again as in March (Part XII). choice

Part Two 第二編 [the Black Rose Book, 黒薔薇の巻] · chapters 14–24 · Jiyū no Tomoshibi, renamed Tomoshibi Shinbun on 14 January 1886 · October 1885–February 1886

Between the parts the serial belonged to everyone. Other small papers, which could not print the real thing, printed continuations of their own, unsigned, in which the hunched prince of chapter 13 woke, came down from his sphere and claimed Utena in a single installment; one ran for three weeks before its readers stopped buying it. choice Racing one another to cash in on a story everyone was reading was an old habit of the trade: when Takahashi Oden, whom the papers called a "poison woman", was beheaded on 31 January 1879 for killing a man with a razor, four papers ran her story at once, and one of two rival books boasted in its seventh part that it had been finished "in barely sixty days" because "a rival edition was coming out". documented The paper's three illustrated volumes of Part One appeared in September. choice It was also the season of the bundled-hair craze: a society founded in July to replace the Japanese coiffure with Western styles had over two thousand members by November, and a count on Nihonbashi on 15 September found about one woman in five with her hair done the new way. documented The girls who had begun to wear a boy's jacket that summer were, the shopkeepers' letters complained, the same girls. choice On 1 September a writer in the paper conceded what every editor knew, that small-paper readers outnumbered big-paper readers, so that "today's society may fairly be called the society of the small papers". documented The same month Tsubouchi Shōyō began to publish The Essence of the Novel in parts (Part V). documented When the serial came back on 13 October, some of its readers had met Part One only in the book. choice

14
黒薔薇の少年等Kurobara no shōnen-raThe Boys of the Black Rose

Episode 14: The Boys of the Black Rose · 13–21 October 1885

The chapter

Under Nemuro Memorial Hall two boys tend a black rose growing from a glowing jar: Mikage, and Mamiya, whom the cut draws dark like Anthy. Anthy visits her brother every Saturday night, and Utena goes with her up the tower. Its round room holds an orrery and a magic lantern that throws the stars on the dome. Akio Ōtori appears, kissing Kanae on a stepladder: acting chairman, betrothed to the chairman's daughter. Over tea he remarks that students here never fight, surely. To an 1885 reader the different surnames of Anthy Himemiya and her brother explain themselves, though the chapter, like the episode, never says why: he must have been taken into the Ōtori house as adopted heir and son-in-law to be, a common arrangement in Meiji families. Among rows of empty shoes under the hall, Mikage and Mamiya plan to take the Bride and kill her. Mikage interviews the troubled in a descending lift whose framed specimen regresses from butterfly to leaf, and Kanae goes down in it from her love for Akio to his sister, whom she cannot like. White lilies stand on the desks in the duelling garden: the Easter lily, which Yokohama nurseries were beginning to ship to America. Utena cuts Kanae's black rose with one low lunge, and Kanae remembers nothing. On a rainy night Anthy goes up alone and lays her spectacles on the table; asked whether she missed her brother, she says yes, and the lantern lights.

As it came out

Akio's surname puzzled nobody: readers decided within days that the siblings' different surnames meant an adopted heir, and the paper received no letters asking why, which in 1885 was itself the answer (Part V). choice Kanae, kissed on a stepladder, drew the first letters from engaged girls. choice The chapter ran in the weeks the Meiji Girls' School opened at Kudanshita (on 30 September or 15 October; the accounts differ), a Christian school founded without mission money by the pastor Kimura Kumaji and his wife Tōko, with the young Iwamoto Yoshiharu among its backers. documented Its pupils came to sit on its governing council and to run their own dormitory. documented It was the nearest thing in Japan to the serial's council (Part III). inference Readers saw the academy in it at once, and in the Peeresses' School too, set up that autumn by the empress's order, which had begun its classes on 5 October and which she would open formally on 13 November. documented for the schools; choice for the readers. The black rose was the chapter's other sensation: the Yokohama nurseries had none to sell and said so in their advertisements, the first sign of the rose fever of 1886 (Part XII). choice

15
其の梢の指す景色Sono kozue no sasu keshikiThe Landscape the Treetop Points To

Episode 15: The Landscape Framed by Kozue · 22 October – 1 November 1885

The chapter

Kozue, who drives off everyone near her twin. A music teacher who lays a ringed hand on Miki's shoulder falls down a staircase; Kozue tells Juri she cannot forgive anyone who would hurt Miki. The milkshakes become sweetened iced drinks, sold in Yokohama since its first ice-water shop opened in 1869, which Kozue refuses from Miki's hand. Nanami presides over the council in Tōga's place, and the creed is heard once with "cage" in place of "shell". Utena, an only child, asks Akio what a brother is to a sister, and he gives her a magic-lantern slide of the moon: a brother is something useless you look up at now and then, and it makes you feel better. Yoshitoshi, in the first year of his One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, gives the slide a cut of its own. Kozue bends tenderly over her brother asleep at the piano and sees Anthy at the door. After her interview she nearly kisses him and shows him a black ring like his, and in silhouette, among black butterflies, a hilt rises from his chest: the first sword drawn from a council member. A glass of the iced drink stands on every desk in the duelling garden; Anthy drinks from one of the glasses, and Utena wins with the low lunge. Kozue remembers nothing and asks Miki to make her the drink again. That night Anthy takes off her spectacles for her brother, who says he will comfort her, as always.

As it came out

Readers noticed "cage" at once. The creed they had been chanting since April had a shell in it, and chapter 15's has a cage, and for a month the letters column argued over whether a compositor had picked up the wrong block or the author had meant it. choice The paper said nothing, which settled it for most readers: a misprint is corrected. choice The 1888 book printed "shell" (Part XVIII), and whether that was a correction or a retreat has been argued ever since. choice Kozue had no defenders at all. Akio's line about brothers, something useless one looks up at, became a saying among sisters, and the cut of his moon slide, drawn in the year Tsukioka Yoshitoshi began his One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, was cut out and kept. documented for the moon series; choice for the rest.

16
幸福の牛鈴Kōfuku no kauberuThe Cowbell of Happiness

Episode 16: The Cowbell of Happiness · 2–10 November 1885

The chapter

The shopping channel becomes a newspaper advertisement for a foreign jeweller, which only Anthy is shown reading. Upstaged at her own party by Juri's necklace, Nanami opens the unsigned casket that comes for her and buckles on a collar with a bell the size of a fist. The bell bears an English maker's mark, "Bullock & Co., Jewellers", which she cannot read; Miki's one word for it, 牛鈴, the paper glosses カウベル, as if it were the maker's name. Whenever anyone starts to say what such a bell is for, the sentence breaks off and the cut shows a farm. She wears the bell with every outfit and turns, by degrees, into a cow, an animal Tokyo had only lately learned to eat: in her dream a faceless Tōga forks her hay, sees her off in a cage cart and sits down to a beefsteak. By moonlight she is found nibbling leaves in the park, which by the next cut has become an alpine pasture. Utena tells her what a bullock is. Nanami grows horns and charges the red shawl Anthy has been knitting; Utena plays matador with it, then cuts the collar with the pitchfork Tsuwabuki throws her, in a flash borrowed from the duels. The bell ends on Anthy's own cow, also called Nanami: the carrier confused the two, Utena decides, and no sender is ever shown. Next morning Nanami asks whether it suits her, and the cut stops at her chin.

As it came out

Cowbells sold. Within a week ironmongers near the Bluff were selling small brass bells on red cord as charms, and girls tied them to their satchels; the boys of Kanda tied larger ones to each other. choice The English maker's mark sent at least one party of readers into the foreign settlement to look for Bullock & Co., Jewellers, who did not exist, and a Yokohama watchmaker put a card in his window saying that he was not Bullock & Co. either. choice Every reader noticed the sentences that break off whenever someone begins to say what such a bell is for, and the letters column became a contest in finishing them, which the editor stopped after a week. choice Suimutei thought it the best of the comic chapters: "Nanami is a cow for six days and a girl for a week afterwards, and the second is funnier." choice Nobody found out who sent the casket, and nobody has. choice

17
死の棘Shi no togeThe Thorns of Death

Episode 17: The Thorns of Death · 11–20 November 1885

The chapter

Shiori Takatsuki comes back, watches Juri fence from the gallery, and tells Utena, all self-reproach, that Juri always protected her. Under Nemuro Memorial Hall the rose in the glowing jar is orange this time, and Mikage and Mamiya mean to take its thorns through the rose's natural enemy, an insect. On a terrace Shiori apologises to Juri's back for the boy she took and has since dropped; Juri says she never cared for him, and Shiori asks whose picture the locket holds. A small bird lies on the paving. Akio warns Utena that she is as innocent as Ganymede, and that such innocence wounds. Juri makes to throw the locket into a pond; Shiori finds it in her own room, in the water of an overturned vase of orange roses, and nobody is shown carrying it there. She learns whose face it holds, and in the lift, the locket open in her hands, her confession turns from envy to triumph before she breaks down. Ringed, she dangles it before Juri in the fencing hall and draws Juri's sword from Juri's breast. On every desk a small grey bird stands on a perch; Shiori fences in Juri's style until the low lunge, and the birds fly. Juri wakes alone beside the locket, and next day Shiori is gossiping gaily about why she dropped her young man.

As it came out

Christian readers caught in the heading an echo of the "sting of death" of First Corinthians, which the Meiji translators had put into Japanese in 1878 as 死の刺, read しのはり. documented for the translation; choice for the readers. The missionary teachers on the Bluff, who had disapproved of the serial in a general way, now disapproved of it in particular: one wrote home that it "quotes Scripture to the girls in a love story between girls", which was accurate. choice Shiori became the most disliked character in the serial within a week, and stayed so until 1887; many of the letters about her came from readers who said they knew someone exactly like her. choice The locket that reaches Shiori's room without anyone being shown carrying it started a new argument. Readers who had decided in May that the serial was about love between girls now argued about whether it was for such love or against it, and the answer depended, as Suimutei said, on which chapter one had read last. choice

18
美蔓もどかしMitsuru modokashiMitsuru Impatient

Episode 18: Mitsuru's Impatience · 21 November – 1 December 1885

The chapter

The heading keeps the anime's pun, mitsuru being both the boy's name and, written 満つる, the literary verb for coming to the full: Tsuwabuki wants to be grown up at once. Mari, a year older, scolds him, eats his chocolate, a confectioner's novelty in Tokyo, and hands back the bitten bar, which he stops short of biting. Nanami leaves the lunch he made her to go off with Mikage. He asks what being grown up means; Utena says experience of certain things, and Anthy, smiling, that they are grown up in all sorts of ways. He studies kissing, for which the translated fiction of the next year or two would make 接吻 the standard word, in a translated English novel of the kind that had been a runaway success in 1878–79, instead of the anime's films, tries it on Mari, and is slapped. In the lift he wants to kick the whole world over; then he lays a ringed hand over Nanami's, and two hilts rise from her silhouette, sabre and dagger. On every desk a clay tomb figure, a haniwa, grips a bitten bar; in the Nihon shoki such figures stand in for the retainers once buried alive at a royal tomb. He attacks before Utena is armed and his blade takes a lock of her long hair, and in 1885 even that was a shock: a woman's cropped hair had been forbidden in Tokyo from May 1872, and a fineable offence from that December until the Penal Code of 1880 took effect in 1882, and in 1885 it still made people turn in the street. She locks both blades and comes down on him from above. Next morning he runs off with Mari, and Nanami is the one left flustered.

As it came out

The chapter printed the kiss with 接吻, a word readers had met only in translated novels, and the boys of Kanda used it for a month to mean anything at all. choice A handful of girls in Tokyo and Yokohama cut their hair short after the cut in which Tsuwabuki's sword takes a lock of Utena's hair, and the papers that disliked the Liberals made the most of them. choice Cropped hair was still a public matter for a woman: Tokyo had forbidden it in 1872. documented Before that cut appeared, on 23 November, two days into the chapter, the police had begun arresting the Osaka plotters, and among those taken, it emerged, was a former schoolmistress of twenty, Kageyama Hideko, who had worn boys' clothes and cropped hair until she was sixteen. documented The rival papers called her "the Utena of Osaka" (Part VI), and for the rest of the chapter's run the letters were about her, not about Tsuwabuki. choice

19
