今は亡き王国の歌Ima wa naki ōkoku no utaSong of a Kingdom Now Lost

Episode 19: A Song for a Kingdom Now Lost · 2–7 and 18–22 December 1885

The chapter

Opens on Wakaba's daydream: a curtain rises on a moonlit castle, and she is a princess in the arms of a prince whose face is not drawn. Tatsuya Kazami hands Utena a love letter, and Wakaba recognises her "Onion Prince" from elementary school. In her childhood memory Wakaba is taunted as "Onionhead", a joke about her hairstyle that turned on a Western vegetable newly grown in Hokkaido; a boy takes her hand, and it is she who announces that the Onion Prince will protect her. Akio tells Utena that the princes other people keep in their hearts are seldom understood. Utena plays matchmaker in a teahouse, where the anime has a café, and takes Wakaba's advice to "muddy the tea", the old idiom for fudging a thing, by slurping hers. Tatsuya admits his letter was only a way to be near Wakaba, and Utena tells him to say so. Where the card announcing each Black Rose duel usually hangs, there is this time a rude note from Wakaba. At sunset Tatsuya believes they are confessing to each other; Wakaba asks him to keep her secret, wishes him happiness with someone too, and runs off to her prince. Tatsuya is turned away from the Mikage lift for being a good person: he breaks down, the specimen stays a butterfly, and Mikage tells him that his path does not lie there. Wakaba opens her door and says she is home. Saionji is in Wakaba's room, at the window, and welcomes her.

As it came out

The chapter was cut in two. On 8 December the Home Ministry suspended the paper for ten days over its reporting of the Osaka arrests (Part VI), and Utena was left in the teahouse for ten days with her tea unmuddied. choice Readers spent the suspension guessing whether Wakaba would win her Onion Prince, and were disappointed when, after the paper came back on 18 December, she turned him down. choice The chapter ended on 22 December, the day the cabinet replaced the old council of state and Itō Hirobumi became Japan's first prime minister. documented Nobody connected him with the serial until the next spring. choice Saionji at Wakaba's window, in the same issue, was the paper's best-selling last line of the year. choice

20
若葉繁れるWakaba shigereruWakaba Flourishing

Episode 20: Wakaba Flourishing · 23 December 1885 – 12 January 1886

The chapter

The heading, archaic in 1997, is plain literary Japanese in 1885, and its pun on wakaba, young leaves, works unchanged. Wakaba's walk home is the same chain of cuts each time, ending at her door with "Welcome home" and "I'm back"; only the vehicle passing in the street changes. The expelled Saionji is hiding in her room. With a secret to keep she shines at everything, and Akio tells Utena that most people are one among many and may shine for a while, though not for long. Saionji carves Wakaba a leaf-shaped hairpin, a kanzashi rather than a clip, and sets it, unfinished, in her hair at the mirror; she cries. Then Mikage is simply there in her darkened room, offering Saionji reinstatement for one small thing, and soon afterwards Wakaba passes Anthy in the street and sees the leaf, gilded, in Anthy's hair. In the lift she never names Anthy, only "that girl" who looks so special: "I'm a face in the crowd." Saionji packs, promising to send her something expensive; she has something better, a black ring, and a sword is hauled out of a spiky silhouette whose face is not drawn. A leaf hairpin lies on every desk. Utena will not draw on a friend, though Anthy urges her four times. When Wakaba goes for Anthy, Utena stands in the way and is hauled up by the hair, blade at her throat, while Wakaba cries that special people trample the rest. Utena steps inside the swing, holds her, takes Wakaba's own sword from her, and cuts the rose. Saionji struts back into school, and Wakaba says "I'm back" to an empty room.

As it came out

The chapter ran over New Year, when the paper took its holiday, and Wakaba's "I'm a face in the crowd" reached households with time to read. choice It brought the largest bag of letters the paper had ever had, and for once they did not come from the Bluff. They came from girls in the shitamachi, shop-girls and apprentices' sisters and pupils of ordinary elementary schools, many of them written in kana alone, saying that Wakaba was the first girl in the serial who was like them. choice The schoolgirl of Yokohama wrote again, to say that the girls of the Bluff had read the chapter as being about themselves, and had not liked it. choice Suimutei printed the first of his two serious columns of the run, in which he admitted that he had been reading the serial for nine months in order to laugh at it, and had cried. choice

21
悪しき虫Ashiki mushiVermin

Episode 21: Vermin · 13–25 January 1886

The chapter

In the heading's idiom an "evil insect" is an unwanted admirer who fastens on a daughter; Nanami turns it round to guard a brother. Keiko and two other girls asked Nanami into their circle on entrance day before learning whose sister she was, and have told it ever since as having been chosen. Tōga sits motionless at home, seen from behind. Nanami gives a party to cheer him and sends Keiko off on an errand, and Keiko ends up outside the window, looking at his back. Under the lantern's stars Utena repeats what Akio has taught her of the Pleiades, which every reader knew as Subaru, the first of the stars in The Pillow Book's list; when she has gone he tells Anthy to stay good friends with her, like Castor and Pollux, whose names few readers knew. In the rain Keiko lends Tōga her umbrella, a Western "bat umbrella" and a status object in its own right, and he takes the handle without a word. Nanami sees, casts Keiko out of every society and committee, and promises to exterminate such parasites; the other two pretend not to hear Keiko's plea. In the lift Keiko admits she served Nanami only to be near Tōga, and in his room she lays a ringed hand on his bare chest and a sword rises from it. An open umbrella stands on every desk, and Keiko names Nanami the real vermin before the low lunge. Next morning the four are together as before, and Anthy tells the baffled Utena that for someone you love you can deceive yourself as long as you need.

As it came out

On 14 January the paper changed its name to Tomoshibi Shinbun. documented The first installment of the chapter had run in the last issue of Jiyū no Tomoshibi and the second ran in the first of Tomoshibi Shinbun, and readers said that the paper had changed its name and the serial had not noticed (Part VI). choice The umbrella was the chapter's object: Western "bat umbrellas" were a status article of the decade, and an umbrella shop in Ginza advertised one "for lending in the rain". choice Keiko drew sympathy and Nanami drew none. choice Akio's Pleiades and his twins sent students to the few star charts in Tokyo's bookshops, and a Kanda bookseller with a Western celestial atlas charged them a sen a look. choice On 24 January Prince Arisugawa Takahito, the emperor's old calligraphy teacher and father of the head of the princely house whose name Juri bears, died. documented By the editor's later account, the Home Ministry's readers began from that week to underline her surname, which the 1888 book would change (Part XVIII). choice

22
根室紀念館Nemuro kinenkanNemuro Memorial Hall

Episode 22: Nemuro Memorial Hall · 26 January – 7 February 1886

The chapter

The serial's longest chapter, nine installments with no duel. Mikage meets Utena on the steps of Nemuro Memorial Hall, invites her to his seminar, and tells the legend of the fire as someone else's. A dark hand in a red sleeve lays a sealed letter on his desk. Then the past: Professor Nemuro, a prodigy no older than the hundred boys he leads toward "eternity", who wear rose rings and call him a living abacus behind his back, where the anime says a computer; Tokiko, the woman inspector sent by the board, who brews tea by an hourglass and preserves roses in sugar because she cannot bear to watch them die; her dying brother Mamiya, who believes nothing is eternal. A visitor drawn only as hands and a smiling mouth offers Nemuro the Rose Crest as a contract and leaves the ring in a cup marked with Tokiko's rouge; through a door Nemuro sees her kissed by a man never drawn whole. Then the fire. Tokiko accuses the boy at the railings and a voice says yes. Nemuro, outside, says that ancient creatures died to make the coal and oil of the present age and that such sacrifices are always required, an argument the age of steam and lamp oil could follow exactly. Nobody is shown lighting the fire. In the present Tokiko, grown older, comes back and is the listener when the shadow girl plays a clockwork doll, the anime's robot, that never ages or tires; then she visits an Akio who has not aged and says she has come to see her brother's grave. Mikage overhears Utena scold Anthy in Tokiko's own words.

As it came out

The longest chapter began on 26 January, the day the government abolished Nemuro Prefecture, with Hakodate and Sapporo, and put all of Hokkaido under a single administration. documented Readers noticed; the paper did not mention it. choice The serial says only "long ago", and readers placed it where 1885 kept its own dead boys: the Aizu youths of 1868 and the Kagoshima academy students of 1877. inference Letters came from Aizu and from Kagoshima, each claiming the hundred boys (Part VI). choice Nemuro's argument that sacrifices are always required was read by the Liberals as the government's and by the government's papers as the Liberals'. choice Readers' theories about who lit the fire, most of which blamed the professor, lasted until chapter 23 asked the question again and did not answer it. choice Within weeks the storytellers of the yose were telling ghost stories about the hall, and it became the chapter most often retold as a kaidan (Part XIV). choice Suimutei's column on it ended: "I withdraw everything. Except about the lift." (Part XIX, document 5) choice

23
決闘者の資格Duelist no shikakuThe Terms of a Duelist

Episode 23: The Terms of a Duelist · 8–17 February 1886

The chapter

The heading glosses 決闘者 with the English loanword デユエリスト, a trick the political novels used for liberty and revolution, and the council uses the word: Nanami wants Utena as an ally, and Miki and Juri reply that what they are is Duellists. Mikage courts Utena in the conservatory and sees Tokiko in her place. At the hall he shows her a corridor of photographs: the hundred boys, each black-rose duellist with a sword, and, when he asks about her memories, a small girl with no face. When he begins his formula she pins him to the wall, and pinned he goes on lecturing that they are alike, people who want never to change. Utena challenges him, to prove she is nothing like him, and he takes the last black rose himself. On every desk stands a photograph of Tokiko with Mamiya. Mikage foresees Utena's leap and Anthy catches her; the boy in the photograph becomes someone else, dark-haired and freckled; Anthy runs a hand along the blade; and the fire is told a third time with new cuts, among them Nemuro walking away with burning tapers in his hand, while a voice asks who really set it. Akio ends him by telephone, an instrument a few ministries had and no school did: Mamiya died long ago, and Akio made use of the illusion. Utena runs in, the black rose shreds, and Akio's voice says "graduate from this place." The hall is a ruin. Miki recalls an old fire in which nobody was hurt and cannot remember the name, trying Kushiro and Noboribetsu, places in Hokkaido like Nemuro, whose prefecture had been abolished on 26 January, the day chapter 22 began. "Mamiya" was Anthy: Akio lays a hand on the boy's shoulder, and she glances back in her own spectacles.

As it came out

The telephone, which almost no reader had seen, made Akio's voice from nowhere the most uncanny thing in the serial so far, and his order to "graduate from this place" became slang. By the spring a girl dropped by a friend, or a clerk dismissed by his master, had "graduated". choice In this timeline it is still the word for being cast off by someone who has used you (Part XV). choice The Kanda students, who had been a reading circle without a name, took the chapter's gloss and became the 決闘者会, read as the serial reads it, the Duellists' Society, with a register, a creed and dues. choice Readers who had followed Mamiya for nine chapters learned who he had been, and those who had guessed wrote to say so. choice On the evening of 16 February the Gakushūin, the peers' school in Kanda, burned, the fire starting in a second-floor classroom after the pupils had gone home. documented Miki's memory of an old fire in which nobody was hurt had run the same week, and readers took it as a comment, which it cannot have been: the manuscript had been posted weeks before. choice

24
七実様内証日記Nanami-sama naishō nikkiMiss Nanami's Secret Diary

Episode 24: The Secret Nanami Diary · 19–27 February 1886

The chapter

The second "story so far", done as Tsuwabuki's pocket diary read aloud at his bedside, with Nanami, Utena and Anthy drawn as shadows on the bed-curtain. He saves Nanami from a second runaway horse and is put to bed; the girls find his diary, and Anthy reads it out over every objection while he lies awake behind the curtain. Like the anime, it re-tells only Nanami's misadventures, since the Black Rose duellists remember nothing: the ruined ball gown, the curry and the road to India, the snail, snake and octopus, the kangaroo, the cowbell. New cuts put the boy at each scene, taking notes unseen, and reveal that the banana whose peel cost Nanami the spice was his present to Chu-Chu. Two of his numbered "Operations" are pictured: make Nanami forget everything and become her elder brother, or, should she turn into a cow again, become a calf beside her. When Utena calls a halt, Nanami asks after the weight of her own feelings, and the pun on omoi, which means both feeling and heavy, lets Utena guess it at thirteen kan. Nanami leaves by the window and wakes bandaged in the bed, Tsuwabuki beside her, to read his Operation the Twenty-fourth, which is also the chapter's number.

As it came out

After Nemuro the second recap came as a relief, and it belonged to the comic hand. choice It made Tsuwabuki a favourite: his numbered Operations were copied into schoolchildren's notebooks, and the guess at the weight of Nanami's feelings, thirteen kan, about forty-nine kilograms, was the joke of the season. choice Nanami's popularity, growing since chapter 10, was now beyond argument; when the paper announced a pause until May, the letters asked for a Nanami chapter first. choice The diary form was imitated at once: boys kept diaries "in the manner of Tsuwabuki" for the pleasure of having their sisters find them, and a stationer in Kanda sold a pocket diary with Operations numbered in advance. choice

Part Three 第三編 [the Carriage Book, 馬車の巻] · chapters 25–33 · Tomoshibi Shinbun, May–October 1886; suspended for nineteen days after chapter 31, and given up after chapter 33

In the ten weeks between the parts the serial became a business. The volumes of Part Two came out in April, the rose fever began (Part XII), and the women's companies played their Rose Bride wherever they could find a stage (Part XIV). choice The newspapers were changing around it. On 27 December 1885 the Yomiuri had printed an essay reporting that "a certain person", whom the historian Honda Yasuo identifies as Tsubouchi Shōyō, had urged it to give novels a column of their own; the paper conceded that "a newspaper is merchandise" and that readers "look at the soft continued stories rather than stiff editorials", and from 4 January 1886 it ran a separate novel column at the foot of its second page. documented In this timeline everyone in the trade knew which soft continued story had made the case. inference The same year Iwamoto Yoshiharu, who took over Jogaku zasshi when its first editor died in May, complained in its pages that the fiction women liked to read showed them only men lost in lust and women who sold themselves for them, and urged women to write better novels themselves. documented He never named the serial (Part VI). His readers named it for him. choice Part Three was the part readers were most impatient for, and the part the government read most closely.

25
二人の永遠黙示録Futari no eien mokushirokuThe Eternal Apocalypse of the Two

Episode 25: Their Eternal Apocalypse · 11–22 May 1886

The chapter

The girls move into the tower. At the council's table a game of baseball goes on, and nobody remarks on it. Under the dome Akio explains his name: the morning star, Lucifer, who chose to be king of hell; 黙示録 was the new Bible's word for Revelation. Then the ride. Tōga finds Saionji scrubbing the kenjutsu hall and cups his ear for the sound that races through the End of the World, and the sound is hooves and iron tyres: Akio's light open carriage, crest on the door, which he drives himself at night along roads lit by gas lamps, and which stands waiting inside the hall. There were fewer than two thousand passenger carriages in all Japan, and a minister's had a coachman on the box: Ōkubo Toshimichi's had died defending him in 1878. Akio drives his own, and readers took the detail as the measure of the man. Tōga speaks of the coffin girl of their boyhood, whom Akio saved by showing her something eternal. At the moment the anime has Akio vault onto the bonnet, he stands up on the box and lets the reins fall, and the horses run with nobody driving. In the duel, overturned carriages rise through the garden floor, Akio watches through opera glasses, and the Sword of Dios thins to nothing. Anthy carries Utena clear and draws a new sword out of Utena; then the carriages' lamps throw their beams upward. That night Akio calls Anthy to him, and the last cut shows her spectacles laid aside and her loosened hair under the magic lantern's stars, a dark hand above her.

As it came out

Part Three opened with a carriage, and within a month the press was attaching Akio's name to every young man who drove his own (Part VI). choice The sons of the rich took up driving themselves at night, with no coachman on the box, and the first collision on the Ginza between a self-driven carriage and a rickshaw, that June, was reported under the serial's heading. choice Christian readers had a harder week, since "Lucifer" was the first time the serial had named the Devil; a mission teacher in Tokyo took the chapter from a pupil's desk and read it to the end before confiscating it. choice The joke that Akio was Itō Hirobumi, prime minister for five months, began with this chapter, and stayed a joke until the following April (Part VI). choice The last cut, of Anthy's spectacles laid aside and a dark hand above her, drew no letters at all. The editor wrote in his memoir that he had expected some, and that their absence frightened him more. choice

26
幹の巣箱　光さす庭 替手Miki no subako: hikari sasu niwa, kaeteMiki's Nest Box: The Sunlit Garden, Alternate Part

Episode 26: Miki's Nest Box (The Sunlit Garden: Arranged) · 24 May – 5 June 1886

The chapter

The anime's "Arranged" becomes kaete, the shamisen term for a second part played against the first. Kozue, hanging from a ledge with a nest of chicks, sees Miki below and lets go, and he and Utena break her fall. A letter from the twins' mother goes into the waste-paper basket. At the council Miki refuses the sealed letter: adults who talk of "your own good" are never to be trusted. He learns that his father is to marry again and writes to him about the wedding, and the cut shows the new stepmother who answers, drawn from the neck down, faceless, in the Rose Bride's gown. Kozue waits at night for her "patron", a word that in 1886 meant what it means in the licensed quarters, where the anime has her "Daddy Long Legs" (a book not yet written); a tall man in silhouette, his hair tied back, puts an arm round her. When the carriage comes for Miki, Kozue rides on the box beside Akio; Miki sits alone behind. She does the talking: she is out with Akio, Miki loves Himemiya, and among the impure one has to become impure. The ribbon at her collar blows back across Miki's eyes, and for a moment he holds the reins himself, with Anthy leaning back beside him. In the garden Kozue, in a pale-blue copy of the Bride's gown, draws Miki's sword from his breast. Mid-duel Anthy is suddenly beside her in the carriage, which circles the rim with nobody on the box, and Kozue pushes her down out of sight by the throat. Miki turns to shout at his sister and loses. Afterwards he sits by the nest box the twins have put up, where no bird is ever drawn, and Kozue, leaving, calls him a coward.

As it came out

Kozue's "patron" was the chapter's trouble. The word belonged to the licensed quarters, and the moralists who had been waiting since chapter 5 wrote in to say so; a schoolmaster in Koishikawa demanded that the paper say whether its author knew what the word meant, and another reader answered that the author plainly did. choice By the editor's later account the Home Ministry's press officials, who had been underlining Juri's surname since January, began with this chapter to read the whole serial as closely as the paper's politics. choice The cut of Kozue on the box beside Akio was sold as a print for a week, and then not: the print-sellers had been warned. choice

27
七実の卵Nanami no tamagoNanami's Egg

Episode 27: Nanami's Egg · 7–17 June 1886

The chapter

A comic interlude: no council, no Akio, no carriage, no duel. After a dream of digging a patterned egg out of a sandpit as a little girl, Nanami wakes beside an egg on her sheet and decides she laid it. Four times she pictures being found out; each time the cut draws the onlookers pointing, their faces inked solid, calling her a creature from the moon, and she ends in a cage at the Ueno zoo, opened in 1882, beside a hen, a frog and a turtle. Miki knows no bird or reptile that lays such an egg; some mammals lay eggs, he begins, and she is gone. Juri's line about "my ball" survives because she bowls; Japan's first bowling alley had opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement in 1861. Nanami sings to the egg, bathes with it and sleeps with it. Anthy remarks that her hen, also called Nanami, was just the same, and wonders who the father is. Tōga's verdict on girls who lay eggs: such a girl would betray her family. She leaves the egg in the woods, cannot bear it, and goes back to find Saionji camping there, frying eggs in a frilled apron, with hers on top of his supply. Then the egg, grown as big as a house behind a police notice, lights up and bursts. Next morning the shell lies broken and empty on her bed, and the text never says where the dreaming stops or whether anything hatched. Chu-Chu, missing all chapter, comes home to the tower in a jacket and tie, and Anthy lowers her eyes over her tea.

As it came out

The egg came as a relief, and the letters said so. After Kozue, a chapter with no council, no Akio and no carriage, in which Nanami merely lays an egg, was what the paper's family readers had wanted for a month. choice Egg jokes filled the comic papers, and a confectioner in Asakusa sold "Nanami's eggs" in white sugar. choice The empty shell on her bed started a quieter argument, about whether anything had hatched, and what; the cut of Chu-Chu coming home in a jacket and tie was, by common consent, the answer, and nobody could say why. choice On 14–16 June, while the chapter ran, more than a hundred women of the Amemiya silk mill in Kōfu struck, the first factory strike in Japan. documented Nothing connects the two (Part VI).

28
闇に囁くYami ni sasayakuWhispers in the Dark

Episode 28: Whispers in the Dark · 19 June – 1 July 1886

The chapter

A masked fencer touches Juri's breast with his point and calls her captain: Ruka Tsuchiya, who taught her, comes back to the fencing club after a long illness that the chapter never names; readers of 1886, who lost so many young people to consumption, named it for themselves. At sunset he finds Shiori in the changing room holding a sword; his cupboard there is next to Juri's. He asks whether it was she who polished his sword while he was away. Shiori says it was, repeats his story back to him, and is kissed. Juri tells him to keep his hands off Shiori, an old friend. At a fountain by night he kisses Shiori with one eye open and turned aside, while Juri stands in an archway in her nightdress, her hand on her locket chain. Tōga brings the summons to Shiori, and in the carriage Ruka talks her round: she is grown up now, and a miraculous power can be theirs. The shadow girls go fishing and land a shoe, a kettle and a rickshaw wheel. In the garden Shiori, in a magenta copy of the Bride's gown, opens her hands and his sword rises between them. He toys with Utena and leaves her against a carriage; behind her Anthy clasps her hands and shuts her eyes, and Ruka says that now he sees. He is left composed with a bare stem; Shiori's carriage lies wrecked against the parapet and her face is scratched. "I failed because of my bride," he tells her, and when she says she polished his sword, he answers that it was not his. Juri, he says, knows better than anyone why he did it.

As it came out

Ruka's illness, which the chapter never names, every reader named: consumption, which killed more young Japanese than any other disease. inference Letters came from the sick and from those nursing them, and Ruka, the serial's most calculating suitor, had defenders among them who would not hear a word against a dying man. choice The week the chapter began, the E-iri Chōya shinbun printed a letter from a woman reader who loved its serials but asked for stories of the civilised West instead of the barbarous past, and its editor replied over three days that he had twice tried serials "in the Western-novel style" and both times provoked "bitter complaints", adding that many women readers would call such things "long tales aping hairy foreigners". documented In this timeline his reply was quoted against him all summer by readers who could name a Western-style serial that nobody found boring. choice Cholera, which had spread through Osaka and Kyoto in May, came east that summer by way of Yokohama to Tokyo. documented

29
空より淡き瑠璃色のSora yori awaki ruri-iro noAzure Paler than the Sky

Episode 29: Azure Paler Than the Sky · 3–15 July 1886

The chapter

The heading's 瑠璃, lapis, joins the first character of Ruka's name to the second of Juri's. Ruka leaves Shiori on the paving of a courtyard with the whole school at the windows. Juri asks him to take Shiori back. He calls Shiori a spoilt liar, pins Juri's wrists to the wall and kisses her by force; when he steps back her locket hangs from his fist, and then it lies under his shoe. She strikes him and challenges him: if she loses, she will do as he likes. The bout is two silhouettes under great beams, and then Juri is on the ground. Ruka cups his own ear for the hooves and cues Tōga for the invitation. In the carriage he tells her a miracle needs a sacrifice, and she goes along to set Shiori free. The shadow-play slot before the duel holds only Shiori, standing before the rose wall. In the garden Ruka draws Juri's sword from her, and her point stops beside Utena's eye while the earlier bout is told again beneath the duel. The carriage lamps flare; Utena's stroke cuts the locket's chain and leaves the orange rose untouched, and Juri pulls the rose off herself. The locket breaks in the rain, and Ruka says twice that it will be all right. Afterwards he stops coming to school. The shadow play proper comes after the duel: two nurses gossiping in a hospital corridor about a patient who died yesterday, who had gone back to school to give someone in the fencing club the power of miracles. Neither names him. Trained nursing was the newest profession open to women in Japan (the first schools opened in 1885–86), so the scene was also news.

As it came out

Cholera was spreading through Tokyo. In July the papers found the city's restaurants empty, and soldiers were forbidden to eat or drink outside their barracks. documented The letters column shrank to a few letters a week; readers had other things to write about. choice More than a hundred thousand people died of the disease in Japan that year, some eight thousand of them in Tokyo. documented The two nurses who gossip about the dead patient were news in their own right, since trained nursing was barely a year old in Japan: the first nursing school had opened at a Tokyo hospital in October 1885, and a second, in Kyoto, would begin teaching that September. documented Readers who had nursed someone through the epidemic found the scene hard to bear, and said so. choice Ruka's assault on Juri was read that summer as of a piece with the disease: something that happened to people without warning, in public, and was not spoken of afterwards. inference Girls who wore lockets put them away for a while. choice

30
跣足の少女Hadashi no otomeThe Barefoot Girl

Episode 30: The Barefoot Girl · 17–30 July 1886

The chapter

Wakaba talks of first kisses, and Utena, in a flash of memory or fancy, sees a figure in a white uniform with epaulettes kissing her, and touches her lips. Akio has baked a Western cake for tea; behind it stand three candles in a branched candlestick, and two go out as the chapter runs. The woman teacher of chapter 1 and the vice-principal scold Utena's boys' clothes, and Akio charms them away, walks her off with an arm round her shoulders and calls himself her hiiki, a theatregoer's word for his devotion to one actor, as though her jacket were a role. Leaping at lawn tennis, Utena sees a figure at an upper window and twists her ankle; Akio drives her to the doctor and leaves Anthy waving from the shadow. In an arcaded court Akio kneels and takes off Utena's buttoned boot, the footwear of a schoolgirl who has given up clogs, tells her they are alike, and bends her back against the carriage. The second candle goes out in Anthy's hands as she stands in the dark, and for a moment she is in the arch behind them; then he kisses her beside the carriage. That night Anthy says she has a prince of her own, and the girls clasp hands across the gap between their beds. Tōga, riding in the carriage, holds up a boot like hers and asks after the owner of the glass slipper. Next morning Akio takes off his fiancée's mother's shoe in the same way: "My only prince." Utena tells herself she loves only the prince, and the last candle burns on, its flame blown flat.

As it came out

The boot and the kiss brought the warning. At the end of the chapter's run the Home Ministry's press section summoned the serial editor and warned him; nothing survives of the warning but his account of it, which says that the official had read every installment and asked him whether the author was a woman. choice The Home Minister was Yamagata Aritomo. documented The letters divided as they had not since chapter 7. Girls who had loved Akio since chapter 14 wrote that he was wicked and that they loved him still; their mothers wrote that they had always known. choice The fiancée's mother's "My only prince" became, in the comic papers, the motto of every mother-in-law in Tokyo. choice Mori Arinori's Ministry of Education was not consulted, and while Mori lived it never joined the Home Ministry against the serial (Part VI). choice On 30 July, the day the chapter ended, the empress wore Western dress in public for the first time, at the first graduation of the Peeresses' School, and the schoolgirls who read the serial took the boot as a fashion plate. documented for the empress; choice for the girls.

31
彼の女の悲劇Kano onna no higekiHer Tragedy

Episode 31: Her Tragedy · 1–21 August 1886

The chapter

The heading writes "her" as 彼の女, read かのをんな, the older of the two ways the translators of the day rendered the Western she; the newer 彼女, read かのぢよ, was just entering fiction. Tōga asks Nanami whether she will join him in the bath and says he is joking; secure in being his sister by blood, she kneels before his shadow on the bath's paper screen, takes from his clothes the letter-case that holds his girls' notes, and next day answers them herself. About to brain Utena with a plaster bust, she slips on the skin of the banana Anthy is eating and is caught in mid-air by Akio, who binds her ankle in the tower while Anthy feeds him shaved ice from a spoon. Nanami's discovery comes from the family register, where the anime has blood types (discovered in 1901): one of her followers remarks on Tōga's entry, and what the register shows Nanami about her brother and herself is not what she expected, though the chapter never prints it. She leaves home, and Akio, at croquet on the lawn, cites a school rule and lodges her in the tower; his dream, he says, is to make it his own ōoku, the shogun's women's quarters, and he says he is joking. On the tower room's blind the shadow girls show a cuckoo's egg hatching in another bird's nest, as in the Man'yōshū poem of the cuckoo born among the warbler's eggs. She tells Tōga they are not really brother and sister; he asks how she found out, and she sends him away, loving him still. Lost at night in the tower, she comes round the back of the sofa, and the chapter ends on what she saw, which it never names.

As it came out

The chapter ran for three weeks, and readers knew from its first installments that something was wrong: Nanami at her brother's bath screen, the family register, a cuckoo in another bird's nest. choice Its last installment, on 21 August, ended with Nanami coming round the back of the sofa and seeing something the text does not name. The Home Ministry ordered the issue seized the next day and suspended the paper for "injury to public morals" (Part XIX, document 6). choice Most of the issue had been sold or delivered before the order came, and the police took only what was left at the paper and the newsagents; about forty copies survive (Part XVIII), and the lending libraries' scrapbooks of the confiscated installment, cut from copies already delivered, rented at a premium all autumn (Part XII). choice The seizure was read as an answer: if the police had seized it, readers reasoned, there must be something in it to seize. inference The text still does not say what. For nineteen days, while cholera was still killing in Tokyo, there was no paper at all. choice The epidemic had already taken Kimura Tōko, co-founder of the Meiji Girls' School, who died of cholera on 18 August, ten months after the school opened. documented

32
踊る女等の恋Odoru onna-ra no koiThe Romance of the Dancing Girls

Episode 32: The Romance of the Dancing Girls · 10–25 September 1886

The chapter

Nanami cannot say what she saw. At breakfast, with Akio in an apron, she sees the night again whenever brother or sister greets her. Under the conservatory sill she hears Tōga tell a girl that he has no sister and that the perfect brother was a part his father ordered. The girl is her own follower Keiko; Nanami goes in swinging and is knocked down by her among the yellow roses while Tōga stands by. Nanami flings his letter-case at a wall. Kanae sits slack on the sofa while hands whose owner is never drawn lift her chin and feed her slices of apple, a scene that its first readers, in the book of 1888, read through the "poison-woman" stories the papers had sold since Takahashi Oden's trial. The letter-case comes back to Nanami without explanation, holding a note signed End of the World: Tōga Kiryū is waiting. At home, as she tells her brother she has asked to change schools, he cups his ear, the carriage comes in through the window, and Akio calls down from the box. Between the two men she begins "I saw him" and cannot finish. After a mutiny her three followers stand behind her again in bandages; Anthy is found face down in the conservatory, and Keiko holds Chu-Chu hostage. One shadow girl plays at kokkuri, the table-turning game then spreading through Japan, and the other heckles her, calling it a trick to the end. Tōga draws a single sabre from Nanami; she fights without her dagger and loses on her feet. On a red bed Tōga tells Akio that he and Nanami are brother and sister by blood, both taken into the Kiryū house when she was a baby, and that he finds her version more romantic. The letter-case is the last thing drawn.

As it came out

When the paper came back, the chapter appeared with two passages printed as rows of circles, blanked by the paper itself (Part XVIII). choice Readers filled them in. Lending libraries in Kanda ran guessing contests with a free rental as the prize, and most of the guesses were about the sofa. choice They were wrong: the book of 1888 printed the two passages, which are the hands feeding Kanae the apple and the red bed on which Tōga talks to Akio, and neither says what Nanami saw. choice Kokkuri, the shadow girls' table-turning game, was coming up from Kyoto and Osaka and reached Tokyo that autumn, and the young philosopher Inoue Enryō was collecting reports of it for the account, published in 1887, in which he explained it as the sitters' own unconscious movements. documented All month Chiarini's Italian circus played in tents at Akiba-ga-hara in Kanda, with an elephant and a monkey that rode a horse, and readers wrote to ask whether Chu-Chu had joined it. documented for the circus; choice for the letters. When the book of 1888 printed Tōga's account on the red bed, that he and Nanami were siblings by blood, half its readers took it for a lie and the other half for the only true thing he ever said. choice

33
夜を走る王子Yoru wo hashiru ōjiThe Prince Who Runs Through the Night

Episode 33: The Prince Who Runs Through the Night · 27 September – 19 October 1886

The chapter

The serial's third "story so far" opens on the fairy tale, unboxed and unillustrated, and braids three strands. Anthy, alone under the stars her brother's lantern throws on the dome, sends a note by the house messenger asking whether he got tonight's roses. The radio quiz becomes the prize-riddle column of a newspaper inside the novel, kept by two girls, the shadow players without their silhouettes; Akio, who writes in to it under the pen name 世界の果て, turns its riddles over as he drives his carriage through the night, and answers neither. Which is eternal: a diamond, a beautiful memory, or tinned peaches? Which is a miracle: Edison's inventions, meeting a prince, or a tinned mermaid? A mermaid, in place of the anime's coelacanth, was a sideshow fake and, in legend, the flesh that gave a nun eight hundred years. Each riddle calls back two of the Carriage Book's duels, none told to its end, and Nanami's is not among them. Utena spends the evening at an inn on the Sumida on the night of the river fireworks, a setting no 1886 reader needed explained, talking to someone who is never drawn and never answers. The Reversi game becomes go, the board turns against her, and the proverb she half-says is 待った無し, no taking moves back. The lamp goes out; lying down, she talks about tomorrow's lunch, loses the thread, and asks what eternity is. The messenger comes back to the dome with his answer: yes, he got them. Afterwards Utena sits on the box beside Akio as he drives, eyes closed, thinking that she came only to deliver the roses. In the newspaper most of the inn scene was printed as rows of circles, and the chapter's last illustration was a blank frame, captioned "this picture withheld."

As it came out

After the suspension the paper ran the serial less often, and the three installments of the last "story so far" were spread over more than three weeks. choice Most of the inn scene was printed as rows of circles, and readers who had been filling in the circles of chapter 32 since September read these as they had read the sofa: the more circles, the worse it must be. choice On 19 October the last installment ended on a blank frame captioned "this picture withheld", with the serial editor's notice that the story would be finished as a book (Part XIX, document 7). choice There was no uproar. choice Five days later the British freighter Normanton sank off Wakayama, its captain and European crew took to the boats and left every Japanese passenger to drown, and when the details came out in November the papers had a scandal that was not fiction (Part VI). documented On 7 October a new small paper, the Yamato shinbun, had begun with Tsukioka Yoshitoshi's illustrations. documented In this timeline he went on drawing for the serial as well, and the withheld picture of 19 October was, by the editor's account, the last cut the serial asked of him. choice Readers wrote to ask when the book would come, and were told the spring. choice Suimutei wrote that he had no column left to write, and wrote one anyway, about the prize-riddle column inside the novel: Akio, he pointed out, never sends in his answers. choice

Part Four 第四編 [the Apocalypse Book, 黙示録の巻] · chapters 34–39 · published as a book only, Shun'yōdō, April 1887

The book was six months coming, and the gap was filled. Fake endings were sold through the winter of 1886–87 in paper covers copied from the part-volumes, several of them claiming to be the author's own: in one Utena marries Akio, in another Anthy dies and Utena takes the veil, and in the best-selling the two girls sail for France. choice In February the authorities announced strict rules for boarders at private girls' schools, citing their "misconduct"; the papers did not need to say which book the boarders were reading. documented for the rules; choice for the rest. Counterfeits were an ordinary hazard of a hit. In April 1887 the publisher of Suehiro Tetchō's political novel Setchūbai warned readers that "cunning men" had published books of the same title under "a writer of the same surname". documented The real Part Four came out the same month, after the Home Ministry's censor had cut one passage (Part XVIII), and sold its first printing of 3,000 copies in nine days and 10,000 by the summer (Part VI). choice For the first time readers met new chapters six at once instead of one installment a morning, and many read all six at a sitting, at night. The notes below record how each chapter was received in the weeks after publication; the argument about the ending has never stopped, and Part XIII follows it. choice

34
薔薇の刻印Bara no kokuinThe Rose Crest

Episode 34: The Rose Crest · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

Anthy is in none of Wakaba's photographs, so Utena asks for one of the three of them; Akio uncaps the lens and steps into the picture, and Anthy, between Utena and her brother, shuts her eyes for the exposure. The shadow girls, who have already stepped out from behind their wall to leave Utena holding a ticket, stage the Kashira Shadow Players' thirty-fourth performance, The Tale of the Rose, in silhouette before Utena, Anthy and Akio: a Rose Prince on a hobby-horse, the harukoma of the New Year street players; the light of the world in four phrases over four council silhouettes; a cage; a witch who is his little sister; and a lamp's beam that finds Akio, then Anthy. Then the memory: a child in a coffin, and a youth in white who shows her a figure pierced by blades at the heart of a dark rose, the Rose Bride; the barn, the prince in the straw, a telegraph key clattering on its own, and outside a mob of faceless men in Western suits with sabres demanding he save their daughters. A short-haired girl holds him down and goes out to them alone. "Dios is no longer here!" They call her 魔女, glossed with the English "witch", and the million swords, not yet named, fly at her. The prince is now 世界の果て; the child vows to become a prince and is given the ring. The play blames the sister and the memory shows her taking the blades; the chapter prints both. Utena wakes having forgotten, and Anthy, lying at her pillow, asks her, "Who are you?"

As it came out

The mob of faceless men in Western suits with sabres, demanding that the prince save their daughters, was the first thing readers of 1887 talked about. They read the men as the oligarchs, or the Rokumeikan's guests, or simply as fathers, depending on who they were. choice The proof the censor sent back marked that picture, the serial editor recalled, and the picture was left in. choice The shadow players' Tale of the Rose divided readers along a line that has held since: those who believed the play, in which the sister is a witch who sealed the prince away, and those who believed the memory, in which she takes the blades in his place. The book prints both and chooses neither. choice The English gloss on 魔女 sent readers to their English dictionaries. choice Anthy's last question, "Who are you?", became the most quoted line in the book after the creed and "Let's just go home". choice

35
冬のころ芽生えし愛Fuyu no koro mebaeshi aiThe Love That Blossomed in Wintertime

Episode 35: The Love That Blossomed in Wintertime · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

The heading, like the anime's title, is built on the two characters of Tōga's given name, 冬 and 芽. The poppy maze, in the decade when Japan's papers were full of opium in China; Akio's lecture on the flower tells a story Meiji readers knew from their Chinese reading, of Lady Yu, consort of the defeated Xiang Yu: the corn poppy, 虞美人草, grew from her grave. Tōga photographs Akio sprawled on his carriage, which stands on a pyramid of other carriages, and is sent with Akio's present. Tōga delivers earrings, a foreign ornament, since Japanese women did not pierce their ears, then takes Utena riding on a dark horse; she is thrown at a jump and caught by Akio, who courts her on a white horse, the mount of the princes in the new foreign picture books and, in the Buddhist story of the Great Departure, of Prince Siddhārtha, who rode his horse Kanthaka out of his father's palace; the proof the censor sent back marked the passage, the serial editor recalled, and that tells us what the censor thought a white horse meant. The shadow players' fisherman lands a fish that says it is a koi, carp and love, a pun that needed no change. The lift rises to the coffin dialogue of chapter 9 in place of the creed; Tōga and Saionji meet among reporters with notebooks and the sketch artists of the illustrated papers, and strip to the waist; Saionji names the girl in the coffin, Utena Tenjō, and Tōga, who holds End of the World's letter for the last council duel, cannot say whether he loves her. Utena puts both earrings on and laughs, and Anthy watches, the sight reflected in her spectacles.

As it came out

The passage in which Akio courts Utena on the white horse had been cut short, and readers noticed the jump where the censor's cut had been (Part XVIII). Since all anyone could see on either side of the gap was Akio on a white horse, they drew the conclusion the censor had drawn. inference The rest of the chapter belonged to Tōga, and it made him, late, the favourite of a new set of readers: the boy who cannot say whether he loves her. choice Earrings, which Japanese women did not wear, were worn for one summer by girls who had their ears pierced in Yokohama, and school inspectors noted them in two prefectures. choice Lady Yu and her poppies were read in 1887 as a lesson in how women die for men who have already lost. inference

36
斯くて夜の扉開くKakute yoru no tobira hirakuAnd Thus Opens the Door of Night

Episode 36: And Thus Opens the Doorway of Night · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

Akio and Utena ride double to a lake, and he kisses her; Tōga is waiting when the horse comes back. The carriage ride is parodied on a two-seated "sociable" tricycle, the boys' tricycle of chapter 9 grown up: Tōga pedals, and Saionji, who hates not being in control, stands up in his seat to declare it time to rise from their coffins. Tōga takes Utena up to the duelling garden by night with no ritual, under coloured lamps and the northern lights, tells her he loves her, and kneels to ask for one night beside her; she agrees. Next day he pins her to a tree and sets his terms: if he wins, she must become his woman. The shadow players' Prince of the White Horse rides a rocking horse, and the lady admires the horse. In the last council duel Saionji draws Tōga's sword and Anthy draws Utena's; Tōga holds her ringed hand until a carriage drives between them; she falls into Anthy's arms and swears to protect her, and Anthy runs her hand along the blade until it turns to light. Carriages charge and are cut apart, and Saionji rides at her on the tricycle with Tōga standing on the saddle. Both end on their backs, Tōga warning her against End of the World "or the Rose Bride". That night Utena crosses the tower room and finds Anthy with Akio. Nobody speaks; the chapter ends on the two girls' eyes.

As it came out

Lending libraries hid this volume. The chapter ends with Utena finding Anthy with Akio, nobody speaking, and the two girls' eyes. The libraries that rented the book to schoolgirls kept the volume under the counter for adult borrowers, and the girls borrowed it from each other instead. choice The sociable tricycle, with Saionji standing in his seat, was the comic relief of the season and its toy: a Tokyo tinsmith sold tin sociables with two small boys on them, one standing. choice Tōga's night beside Utena in the empty garden, which the chapter passes over between his request and the next morning, was its other scandal, and readers who wanted it to mean something filled the gap as they had filled the circles of chapter 33. choice

37
世界を革命する者Sekai wo kakumei suru monoThe One to Revolutionize the World

Episode 37: The One to Revolutionize the World · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

Utena takes off the ring at dawn and lets it fall, and Anthy's eyes open. At breakfast Akio notices the bare hand, and a date is made over Chu-Chu's toast. The evening ends in the halted carriage, where Akio confides that the stars do not interest him at all. Anthy has waited up and says that in the end girls are all like Rose Brides; in front of her, Utena tears up the letter that promises her prince at the castle. The badminton becomes hanetsuki, the girls' New Year battledore game, played out of season: Utena says she has only been playing prince, cannot finish a sentence when Juri asks whether she loves Anthy, and is warned off the chairman and his sister by Nanami. Akio drives Anthy in the Bride's gown and tells her it is the world that hurts her; for an instant blades stand out of the seat. Tea and talk of cantarella, the Borgias' poison: Anthy has baked the biscuits, Utena says she has poisoned the tea, and both go on eating; Utena hopes that in ten years they will still be having tea and laughing like this. Anthy goes off the edge of a roof cornice and Utena catches her cuff. At sunset Tōga and Saionji, who had not expected Utena to go to the castle after all, ask her why she is going, and Tōga tells her what he wrote in chapter 9, that anyone who believes in true friendship is a fool; she says she is one. On the steps Anthy holds out the letter, pasted back together, with the ring lying on it; Utena shows her hand, and the ring is on it, though the chapter passes over the moment she puts it on. "Let's go."

As it came out

Readers took the tea. Utena's hope that in ten years they will still be having tea and laughing became a promise girls made to each other on leaving school, and from 1897, ten years after the book, the alumnae of several Tokyo girls' schools held a "ten-years tea" for each class a decade after it left, a custom that spread and survives (Part XV). choice The cantarella exchange, poisoned biscuits answered with poisoned tea, was read aloud in dormitories as comedy and taken in staff rooms as a threat. choice "Let's go", after "Let's just go home" in chapter 12, persuaded most readers of 1887 that the book would end happily. inference They had two chapters left. choice

38
世界の果てSekai no hate (the book gives no reading)End of the World

Episode 38: End of the World · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

At the head of a red stair a caped figure sits on a great sphere, and Akio waits in a prince's white uniform: so he was End of the World, and still her prince. He draws Utena's sword from her himself, with no formula, and she stands in a pink gown and crown in the crook of his arm. What happened on the roof is told now: above the city's gas lamps, Anthy confesses that she used Utena from the first, and Utena that her protecting was for her own pride. Utena takes the sword back to free Himemiya, and Akio says that he will show her reality. Then the reveal, which 1887 understood instantly because its readers knew what a magic lantern did: the castle is a slide in Akio's magic lantern, thrown on the dome of his room, and there is no higher place. He calls his pictures illusions, and the instrument's Meiji name, 幻燈, "illusion lamp", has said so all along. He throws her own evenings with him on the dome, then the church and the coffins, calls Anthy, her head in his lap, a witch, and names the seated figure the grave of Dios. He draws his own sword from among the blades where Anthy lies. Hands drop roses of five colours into a watering can as the creed is spoken for the last time, and the can ends holding only white ones. The duel; "I'm going to be a prince!"; the lantern flares and the castle breaks up. Akio sends Anthy forward, Utena shelters her, and the blade comes from behind, from the girl she is shielding.

As it came out

The castle was a lantern slide, and readers of 1887 understood at once, because they knew what a magic lantern did. The Ministry of Education had sent lanterns to the normal schools from 1880, a slide-maker had been giving free lantern evenings in Tokyo since 1883, and the boom in lanterns was just beginning. documented for the lanterns; inference for the readers. The reveal took the castle away from the readers as completely as from Utena, and many of them said so in the margins of their copies, which survive in some numbers. choice The blade from behind, from the girl Utena is shielding, was the hardest page in the book for its first readers. Girls who had loved Anthy for two years wrote that they could not finish the chapter, and finished it. choice On 20 April the prime minister, Itō Hirobumi, gave a fancy-dress ball at his official residence; a scandal about him and a nobleman's wife followed, and the serial's own paper, renamed Mezamashi Shinbun three weeks before, reported it and was suspended for eight weeks. documented Within the month, then, the chapter had a reading nobody had planned: readers who had just met End of the World on his red stair stopped treating the joke of chapter 25 as a joke (Part VI). choice

39
何時か共に輝かんItsuka tomo ni kagayakanSomeday, Together, We'll Shine

Episode 39: And Someday, Together, We'll Shine · April 1887, in the book

The chapter

The chapter opens without its heading. Anthy tells Utena she can never be her prince because she is a girl, and takes her sword. Round a brazier under the stars, Juri tells the council of a boy washed away trying to save her sister, a boy whose name she has forgotten. Akio weeps, and Anthy gives him the sword; he walks out along a causeway to the Rose Gate. Anthy slips from her gown and Utena's grip, and the million swords that shine with human hatred rise to cries of "witch" and close on her where she hangs in the prince's place. The anime's merry-go-round becomes a revolving lantern, 走馬燈, whose paper horses run in circles, and beside it a kind voice tells Utena that what lies beyond the gate is too much for a girl. The sword breaks on the gate; Utena pushes Akio aside and pulls at the seam with her hands, and a tear falls. The gate becomes a rose with a coffin at its heart; Utena's bloody fingers drag the lid aside; Anthy refuses, then lifts her hand; fingertips. The coffin falls away and the swords dive at the slab where Utena lies. The school forgets her within a season. Anthy leaves her spectacles on Akio's desk and tells him Utena has only vanished from his world. At the gate, in a pink travelling suit, with a trunk and Chu-Chu, she asks the absent Utena to wait for her, calling her plain "Utena", without 様, for the first time, and walks out down a road over green hills. The book's last plate is a photograph in a rose-coloured mount, with a third figure cut off by its edge, and under it, at last, the chapter's heading.

As it came out

The ending was argued about from the week it appeared. Readers divided at once: over whether Utena was dead, gone or somewhere Anthy could reach; over whether Anthy's walk through the gate was an escape, a pilgrimage or another kind of death; and above all over whether fingertips touching across a coffin lid were enough. choice The book does not say, and the answers critics have given since are in Part XIII. choice Suimutei, who had written in October that he had no column left to write, wrote one more, on the last chapter: the author, he said, had given readers "a heroine who disappears and a bride who walks", and asked them which of them was the story (Part XIII). choice Nobody disputed the walk itself. A young woman leaving her brother's house alone, with a trunk and a small animal and no destination, was a scandal in 1887 and a promise (Part VI), and the pink travelling suit was in the Yokohama tailors' windows by the summer. choice The last plate, the photograph with a third figure cut off by its edge, was the most argued-over picture in the book, until the blank frame of chapter 33 overtook it. choice

The recurring machinery

The anime's set pieces have to survive as print, and they do, in forms the Meiji press already had.

The storybook prologue
A boxed "Western tale" opening chapters 1, 3, 8, 13, 16 and 31, set in a heavier rule like the imported picture books sold at Maruzen. The prince's face is never drawn.
The creed
Printed in proclamation style, unattributed, as the council rides the lift in Part One; once more in chapter 15, with "cage" for "shell", and a last time in chapter 38. In between, the lift often rises in silence. From 1886 it was among the most quoted passages in Japanese. choice
The shadow plays
Two girls drawn as black silhouettes against a rose-patterned wall, in the convention of kage-e shadow prints, trading a riddle or a skit in nearly every chapter, duel or none, most often just before the duel; in Part Two a single girl performs for a listener at the lockers. Some open with a short formula, which readers chanted choice; the serial gives the girls no names.
The duel songs
Each duel installment prints a chorus in the new-style verse of the 1882 Shintaishi-shō, packed with the vocabulary of the decade's science (evolution, embryology, the galvanic cell) wound round Buddhist terms. They were set to music by the 1890s, and the stage versions sang them. choice
The descent
In Part One the figure who dives from the castle is drawn whole only twice, in chapters 2 and 11, as in the anime's first arc; later chapters give him a line of text and, in the cuts, a small diving shape, as the anime gives him a few frames.
The previews
Each chapter but the last ends with a 次回 notice naming the next heading and closing on the same cryptic tag, 絶対運命黙示録, "Absolute Destiny: Apocalypse". Nobody in the serial explains it.
The recaps
Chapters 13, 24 and 33 are the serial's three "story so far" chapters, placed where a newspaper needed them, at the end of a part.
V

How 1885 read it

Seven readings, all of them partly right

Meiji readers were trained to look through a story for the thing it was really about. The Edo habit of reading comic fiction and prints as coded comment on the authorities, and the 1880s fashion for political novels set in Greece or Ireland that were obviously about Japan, made every serious reader a decoder. documented Utena gave them almost too much to decode.

1. A political novel in disguise

The paper's own readers, Liberal men who had lost their party in October 1884, watched the Chichibu rising crushed a few days later, and spent the winter reading about Sophia Perovskaya in the same column, read it first as a political novel. documented for the dissolution and Chichibu. The creed of the chick that must break the world's shell read like a handbill. The Student Council, sons and daughters of rich houses who rule the academy from a balcony in the sky and take their orders from sealed letters signed "End of the World", read like the oligarchs of Satsuma and Chōshū and their circle, who governed by rescript from behind a screen. The Rose Bride, who belongs to whoever wins her by the sword, was "the people's rights": prized, fought over, and never consulted, like the geisha O-Ken ("Rights") of the first political novel, courted in 1880 by "People" and "Government". documented for the 1880 novel. Utena, the commoner in borrowed clothes who fights for the Bride and is not a prince, was the movement itself. inference The police read that way too. When Kishida Toshiko spoke on "daughters in boxes" at Ōtsu in October 1883, the inspector's report took the box for the government's press and assembly laws, the parents for the government, the daughter for the people, and the servants sent after a daughter who elopes for the police in the hall. documented Anyone who could decode a speech about daughters could decode a novel about a bride.

The names helped. Saionji, the hot-tempered vice-president who strikes the Bride and wants to possess her, shares a surname with Saionji Kinmochi, the young noble back from Paris whom an imperial order had forced out of a liberal newspaper in 1881. Arisugawa, the cool fencer who duels to disprove miracles, shares a name with an imperial prince's house. documented for the real Saionji and Arisugawa. Readers could take the borrowings as satire, as homage or as carelessness, and argued about which. inference When the Osaka Incident broke in November 1885 (Liberal activists arrested for a plot to start a revolution in Korea, with a twenty-year-old former schoolmistress, Kageyama Hideko, among them), the papers that disliked the Liberals had their headline ready: the Liberals' girl revolutionaries were no longer only in their fiction. Kageyama had, by her own account, cropped her hair and dressed entirely as a boy until she was sixteen, while the local children jeered at her as a "fake", and she had carried the plotters' explosive chemicals in a trunk because nobody searched a woman's luggage. documented for the Osaka Incident, Kageyama's arrest and her own account; choice for the headline.

2. A book about marriage

Women heard it differently, often aloud, often in the evening, at an age when few of them could read the paper themselves. inference To them the Rose Bride was not an abstraction. A Meiji bride was chosen by her parents through a go-between, transferred with her goods to her husband's household, entered in its register, and expected to obey its head; that is what "engagement" meant. The serial's word for Anthy's state, 婚約, was still a new and learned one: the dictionary's earliest record of it is the revised philosophers' lexicon of 1884. documented for the marriage customs and the word. Anthy, who is engaged to whoever holds the sword, calls each new owner by a new form of address and smiles, is the most exact portrait of a Meiji wife in Meiji fiction, and she is drawn as a horror. inference

The rest of the household is drawn as exactly. Akio's position, which a modern viewer must puzzle out, needed no explanation in 1885: a young man betrothed to the chairman's daughter and, as every reader assumed though the book never says so, taken into the house as adopted heir, ruling it while the old man is ill; that is why, readers decided, the siblings Himemiya and Ōtori have different surnames. The adopted son-in-law was a commonplace of the Meiji family, and so was his reputation for owing everything to his wife's house and resenting it. documented for the institution. Mrs Ōtori, who calls her daughter's fiancé "my only prince" in chapter 30, was the mother-in-law of a hundred kabuki plays turned inside out. inference And the boxes and coffins that run through the serial (the coffin girl in chapter 9, the box sealed with pasted paper at the sluice in chapter 10, Mikage's drawers dropping into the fire) began arriving less than two years after Kishida Toshiko had told an audience in Ōtsu that Japanese parents kept their daughters like goods "in boxes", and been arrested for it. documented for the speech and arrest. No woman reader in 1885 needed the connection made. inference

3. A schoolgirls' book

The girls of the mission schools on the Bluff read it as a book about themselves, and they were the first to read it in packs. They lived in dormitories, played the piano, learned English and French, had senior girls they worshipped, and were watched for signs of corruption by a press that had decided "schoolgirl" meant trouble. documented for the mission-school milieu and the press's attitude. In Utena they found a school that was theirs made strange and grand, a heroine who answered back to teachers, and a world in which the important relationships were between girls. inference Within a year they were exchanging carte-de-visite photographs in lockets, giving each other white roses, and calling each other by the serial's forms of address; within two, the word Bride had become the dormitory word for a younger girl attached to an older one, and prince for the older. choice In our history the schoolgirls had no name for these attachments until the slang o-me was reported in 1909 and esu ("S", for "sister") spread in the 1910s; the clinical 同性愛 came later still. documented In this timeline the words come a generation early, out of a novel, and carry its romance and its menace together. inference Part VII follows what became of this.

4. A Christian book

Japan's Christians in the mid-1880s numbered a few tens of thousands: about 30,000 Catholics in 1884, a Protestant membership that was growing fast after the revival of 1883, and the Russian Orthodox converts besides. documented They were a small community but a disproportionately literate, urban and female one, concentrated around the very schools where the serial was most read. inference Christian readers recognised what others missed. Akio introduces himself as Lucifer, the morning star who chose to rule in hell. The last arc's word for revelation is the new Bible's. The heroine's prince is called Dios, the Spanish for God. No Japanese text of the period uses that form, but Catholic readers heard in it でうす, Deusu, the sixteenth-century word for God that the French missionaries' catechisms of 1868–72 still printed as a gloss, and that their hidden-Christian grandparents had prayed to in secret. documented for the catechisms. And the Rose Bride, pierced by a million swords of human hatred and unable to die, comes out of a devotion the French priests had brought with them: Our Lady of Sorrows, whose soul, in Simeon's prophecy in Luke, a sword would pierce. documented for the devotion and the verse, which the New Testament of 1880 had put into Japanese; whether any Japanese church had an image of her with swords is not known. The missionaries were divided. Some preached against the serial's incest and its girls' love; some of their Japanese teachers, women above all, read it as a parable of the soul held captive by the world and of the one who reaches into the coffin to save it. inference

5. An allegory of the throne

The most dangerous reading took longer to form, and the government was quicker to see it than most readers were. The castle that hangs over the duelling garden is "the castle said to hold eternity". Japanese political rhetoric of the 1880s already described the imperial line as unbroken for ages eternal, and in 1889 the constitution would put the phrase in its first article. documented A castle said to hold eternity, a prince on a white horse whom everyone worships and who turns out to have fallen, a man who rules from a tower by projecting the castle onto the sky with a lantern, and a girl who is told that she cannot be the prince because she is a girl: by 1889, each of these had a meaning in Tokyo that the author of 1885 may or may not have intended. inference The parallel with Princess Kazu was easier still. Engaged as a girl to Prince Arisugawa Taruhito, she had been given instead to the shogun Iemochi in 1862 to bind the court to the shogunate, a Rose Bride transferred from one champion to another for reasons of state, and she had died only in 1877. documented Older readers who remembered her journey to Edo did not need to be told why a girl called Arisugawa stood on the council. inference Anthy's own surname made it worse. 姫宮, himemiya, is the word The Tale of Genji uses for an imperial princess, and in the 1880s, when each child born to the emperor was given a personal title ending in -miya, a commoner girl called Himemiya sounded at best presumptuous. documented for the word and the custom. A princess of the blood, kept in a tower, engaged to whoever wins her: on the proof of the 1887 book that the censor sent back, the serial editor recalled, the surname was marked every time it appeared. choice

6. A comic novel with a modern heart

The literary men read it as a gesaku, the comic popular fiction of Edo that the new criticism was trying to bury, and were unsettled to find it moving. Tsubouchi Shōyō was publishing The Essence of the Novel in parts from September 1885, arguing that the novel's subject was human feeling, shown truthfully, not moral lessons or marvels. documented In this timeline the treatise never mentions the serial, but the younger critics who took up its terms applied them to it at once, as a case of feeling truly observed inside a frame of marvels, and regretted the marvels. choice The verdict stuck to the book for a generation: true in its people, false in its castles. It took the critics of the 1920s to argue that the castles were the truth, and the people's feelings the projection. inference

7. A scandal

The police and the moralists read it as a list of offences. A girl in a man's coat: Tokyo's minor-offences ordinance had punished "women who dress as men" from August 1873, with exemptions for actors and for women in hakama, and in April 1881 the Yomiuri had reported a crop-haired fishmonger's daughter in Shiba, in a workman's coat and tight trousers, being summoned and "admonished" under it, after which she eloped with a girl from a tea stall at the Shiba Shinmei shrine. The reporter found a woman falling for a woman "too strange". documented The ordinance had lapsed when the new Penal Code took effect on 1 January 1882, and the Penal Code had dropped the clause; whether Kanagawa's police rules kept one is not known. documented So Utena broke no law that anyone could name, which annoyed the moralists more. Girls who love girls. A brother and sister. A grown man, engaged to be married, who courts a schoolgirl, and his fiancée's mother besides. Schools where boys and girls are taught together, which the Education Order of 1879 had forbidden above the elementary level. documented And the word revolution in the title, in the paper of a party that had just been dissolved. The surprise is not that the serial was suspended in 1886 but that it ran for nearly seventeen months before it was. The answer, in this timeline, is that for most of its first year the Home Ministry was watching the paper's politics, not its fiction: when it suspended the paper for ten days in December 1885, the order named its reporting of the Osaka arrests. The ministry's readers began to underline Juri's surname only in January 1886, and its press section warned the serial editor in July (Part IV); it did not treat the fiction as an offence in itself until chapter 31 gave it one. inference

Who was who

By the end of 1886 the guessing game had settled into a set of identifications that every reader knew and no editor would print. Akio was Itō Hirobumi, prime minister from December 1885, whose charm and appetite for women were common talk. documented for Itō's reputation; choice for the identification. Nemuro's hundred boys were the boys of Aizu who died on Iimori Hill in 1868, or the students of Saigō Takamori's academies who followed him to death in 1877; readers chose by region. documented for both events; choice for the readings. End of the World was the oligarchy, or the emperor, or the West, or simply adulthood, which is the reading the anime's own writer arrived at a century later. choice for the readers; documented (makers' statement: Enokido Yōji, 1998) for the writer's. Nobody identified Utena. She was, as the girls of the Bluff said, whoever was reading.

Her name did its own work. うてな was a word every reader knew from Buddhist sermons and the theatre: the lotus seat of those reborn in paradise, the seat that the lovers of The Tale of Genji vow to share, and so, through the puppet plays of Chikamatsu, the "one lotus" (一蓮托生) that lovers hope to share by dying together. documented for the senses of the word. A heroine called "the lotus seat" whose last meeting with another girl is a hand reached across a coffin lid was read in 1887, by everyone who knew their Chikamatsu, as a love-suicide refused, or postponed. The book does not say which, and the argument has never stopped. inference Older readers had a word for what she was, too: 変成男子, henjō nanshi, the Lotus Sutra's dragon king's daughter who becomes a man in an instant so that she can become a buddha, a phrase Edo comic verse had used since at least 1753 for a woman in men's clothes. documented In the serial's first year the word came back into the street as the name for a girl who dressed like Utena. choice

Shadow play · Part V

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-ko(A fortune-teller, rattling her sticks.) Ohh, the sticks have spoken! A girl in a boy's coat, picking a fight with the whole sky!

A-ko(Top hat.) The girl is the people! So the sky must be… the government!

B-koOne sen.

A-ko(Pince-nez.) Low comic fiction. Vulgar. …Why am I crying?

B-koHandkerchief, one sen.

A-ko(Police cap.) A girl in a boy's coat? That's an offence! …Isn't it?

B-koNot any more, sir. One sen.

A-ko(School ribbon, running up.) Wait! Wait! That one's mine!

B-koNo charge, miss.

A-koDo you know? Do you know…

B-ko…whose fortune that was?

(The schoolgirl sits down on the kerb and reads it aloud. The top hat, the pince-nez and the police cap sit down beside her to listen.)

VI

Chronicle, 1885–1890

The serial years, and the six years in which Japan began to write down what a woman was

For five years Utena was news. It ran, it was stopped, it was staged, it was argued about in the letters columns and the lecture halls, and it gave a generation of girls a way of speaking, dressing and pairing off that their elders could see and could not stop. Its first effect on the law was the opposite of what its readers hoped.

Each year below threads the serial through documented events. Entries marked documented happened on those dates in our history; the threads are marked inference or choice.

1885The Council Book

Winter. The Matsukata deflation is at its worst; rice is cheap, farmers are selling land to pay taxes, and the Chichibu rebels of the autumn before are being tried. The Liberal Party has been dissolved since October. documented In February the first three chapters of a serial arrive at Jiyū no Tomoshibi by post. choice

2 April. Chapter 1 appears. It runs for a day beside Miyazaki Muryū's nihilist serial, which ends the next day and leaves it the space, and for a month it is one entertainment among several in a paper that already has one of the largest sales in Tokyo. documented for Kishūshū and the paper's standing; choice for the rest. The first sign of something else comes from Yokohama, where the paper is sold at the station and in the foreign settlement's Japanese shops: the agent there orders more copies every week from the serial's second week, and by May the paper's Yokohama sale has trebled. The mission schools on the Bluff are reading it. choice

18 April. Itō Hirobumi and Li Hongzhang sign the Tianjin Convention, withdrawing both countries' troops from Korea. documented

May–June. Chapter 7, Juri's chapter, ends with the photograph in the locket. Within days the letters column, which normally prints three or four letters a week, prints eleven in one issue, most of them from women, and the paper runs a second column of letters for the first time in its history. choice Some are outraged; more are grateful; one, signed "a woman of Kōjimachi, aged forty", says only that she had a friend like Shiori once and had not thought of her for twenty years. choice This is the moment when the serial stops being a political novel in disguise and becomes the thing its readers will remember: the first story in modern Japanese print in which a girl's love for a girl is the point of a chapter, stated in a picture and left without comment. inference

4–12 June. Fukuzawa Yukichi's editorials "On Japanese Women" run in his Jiji shinpō, with a continuation in July: Japanese men should imagine their positions and their wives' reversed, and a society that expects women to bear what men could not is not civilised. documented Tokyo's most influential liberal and its most popular serial are arguing about the same thing in the same weeks, and readers notice. Fukuzawa never mentions the serial; its letters column mentions him often. choice

June. The serial pauses for two weeks while the paper waits for manuscript. On 19 June a schoolgirl's letter points out that the byline can be read as a girl's name (Part XIX, document 2). choice

Summer. Girls on the Bluff begin to wear black boys' jackets over their kimono on the walk to school. In Tokyo the first are seen in Kanda, near the private schools, by August. choice Girls in men's clothes had drawn official notice before: in 1872 the government's first girls' school had put its pupils in samurai men's hakama, and the same spring Tokyo forbade women to crop their hair, on the ground that it blurred the line between men and women. documented The jackets reopened the question in a new form. Shops near the schools start selling "ウテナ形", Utena-style jackets cut for girls, and stalls near the schools sell cheap brass rings stamped with a rose, made in Tokyo's metalworking quarters, for 5 sen, the price of five copies of the paper. choice The girls' new habit of saying boku draws the letters that document 3 imitates. choice

20 July. Jogaku zasshi, the "Magazine of Women's Learning", begins publication in Tokyo. documented Its Christian editors will spend the next five years arguing with Utena without ever naming it in print. choice

21 August. Part One ends with chapter 13, the "story so far". The paper announces a second part for the autumn and the first three volumes of the book edition. choice By then its daily sale is half as large again as it was in March, and the paper is the best-selling in Tokyo by a distance. choice (Part XII gives the numbers.)

September. Tsubouchi Shōyō begins publishing The Essence of the Novel, in nine parts that will run to April 1886. documented

13 October. Part Two begins, and with it Akio. The same month Tōkai Sanshi's Chance Encounters with Beautiful Women appears. documented for Kajin no kigū; choice for the serial's date.
