For the rest of the decade students will argue about which of the two heroines, the Irish revolutionary Kōren or Utena Tenjō, a young man should prefer, and the girls of the Bluff will settle it for themselves. choice

November. A women's theatre company plays The Rose Bride of the Bluff at a small Yokohama house (document 4). It is the first of more than a thousand unauthorised stage versions, and the first time a Japanese audience sees a woman play a girl who plays a prince. choice From 23 November police in Osaka and Nagasaki arrest some 130 former Liberals for a plot to send explosives to Korea and start a revolution there; among them is a twenty-year-old former schoolmistress, Kageyama Hideko. documented She idolised Joan of Arc, and historians would call her the Joan of Arc of the East. documented In this timeline the papers, which have all read their rival's serial, call her "the Utena of Osaka". choice The Home Ministry suspends Jiyū no Tomoshibi for ten days in December, for its reporting of the arrests. choice The serial stops for ten days.

22 December. The cabinet system replaces the old council of state; Itō Hirobumi becomes Japan's first prime minister and Mori Arinori its minister of education. documented

1886The Black Rose and the Carriage

14 January. Jiyū no Tomoshibi becomes Tomoshibi Shinbun. documented The first installment of chapter 21 runs in the last issue under the old name and the second in the first issue under the new; readers say the paper changed its name and the serial did not notice. choice

26 January–7 February. Part Two reaches Nemuro Memorial Hall, on the day Nemuro Prefecture is abolished (Part IV). The fire, the hundred boys and the professor who calls their deaths a necessary sacrifice arrive in a city where adults remember the boys of Aizu who died on Iimori Hill in 1868 and the students of Saigō's academies who followed him to their deaths in 1877. documented for both. Letters come from Aizu and from Kagoshima, each claiming the hundred boys for its own dead. The serial never says. choice

March–April. Mori's school ordinances reorganise Japanese education from the Imperial University down to the elementary schools, and make normal schools into barracks of discipline. documented The model of schooling the serial mocks (a school that trains its pupils to be pieces in a game run by an absent authority) becomes official policy the same spring. Mori himself, who had once published an argument for monogamy and married by written contract, is the cabinet's leading advocate of women's education, and the oligarchs' least predictable reader. documented for Mori's views; choice for his reading. In this timeline he reads the serial, and while he lives his ministry, alone among the government's, never moves against it. choice

Spring. The rose fever begins. Western roses had come in with the treaty ports, and the first Japanese manuals on growing them, translated from American books, had appeared in 1875; but the rose was still a collector's plant. Tokyo knew what a craze could do. In 1872–73 imported rabbits had changed hands for fifty, a hundred and once six hundred yen, until on 7 December 1873 Tokyo prefecture taxed every rabbit a yen a month and eleven days later a kit sold for two sen; and from about 1877 to 1885 the potted omoto had its own boom of books and prices. documented In the spring of 1886 the rose becomes a speculation in its turn. White roses sold as "Utena" change hands for a yen a plant; a dark red-violet sold as the "Bride" goes for five, then fifteen; nurseries in Yokohama and Komagome import French stock by the crate. choice Part XII follows the bubble to its crash.

1886. A sixteen-year-old samurai's daughter from Sendai, whose father had named her Tarita, "enough girls already", runs away to join a touring troupe of sword-fighters, who bill her as "the beautiful swordswoman"; as Sonobe Hideo she will become the greatest woman fighter of the age, and in 1899, before an imperial prince, she is said to have made a famous swordsman of sixty-one abandon a bout against her. documented In this timeline the troupe's posters that year show her in a black jacket. choice

11 May. Part Three begins, the Carriage Book. Within a month the press attaches Akio's name to every young man with a private carriage, and a fashion for driving oneself at night, with no coachman on the box, spreads among the sons of the rich. choice

14–16 June. More than a hundred women of the Amemiya silk mill in Kōfu walk out against new guild rules that lengthen their day from fourteen hours to fourteen and a half and forbid them to move to another mill, shut themselves in a temple, and win a relaxation of the rules in two days: the first factory strike in Japan. documented Nothing connects them with the serial. Most of the strikers could not read, the paper did not circulate in Kōfu, and the story's academy is the opposite of their dormitories. inference Their strike is a reminder of how narrow the serial's world was: it was read in schools, shops and houses with a newspaper subscription, not in the mills, which held far more young women than all the girls' secondary schools in Japan put together.

Summer. Cholera kills more than a hundred thousand people across Japan. documented The serial's readers, like everyone else, are frightened; the letters column shrinks. choice

21–22 August. Chapter 31 ends with Nanami behind the sofa. The Home Ministry orders the issue seized and the paper suspended for "injury to public morals" (document 6). choice The suspension lasts nineteen days. When the paper returns, chapters 32 and 33 appear with passages blanked; on 19 October the last cut of chapter 33 is printed as an empty frame and the serial editor announces that the story will be finished as a book (document 7). choice

24 October. The British freighter Normanton sinks off Wakayama; its British captain and European crew take to the boats and leave all twenty-five Japanese passengers to drown, and a British consular inquiry at Kobe acquits the captain; after a public outcry he is tried at Yokohama in December and given three months, and the drowned passengers' families receive no damages, only the money raised by public appeals. documented The fury over extraterritoriality fills the papers for months and buries the serial's abandonment as news. inference

December. Yajima Kajiko, acting head since 1881 of the Sakurai Girls' School, a Tokyo mission school, founds the Tokyo Women's Reform Society, the Japanese branch of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, with herself as president. documented Its founders disapprove of the serial. Many of its younger members have read it twice. choice

1887The Apocalypse Book

January. The empress, who had first appeared in Western dress the previous summer at the Peeresses' School, issues a memorandum urging women to adopt it: the kimono of the day, it says, is a bad legacy of the age of civil wars, and Western dress, divided into upper and lower garments, is closer to the dress of ancient Japanese women. documented The girls who have been wearing a boy's jacket since 1885 take it as permission. choice

1 April. Tomoshibi Shinbun becomes Mezamashi Shinbun. documented The same month, Part Four appears as a book, after the Home Ministry's censor has removed one passage about the white horse (Part XVIII). choice It sells its first printing of 3,000 copies in nine days, and 10,000 by the summer. choice Readers who had waited six months for the end got the Rose Gate, the coffin, the fingertips, Utena's disappearance and Anthy walking out of the academy gate in a pink travelling suit. The ending's force in 1887 is hard to recover. In a society where a woman left her father's house for her husband's and her husband's only for the grave, a young woman walking out of her brother's house alone, with a trunk and no destination, to look for the girl who had vanished, was not a romance. It was a scandal and a promise. inference

20 April. Prime Minister Itō gives a fancy-dress ball at his official residence, and a scandal about the prime minister and a nobleman's wife follows it. The paper that had serialised Utena, renamed Mezamashi three weeks before, reports the scandal and is suspended for eight weeks; in all it spends 133 days of 1887 under suspension. documented (Part XXI) Readers who had finished Part Four the week before needed nobody to tell them what Akio Ōtori was. The identification of Akio with Itō, which had been a joke, becomes a political weapon, and Liberal speakers begin quoting the serial's carriage-ride line, "Let me show you the End of the World", in the halls where they attack the government's foreign policy. choice

Summer. Foreign Minister Inoue Kaoru's treaty-revision talks collapse under public anger at their concessions; he resigns in September, and the Rokumeikan era ends with him. documented The book of the ballroom, as some critics called Utena, outlives the ballroom. inference

1887. Roses bloom in the titles of popular fiction: a storyteller's "European novel" called The Yellow Rose, and Cherry and Rose, The Rose in Two Colours and In the Shadow of the Rose, all published that year. documented In this timeline every one of them is sold as being "in the manner of Utena". choice

Autumn. The first kabuki Utena, an authorised adaptation by the house playwright of the Shintomi-za, opens to full houses: a girl playing a prince, played by a man who specialises in women, which kabuki audiences found more natural than the women's companies' versions. choice Its most admired scene is the ball. Its last scene is not the book's: Anthy finds Utena asleep beyond the gate (Part XIV).

25 December. The Peace Preservation Ordinance takes effect the day it is issued, and between the night of the 26th and the 28th some 570 activists are ordered to leave Tokyo, by the rule that bars anyone the police think dangerous from living within three ri of the palace. documented Among them is the paper's founder, Hoshi Tōru; without him Mezamashi falls into a crisis that ends with its sale to the Osaka Asahi. documented Among them too is the Liberal politician Nakajima Nobuyuki, Kishida Toshiko's husband. He goes to Yokohama, and she, then teaching at the Shin'ei Girls' School in Tsukiji, soon joins him there; in March 1888 they settle in Ōta, on the western side of Yokohama, and in May she becomes an honorary professor at Ferris. documented In this timeline the expulsion list also includes the paper's former serial editor. choice The Nakajimas' move to the city of the Bluff, and Kishida's chair at the school every reader thought the academy was modelled on, are the foundation of the Kishida hypothesis about the authorship (Part XVII). inference

1888The collected edition and the crash

Spring. The rose bubble bursts. A dealer in Komagome who cannot pay for forty crates of French roses kills himself, the papers discover that the "Black Rose" plants sold for thirty yen were ordinary crimson roses grown in shade, and prices fall by nine-tenths in a month. choice What survives the crash is the trade: Japan now has a dozen nurseries that know how to grow, graft and ship Western roses, and a public that wants them (Part XII).

June. Tanabe (Miyake) Kaho publishes Warbler in the Grove, usually counted the first modern novel by a Japanese woman, a satire of the Westernised girls of the Rokumeikan years, written while she was still at school. documented In this timeline reviewers compare it, unfavourably, with Utena; Kaho's satire of a Westernised girl is read as an answer to the serial's girls, and the fee she earns will, a few years later, persuade Higuchi Natsu, the future Ichiyō, that a woman can live by writing, as in our history. documented for the fee's effect on Ichiyō; choice for the comparison.

10 July. The Osaka Asahi's owners relaunch Mezamashi Shinbun as the Tokyo Asahi Shinbun. documented In this timeline they pay noticeably more than they would otherwise have done, for a paper whose subscription list had been built by the serial and whose name was still attached to it. choice The collected edition of all thirty-nine chapters appears in four volumes the same year, with Juri's surname changed by one character (Part XVIII). choice

September. The duelling scandal. In June the magazine Nihonjin had exposed conditions in Mitsubishi's Takashima coal mine; when the journalist Inukai Tsuyoshi denied the report in the Chōya, its author, Matsuoka Kōichi, a pupil of the swordsman Sakakibara Kenkichi, challenged him to a duel, with the famous journalists Miyake Setsurei and Shiga Shigetaka as his seconds. Inukai refused, reportedly calling duelling "a barbarous survival". On 30 September, at a debate of the five private law schools in the hall of the Imperial University, the Paris-trained prosecutor Kōmyōji Saburō declared that "the duel is the flower of civilisation", and challenges followed one after another. documented In this timeline the papers have a word ready for every challenger: he is a 決闘者, read, as in the serial, Duellist. choice

December. Sudō Sadanori stages his "political-youth" play in Osaka, the beginning of shinpa, the "new school" theatre. documented Shinpa will stage Utena more often than any other novel of the 1880s. choice

1889The constitution and the duelling law

3–28 January. The Yomiuri serialises A Mirror for Women by Kimura Akebono, the teenage daughter of a Tokyo restaurant owner, written between shifts in the family restaurant: its heroine quarrels with her father, runs away, studies in the women's college at Cambridge, works in a New York factory and comes home to build a factory of her own. It holds the dictionary's earliest example of the word for a woman's men's dress, 男装. Kimura died the next year, not yet twenty-one. documented In this timeline the word is already four years old, and the reviewers call her heroine an Utena who went abroad. choice

11 February. The emperor bestows the constitution on his subjects. Its first article declares that the empire shall be reigned over by a line of emperors unbroken for ages eternal. The Imperial House Law, issued the same day, restricts the succession to males of the male line, the first such rule in Japanese history. documented The same morning the education minister, Mori Arinori, is stabbed by a nationalist; he dies the next day. documented

The rule had not been certain. The Senate's first draft constitution of 1876 allowed a woman to inherit, and its draft of 1880 allowed the female line "if there is no help for it"; a public debate of the liberal Ōmeisha society in 1882, serialised in a Tokyo paper, ended against reigning empresses, the speakers arguing that an empress's husband would rule from behind her and that her son would not be of the unbroken line. Most strikingly, a draft of the house rules drawn up inside the imperial household under Itō in late 1885 and early 1886 provided that if the male line failed the throne should pass through the female line, and said whom an empress should marry. Inoue Kowashi attacked it, quoting the debaters of 1882: an empress's son would bear his father's name, and the dynasty would change. The next draft, in 1886, dropped every female provision, and none came back. The law of 1889 adds that a woman who serves as regent must be unmarried. documented The imperial household's female clause was therefore drafted while the Black Rose Book was running in Tokyo, and was gone from the draft Itō submitted on 10 June 1886, a month into the Carriage Book. documented for the dates. In this timeline Inoue's memorandum does not mention the serial; no paper of his would. But the men who read it had all heard what the newspapers were saying about girls who wanted to be princes, and a clause that had been a lawyer's contingency now looked like an invitation. inference The serial's first effect on Japanese law is to help close the door it was knocking on. inference It will take a hundred and sixteen years for the question to come back in earnest (Part XI).

May. In this timeline the duelling craze of the previous autumn reaches the girls' schools. Two pupils of a Yokohama girls' school fight with fencing foils in a garden on the Bluff over a younger girl, before a ring of classmates, and one loses an eye. choice The papers call it "a duel for the Rose Bride". choice

30 December. The Senate, after readings on 21, 26 and 27 December, passes a short law, promulgated on the 30th, that makes it a crime to issue or accept a challenge (six months to two years), to fight a duel (two to five years), to act as a second or witness "under whatever name", or knowingly to lend the ground; mocking a man for refusing a challenge is punished as defamation. It was passed, in the words of the upper house's legislative bureau today, "for fear that the Western custom of duelling would take root". documented In this timeline the law's text mentions no novel, as no Meiji law would. But the article on lending the ground was read by everyone as aimed at the gardens of girls' schools, and the newspapers called it "the Utena law", a name it has kept. choice It is still in force; police used it in January 2026. documented

1890The settlement

1 July. Japan's first general election, for a lower house elected by about one person in a hundred: some 450,000 men, out of a population of nearly forty million. documented

25 July. The Law on Assembly and Political Associations bars women, along with soldiers, police, teachers, students and minors, from political meetings and political associations. documented In this timeline the women who object are more numerous and more organised than in ours, because they have been meeting for five years in the reading circles, letter-writing clubs and Christian societies that grew up around the serial, and because the government has given them a story about themselves to resent. inference The protests do not change the law. documented for the outcome in our history; inference that it would hold here too, since the oligarchs did not need women's consent for anything.

30 October. The Imperial Rescript on Education: filial piety, conjugal harmony, loyalty, and the duty of every subject to offer himself to the state. Schools begin reciting it in the following months, before the emperor's portrait. documented

11 November. The Ryōunkaku, the twelve-storey tower in Asakusa, opens with Japan's first electric lift, two cars for ten people each, which run from the ground to the eighth floor. Admission is eight sen. The lift breaks down from the first day and is stopped in May 1891; the owners fill the dead stairwell with photographs of a hundred geisha and let the climbers vote. documented Visitors, who have read about the council's lift for five years, call it "Utena's lift", and the nickname outlives it. choice The first Diet opens on 29 November. Its Speaker is Nakajima Nobuyuki, Kishida Toshiko's husband; its Vice-Speaker is Tsuda Mamichi, who in 1875 had written against equal rights for husband and wife and against votes for women. documented Women may not vote, attend political meetings or join parties; they may petition the Diet and, within days of its opening, watch it from its galleries, which is all the political rights they have. documented Even the galleries are closed to women at first. In October twenty-three women, Sasaki Toyoju and Shimizu Toyoko among them, write to the two liberal parties to ask why, and on 3 December the House lifts the ban. documented In this timeline the October letter is followed by a petition of several thousand signatures, presented by a delegation of former mission-school girls wearing black jackets over their kimono. choice On 20 January 1891 the temporary Diet building burns down before dawn, and the lower house moves into the Tokyo Jogakkan, a girls' school then housed in the old Imperial College of Engineering. In March the lower house passes a bill to let women attend political meetings; the House of Peers rejects it. documented

Shadow play · Part VI

C-koExtra! Extra! Extra!

C-koScandal at the house with the old pine!

C-koLittle sister has climbed the family tree!

C-ko(Little sister, from the top.) Everybody bow! I'm the prince up here!

C-koThe uncles sit in council all night, and the cat eats everybody's fish!

C-koNext morning, a board nailed to the trunk!

C-ko"BOYS ONLY, AS IT HAS BEEN SINCE THE BEGINNING OF TIME."

C-ko(Big brother, wagging a finger.) We never needed a board till you went up there!

A-koThen why is the paint still wet?

(The board slides off the trunk. Carved in the bark beneath it, older and deeper: eight women's names.)

VII

Chronicle, 1890–1912

The backlash, the underground, and the girls who grew up on it

From 1890 the state built the family it wanted: a household under its head, a wife who was a minor in law, daughters schooled to be good wives and wise mothers. Utena could not stop any of it. What it did, through the twenty years in which the new order took hold, was to supply that order's daughters with a counter-story and a private language, in dormitories the state had built and could not see into.

1888–1898Women on the stage

1888–1898. The craze for the girl chanters of gidayū. Takemoto Ayanosuke, who had grown up with a boy's crop, was called "the man-woman" and performed in a boy's topknot, and her rival Kotosa, both in their early teens, drew student fan clubs, the dōsuru-ren, who chased their rickshaws and fought over their fallen hairpins; in 1900 the Yorozu chōhō denounced the young men "crazed by such wenches as the girl chanters" as "the great corruption of youth". documented In this timeline a gidayū text of the duel in the forest garden, newly written in 1889, is Ayanosuke's most requested piece. choice

August 1890. The Metropolitan Police announce that men and women may henceforth act together on the same stage, ending a ban that went back to the Edo period; the critic Okamoto Kidō, who recorded it, remembered that the papers printed it in small type and that no major theatre hired an actress. The same month's theatre regulations create a class of "small theatres". documented

1891–1893. The first of the small theatres, the Misaki-za, opens in Kanda on 27 June 1891, on a former army drill ground. In 1893 it becomes the home of a permanent company of women players, the heirs of the women who had performed kabuki for the shogun's and the lords' inner quarters, under Ichikawa Kumehachi, "the female Danjūrō", Danjūrō IX's only woman pupil, whom he expelled that same year for playing Kanjinchō without his leave. For more than ten years the Misaki-za plays every month, to houses with many young women in them, and students, and literary men. documented In this timeline the company's first new piece, in the autumn of 1893, is Utena, the first all-woman staging by a standing company in a Tokyo theatre: Kumehachi, forty-six and famous for her men, plays Akio, and the pit fills with schoolgirls in black jackets over their kimono. choice Kidō, who saw Kumehachi play the mountain witch in 1890, wrote that she had been born forty years too early. documented In this timeline the Misaki-za Utena is revived almost every year while the company lasts. choice It is the bridge between the Edo women's troupes and the Takarazuka of 1914. inference

1891–1893The reaction

January 1891. At the First Higher Middle School the Christian teacher Uchimura Kanzō hesitates to bow low enough before the emperor's signature on the Rescript on Education, and is hounded from his post; a campaign against Christianity as disloyal follows, led by the philosopher Inoue Tetsujirō. documented In this timeline lesser pamphleteers of the campaign, never Inoue himself, cite Utena as an example of what Christian schools teach girls: to love each other and to despise the household. The mission schools on the Bluff, where the serial first found a following, lose pupils for the rest of the decade, as many real mission schools did. documented for the decline; choice for the pamphlets.

January 1891. Shimizu Toyoko, writing as Shikin, publishes The Broken Ring in the Jogaku zasshi: a woman who leaves a husband who keeps a mistress, pulls the stone out of the ring he gave her, and goes on wearing it broken as a reminder of what she will spend her life working to end. It is counted as the first feminist novel in Japanese. documented In this timeline every reader of 1891 sees the ring as the answer to Utena's: a ring not from a prince but from a husband, not a key to a castle but a broken thing kept on purpose. inference Critics here count it the first important work of a genre that will last for a century, fiction read in conversation with Utena, though Shikin never names the serial. choice

1891–1892. The Civil Code controversy. Hozumi Yatsuka's essay, "If the Civil Code comes out, loyalty and filial piety will perish", rallies the opponents of the French-inspired draft; in 1892 the Diet votes to postpone it. documented In this timeline the code's opponents use the serial's last chapter as an image of what the liberal draft would produce: daughters walking out of their brothers' houses. choice The postponement passes, as it did. documented

1893. The Ministry of Education instructs the girls' schools under its supervision to forbid "novels harmful to morals" in dormitories. choice (Part XIX, document 9, imitates the rules that follow.) In our history the ministry sent the girls' high schools a confidential instruction to tighten discipline over their pupils' daily lives in September 1902, and in June 1906 the minister, Makino Nobuaki, told every school to forbid, "inside or outside school", reading that preached "pessimism" or depicted "base passions", and complained of students who "agonise over fantasies". documented In this timeline the same steps come nine years earlier, with one book in view. The ban does what bans do. A book that girls had read openly by day, whatever they did after lights out, becomes one that they read only under the blankets, lend in wrapped covers and quote in code. inference

1890sThe rose and the bride

The girls' school friendship culture that our history calls "S", after "sister", took shape in the 1900s and 1910s: intense attachments between older and younger girls, exchanged letters and photographs, and a moral panic about them. documented (Part XXI) In this timeline it takes shape a decade earlier, in the 1890s, in the mission schools and the new public girls' schools, and it takes its forms from Utena. inference An older girl and a younger one are a "prince" and a "bride"; the relationship itself is "a rose" (薔薇), and to have one is to be "engaged"; a white rose left in a desk is a proposal; a cheap brass ring with a rose stamped on it is worn on a ribbon under the collar. choice In our history, as a girls' magazine reported in 1910, the proposal was a purple or crimson ribbon delivered by the older girl's friends, which the younger accepted by tying it in her hair. documented In this timeline rose became the code word for love between girls, and stayed one. One consequence lies far ahead: in our timeline "rose" (bara) became Japanese slang for gay men after a men's magazine took the name in 1971, and "lily" (yuri) became the word for love between women in answer to it. In this one the flowers are the other way round. documented for our history's terms; choice for the inversion.

Speech went the same way. The new schoolgirl slang of the 1890s, with its clipped -teyo and -dawa endings, appalled older writers in both timelines. documented In this one it also kept Utena's boku, which girls used among themselves and dropped at home. The magazine Shōjo no tomo would later be famous for its readers' "kimi and boku" slang; in this timeline that is simply how its readers' mothers talked. documented for the magazine's slang; choice for the rest.

1894–1899War, and the code

1894–95. The war with China. The stage turns to war plays, Kawakami Otojirō's troupe among them, and the serial's audience turns to the news. documented for the war plays. The only wartime Utena is a shinpa piece in which the prince's sword is a Japanese officer's; it closes in a week. choice

1896. Wakamatsu Shizuko dies of tuberculosis in February, five days after the Meiji Girls' School burns; Higuchi Ichiyō dies of the same disease in November, at twenty-four, having published Child's Play (Takekurabe), whose heroine Midori, a spirited girl at the centre of the neighbourhood children's quarrels, is destined to follow her sister into the licensed quarter. documented In this timeline critics have argued for a century over whether Midori is Ichiyō's answer to Utena: the girl who holds her own among the children, and whom the adult world is waiting to take. choice Nothing in Ichiyō's diaries settles it.

16 July 1898. The family and succession books of the Civil Code take effect: the household head controls the family's property and members' marriages and residence; the wife is legally incapable of most acts without her husband's consent; the household passes to the eldest son. documented (Part XXI) In this timeline the articles on wives' legal incapacity are known, within a year, as "the Rose Bride articles": the wife, like Anthy, can do nothing on her own account and belongs to whoever holds the household. choice The name does not change the law. It changes how the law is talked about for the next thirty-three years, until the articles go in 1931, and it is the reason they are the first thing reformers try to remove (Part IX). inference

1899. The Girls' High School Order requires every prefecture to have a secondary school for girls, and the education minister, Kabayama Sukenori, defines its aim as making "wise mothers and good wives"; Japan's first modern Copyright Act is passed and Japan joins the Berne Convention. documented Under the new act an anonymous or pseudonymous work is protected for thirty years, counted from the year after publication, or, for a work issued in parts, from the year after its last part. Works published before 1899 without registration under the old law, its drafter explained, had no rights to carry over. documented For Utena that means two texts with two fates. The newspaper text had never been registered and was anyone's to reprint once the old law's two years of the editor's control had passed, and pirated editions of chapters 1–33 had been on sale since the late 1880s. Shun'yōdō's book of Part Four (1887) and its collected edition (1888), registered by the publisher with the paper's serial editor named in the colophon as compiler, since the book laws wanted a responsible name there and the author would give none, now run on until the end of 1917 and 1918. choice Shun'yōdō and the Tokyo Asahi, as heir to the paper that had issued the first three parts, dispute the rights in 1900–02 and settle by sharing them until the term runs out (Part XII). choice

1900–1905The second generation

10 March 1900. The Public Peace Police Law keeps women out of political associations and political meetings, in its Article 5. documented The first organised campaign against Article 5, by socialist women, would begin in 1905. documented In this timeline it begins in 1900, with a petition circulated through the alumnae associations of girls' schools, whose members had, in many cases, first met in a "rose". choice It fails. inference

Summer 1900. In Paris, the actress Kawakami Sadayakko plays at Loïe Fuller's theatre at the Exposition Universelle, and plays a fragment of Utena among her pieces (Part VIII). choice

1901. Japan Women's University opens; Kishida Toshiko dies in May. documented Her obituaries in this timeline mention the authorship theory, which she never addressed in public. choice

1902. Shōjo kai, the first magazine for girls, appears, followed by Shōjo sekai (1906), Shōjo no tomo (1908) and Shōjo gahō (1912). documented In this timeline the editors who founded them knew exactly whom they were selling to: the daughters and younger sisters of the girls who had read Utena in 1885, now organised into a reading public by seventeen years of a book their schools had kept out of the dormitories since 1893. inference What the girls' magazines printed most, after poetry and readers' letters, was a genre with no equivalent in our timeline: the "Anthy story" (アンシー物), in which a girl leaves home with a trunk and a small animal and goes looking for someone she has lost. Hundreds were printed between 1902 and 1930, almost all by amateurs. choice They are where the Japanese girls' novel learned its first plot.

1903. Kosugi Tengai's Makaze koikaze in the Yomiuri: it opens with a schoolgirl's bicycle crash, and its hero, a viscount's adopted son engaged to her best friend, a girl who calls the heroine "elder sister", falls in love with her. documented In this timeline it is the first best-seller about schoolgirls that is not about Utena, and its success is read as proof that the genre had outgrown its source. inference

1904–1905. The war with Russia. Thousands of Chinese students come to Tokyo, among them a young woman from Shaoxing named Qiu Jin, who wears Western men's clothes, carries a Japanese sword, and goes home to plan a revolution (Part VIII). documented

1905–1912Toward the Bluestockings

1905–1909. The women of the socialist Heiminsha, among them Sakai Tameko and Nishikawa Fumiko, petition the Diet year after year to amend Article 5; Sekai fujin, founded in January 1907 by Fukuda Hideko, who as Kageyama Hideko had been arrested in the Osaka Incident, campaigns for it until July 1909, when the authorities crack down on its thirty-eighth number and the paper, already short of money, closes. In March 1908, by the usual account, the lower house passes an amendment based on Fukuda's petition and the House of Peers rejects it the next day. Nothing changes until 1922. documented In this timeline the petitions carry many more signatures, because the girls' school networks of the 1890s sign alongside the socialists, and a member of the Peers quotes Utena on the floor, against them. choice

1908. Kawakami Sadayakko and her husband open the Imperial Actresses' Training Institute in Tokyo, for girls of sixteen to twenty-five with two guarantors; Ichikawa Kumehachi, who had founded a smaller actresses' school with a dancer two years before, teaches there. When the new Imperial Theatre opens in March 1911, actresses from the institute, now its training school, appear in its first production, Mori Ritsuko among them. documented The institute's first public performance in this timeline is the ball scene from Utena, with women in both parts. choice

25 January 1911. Kanno Suga, journalist, socialist and the only woman among the twelve executed for the alleged plot against the emperor, is hanged. documented The government's case against the "High Treason" defendants reaches into what they read; in this timeline the prosecution's list of seized books includes a copy of Utena seized at her lodgings, its chapter 38 marked in pencil by a hand nobody has identified. choice No one has seen it since 1945.

September 1911. Hiratsuka Raichō and four other young women found Seitō, the "Bluestocking", whose first issue opens with Yosano Akiko's poem on "the day the mountains move" and then prints Raichō's manifesto: "In the beginning, woman was the sun." documented The same month, on 22–24 September, the Literary Society gives Ibsen's A Doll's House on the private stage in Tsubouchi Shōyō's garden, and in November at the Imperial Theatre, with Matsui Sumako as Nora, the wife who leaves her husband's house and slams the door. documented In our history Nora became the emblem of the "new woman" in Japan. In this one she arrives as a second Anthy, and a reviewer calls her "the Norwegian Anthy": a woman who leaves with no destination, twenty-four years after the first one did. choice The comparison is not flattering to Nora, who has a husband to slam the door on. Anthy had only a brother and a world.

1912. Otake Kazue, a painter's daughter of nineteen who joins Seitō that year under the boy's name Kōkichi and wears men's kimono, falls in love with Raichō, who calls her "my boy"; their affair, her glass of "five-coloured liquor" at a bar and a visit to a Yoshiwara brothel to see the women there make her the press's favourite "new woman", and she leaves the society in October. documented The papers in this timeline do not need to invent a nickname for Kōkichi. Every reader already has one. choice On 30 July the Meiji emperor dies. documented

Shadow play · Part VII

B-ko(A matron, with a lamp.) Inspection! Desk lids up! …And what is this?

A-koA white rose, Miss.

B-koFrom whom?

A-koMy prince, Miss.

B-koA prince! Is he rich?

A-koVery, Miss. Two hair ribbons and a bicycle.

B-koAnd you're engaged?

A-koRing on a ribbon, Miss. Under the collar.

B-koHow modest! A model wife in the making!

A-koDo you know? Do you know…

B-ko…how to read a rose?

(The matron sweeps on down the row. In every desk, a white rose.)

VIII

Abroad

Paris, the Chinese students of Tokyo, Seoul, and the long way round to Europe's girls

Utena travelled by two roads. One ran west through Yokohama's foreign colony and the Japonisme of Paris, and made the book a minor classic of European modernism and a private text of Europe's women. The other ran through the Chinese and Korean students who came to Tokyo in their thousands after 1900, and made it part of the history of revolution in East Asia, in the sense its title meant.

The foreign settlement

The first Westerners to read the serial were the ones who lived beside it: the missionary teachers of the Bluff, whose pupils were reading it under the bedclothes. In this timeline a short-lived English-language weekly of the Yokohama settlement prints a paragraph about "a curious native romance of a girls' school" in the summer of 1885, and a longer, disapproving notice by a missionary in 1886. choice The serial's foreign reputation begins there, as gossip about what Japanese girls were reading, and the gossip is carried home on furlough.

The foreigners' handbooks followed. In this timeline a missionary's guide to Japanese reading, published in Yokohama in 1891 by a writer otherwise forgotten, gives it a short and sardonic paragraph, as a work every schoolgirl admired and no critic would defend. choice

Paris, 1900

The actress Kawakami Sadayakko, a former Tokyo geisha whose patrons had included Itō Hirobumi and Saionji Kinmochi, was billed as the star of her husband's touring company in San Francisco in May 1899 without being told, and found herself an actress. In the summer of 1900 the company played at Loïe Fuller's theatre at the Paris Exposition Universelle; Rodin, by her biographer's account, asked to sculpt her and was refused; André Gide went again and again and wrote that it was "beautiful as Aeschylus"; Picasso drew her; and a kimono-like "Yacco" dress became a fashion. documented Her company's pieces were melodramas built for foreigners, with a geisha's death scene at their centre. documented In this timeline the company adds a short piece cut from Utena: the duel in the forest garden, with Sadayakko as Utena in a cadet's jacket and a younger actress as the Bride, who never speaks. Paris had come to see a geisha die and was shown a girl win (Part XIX, document 10). choice Tokyo, reading the reviews, enjoyed the joke that Paris could not see: the actress playing the girl who defeats the academy's council and defies its master had been the favourite of two of the most powerful men in Japan, and one of them was the man every reader took for Akio. inference

The translation followed quickly. Judith Gautier, novelist and Orientalist, had published Poèmes de la libellule, French versions of Japanese verse, in 1885, and in 1900 she and the composer Louis Bénédictus transcribed the music of Sadayakko's dances for publication; in 1910 she became the first woman elected to the Académie Goncourt. documented In this timeline she brings out La Fiancée des roses in 1902, from a literal version by a Japanese student in Paris. choice Her 1885 poems are often said to have been made from literal versions supplied by Saionji Kinmochi, which, if true, gives the book's French career a pleasing symmetry. documented for the claim being made; whether it is true is unverified. Gautier's version is free, lush and abridged: she cuts most of the comic chapters and all of the curry. It is the version Europe read for twenty years. choice

The women of the salons

In Paris in the first decade of the century a circle of women writers, many of them foreign, made a public culture of love between women: Natalie Barney's salon, the poet Renée Vivien, the young Colette on the stage. documented In this timeline La Fiancée des roses becomes one of that circle's books. It is the one modern novel they know in which two girls reach for each other's hands across a coffin lid, and in which the man is the villain without being the point. inference Copies passed hand to hand; "a reader of the Fiancée" became, for a generation of Parisians, a discreet way to describe a woman. choice The English version of 1911, Utena; or, The Rose Bride, by a translator who signed only her initials, carried the same reputation to London and New York. choice

The Demian question

In 1919 a German novel called Demian appeared under the pseudonym Emil Sinclair; its author, Hermann Hesse, was named only the next year. Its most quoted passage says that the bird fights its way out of the egg, that the egg is the world, and that whoever would be born must first destroy a world. documented In our history that passage is where the 1997 anime got its creed, as its director said. documented (makers' statement) In this timeline the creed was printed in Tokyo in 1885, and a German translation of Utena (from Gautier's French) had appeared in 1909. choice When Demian reached Japanese readers, they noticed. Whether Hesse, who was steeped in Asian thought, had read the German Utena is one of the minor scholarly quarrels of the twentieth century; his papers do not say, and both books were published under false names, which delights everyone who writes about it. choice

Butterfly

Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème (1887), John Luther Long's story "Madame Butterfly" (1898) and Puccini's opera (1904) made the self-sacrificing Japanese woman who waits for her Western lover and dies of it the West's image of Japanese womanhood for a century. Loti took his own rented "wife", a young woman named Okane, in Nagasaki for a month in the summer of 1885, while Part One of the serial was running in Tokyo. documented Nothing in this timeline stops them being written. inference What changes is that they have a rival. From 1902 Western critics who write about Butterfly, more of them each year and most of them once the English version appears in 1911, have read, or have been told about, a Japanese novel in which the girl who looks like Butterfly, the smiling, obedient Anthy, turns out to be the most dangerous person in the book and walks out at the end. The stereotype is no weaker in the opera house. It is a little weaker outside it, especially among the women who read the Fiancée. inference

The other road: Tokyo's Chinese students

The modern Chinese word for revolution, geming, came back to China from Japanese, where kakumei had taken on the sense of the European word; Liang Qichao, who fled to Japan in 1898, took it up there, and a story told by Sun Yat-sen's associate Chen Shaobai, which some historians doubt, has Sun adopting it after a Kobe newspaper called his party "revolutionaries" in 1895; the Kobe paper that has been found calls him only the "ringleader of the Canton rioters". documented for the story and the doubt. Liang complained in 1902 that students back from Japan went about crying "geming, geming" because the Japanese used the word, and the same year called for "a revolution in the world of fiction", on the ground that to renew the people of a nation one must first renew its fiction. documented He was writing in Yokohama, a few streets from the Bluff. His essay names no Japanese novel. In this timeline the Chinese students who read it in Tokyo know that he means the political novels he had been translating since 1898, Kajin no kigū first among them, and add the one about the girls' school on the hill to his list themselves. choice

By the end of 1905 there were about eight thousand Chinese students in Japan. documented Among them was Qiu Jin, a poet from Shaoxing who had left her husband to study in Tokyo, at the Practical Girls' School of Shimoda Utako, the same educator who ran the Peeresses' School. In Tokyo she wore Western men's clothes, and at a meeting of students from her province she drew a Japanese sword from her boot and drove it into the lectern. She went home in 1906, edited a women's journal and planned a rising, and was beheaded at Shaoxing on 15 July 1907. documented

In this timeline the Chinese women students in Tokyo read Utena in Japanese and, from 1906, in a Chinese translation printed in Tokyo, whose title is simply 少女革命: in Chinese, unambiguously, "A Girls' Revolution". choice Qiu Jin's own unfinished verse-novel Stones of the Jingwei Bird, in which five rich girls flee arranged marriages for Tokyo to study and make a revolution, is a work of our history, written in the women's ballad form of tanci, whose most famous heroine, Meng Lijun, had fled a forced marriage in men's clothes and risen to chief minister. documented In this one critics read its opening chapters as a Chinese answer to Utena's last: girls who leave the house, and know where they are going. choice The Qing authorities ban the Chinese Utena in 1907, after her execution, and its readers keep it the way the schoolgirls of Tokyo had. choice When women's units formed in the revolution of 1911, as they did in our history, one in Shanghai took a white rose for its badge. documented for the women's units; choice for the rose. In the 1940s Shanghai's all-female Yue opera companies, whose form had trained girls to play men since the first girls' class opened in the Shaoxing countryside in 1923, put a Chinese Utena on the stage. documented for Yue opera; choice for the play.

Seoul and Taipei

Korean women who studied in Tokyo after 1910 brought back the vocabulary of the "new woman" and were punished for living it. The painter and writer Na Hye-seok, a student in Tokyo from 1913 to 1918 who admired Hiratsuka Raichō and Ibsen's Nora, held the first solo exhibition of oil paintings by a woman in Korea, in Seoul in March 1921, was divorced in 1930, published a frank "confession" of her divorce in 1934, and died poor in 1948. documented In this timeline they also brought back Utena, read in Japanese, since Korean translations were not permitted by the colonial censors until the 1920s and then only in an expurgated form. choice For Korean readers under colonial rule, a story about a school run by an absent authority through sealed letters, in which those who resist are expelled and forgotten, was not difficult to read. inference Taiwanese girls in the colonial girls' high schools read it in Japanese as part of the same curriculum of reading that colonial schools did not set and could not stop. inference

Shadow play · Part VIII

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-ko(A lady, with a parasol.) Rickshaw! To the French boat. Gently, it's fragile.

A-ko(A student in a cap, climbing in beside her.) Rickshaw! To the Shanghai boat. Run, it's explosive.

B-koDarling, that's the same book.

A-ko(Leafing through the lady's copy.) Then where's the curry?

B-koCut. Too comic for Paris.

B-ko(Tilting the parasol over them both, very softly.) Tell me… are you a reader?

A-ko(Holding up her copy.) A READER? IT SAYS REVOLUTION ON THE COVER!

B-koShh!

A-koDo you know? Do you know…

B-ko…which road it took?

(At the fork the rickshaw comes apart down the middle, one wheel to each half.)

IX

Chronicle, 1912–1945

The public domain, the revue, the vote that passed, and the war that buried it

In the Taishō years Utena stopped being a banned book and became a common one: out of copyright, everywhere, on stage, on film and in the cheapest sets of books in Japan. Its readers grew old enough to sit in the Diet's galleries and lobby the Peers. For one decade this timeline's Japan moved towards giving women a share of power, and in 1931 it gave them one, in local government, fifteen years before ours did. Then the army took the country to war, and the book's title was censored, one word at a time.

1912–1922A common book

1913–1916. Seitō changes its rules in October 1913 from "the development of women's literature" to "the awakening of women", is banned for an issue in 1915 over an essay on abortion, and under its last editor, Itō Noe, argues in public about chastity, abortion and licensed prostitution until it stops in February 1916. documented In this timeline its contributors quote Utena as their grandmothers quoted the Classics, by chapter number. choice

1 April 1914. The girls' singing troupe that Kobayashi Ichizō had formed in July 1913 to sell tickets on his Minoo-Arima Electric Railway gives its first performance at the line's hot-spring resort in Takarazuka, in a theatre made from an indoor swimming pool. The bill is a children's opera of Momotarō, a comic piece and a dance; the run lasts two months, and some 1,100 people a day see it free with their bath. documented Kobayashi's company was a business idea before it was anything else, and in this timeline he knows exactly which story every girl in the Kansai already loves. Its first full-length Utena, an operetta in three acts that ends, as the kabuki of 1887 had, with the two girls reunited beyond the gate (Part XIV), opens in 1919, the year the company becomes the Takarazuka Girls' Opera and founds its music school. documented for the renaming and the school; choice for the operetta. In our history the girls played male parts from the first night, when Takamine Taeko was Momotarō; the Western men's dress of the later male-role star came with the move into the Grand Theatre in 1924, and the revue followed in 1927. documented In this one the girl who plays a prince, played by a girl, is the company's signature five years earlier, and has had a name since 1885. choice

1916–1924. Yoshiya Nobuko's Flower Tales, begun in 1916 as a reader's submission to Shōjo gahō and planned as seven stories, grow by readers' demand to more than fifty stories of girls' romantic friendships and make her the favourite writer of Japan's schoolgirls; her 1919 novel of two young women in a hostel attic depicts love between women openly. In January 1923 she meets the mathematics teacher Monma Chiyo, who becomes her partner for life; in 1957, adoption being the only legal tie open to them, Yoshiya adopts her. documented In this timeline Yoshiya is the greatest of the "Anthy story" writers, and the most open: her girls do not only leave home looking for someone, they find her. choice

1918. In July, fishermen's wives in Toyama start the rice riots that spread across the country and bring down a cabinet. documented Nothing links them to the book. The same summer the film theorist Kaeriyama Norimasa, whose 1917 book on the art of film drama called for screenplays, intertitles and actresses instead of female impersonators, shoots The Glow of Life with a young woman, Hanayagi Harumi, in the lead; the narrators who spoke over silent films in Japanese cinemas, whom his reforms would have made unnecessary, delay its release until September 1919, and Hanayagi is remembered as Japan's first film actress. documented In this timeline Kaeriyama also shoots, that summer, a two-reel duel scene from Utena, with women in every part, and the narrators cannot keep it off the screens for long: the cinema owners, besieged by people who already know the story and do not need it told, overrule them. It opens in November 1918. choice Women had appeared in Japanese films before, a women's-kabuki actress among them as early as 1908; but the first actress to reach the screen who had been cast on purpose, as a reform, in place of a female impersonator is therefore an Utena, ten months earlier than in our history. documented for 1908; inference for the rest.

1 January 1919. The last of Shun'yōdō's thirty years ran out at the end of 1918, and the whole of Utena, Part Four and the revised text included, now belongs to everyone. documented for the rule (Copyright Act of 1899, arts. 5, 8, 9 and 47); choice for the registration that set the clock. Within two years there are eleven editions in print, from cloth-bound sets to paper-covered booklets sold at railway kiosks for ten sen. choice

1920–1922. Hiratsuka Raichō, Ichikawa Fusae and Oku Mumeo found the New Women's Association (announced in November 1919, inaugurated at the Ueno Seiyōken on 28 March 1920) to amend Article 5. A revision passes the lower house in 1921 and dies in the Peers after a speech by Baron Fujimura Yoshirō. In February 1922 Sakamoto Makoto and Oku Mumeo call on the baron at his house in Nakano and win him over, and on 25 March, the last night of the session, the Peers pass the amendment at 11:50 p.m.: women may now attend and organise political meetings, though they still may not join parties. documented In this timeline the 1921 revision does not die in the Peers: it passes, after a member reads out the creed of the chick and the egg in the chamber and two dozen peers' wives watch from the gallery. choice The ban on party membership stays, as it did. inference

1923–1931The decade of the vote

1 September 1923. The Great Kantō Earthquake and the fires after it destroy most of Tokyo and Yokohama, the Bluff included, and kill more than a hundred thousand people. documented The fire takes the Home Ministry's censorship records too, so that nothing survives of the files on the serial's suspension. documented for the loss of the records; inference for what they held. The Tokyo Asahi's building burns, and with it all but twenty-three leaves of the serial's manuscripts (Part XVII). choice On 16 September army police murder the anarchist Ōsugi Sakae, his partner Itō Noe and his six-year-old nephew. documented

1925. On 29 March the Diet passes the law giving the vote to all men of twenty-five, and Ichikawa Fusae writes in her diary that she will remember the day as the one on which women's political rights were taken away. On 22 April the Peace Preservation Law is promulgated, and from 12 May it is a crime to organise against the "national polity" or private property. documented The word "revolution" becomes, in practice, a police word. inference

1926–1927. The "one-yen book" boom. In November 1926 the near-bankrupt publisher Kaizōsha offers a thirty-seven-volume set of modern Japanese literature by subscription at one yen a volume, about two per cent of a university graduate's first month's pay, and 230,000 people subscribe, so many that the set grows to sixty-three volumes; its first volume is Ozaki Kōyō. Other houses follow, Shun'yōdō with a sixty-volume set of Meiji and Taishō literature from June 1927. documented In this timeline Shun'yōdō's set opens with the book it had published in 1887, and its Utena volume outsells every other in the set. choice A generation of young women who had never seen the serial reads it now, in standard type without ruby, as Shōjo Kakumei.

1930–1931. The women's suffrage movement reaches its high point. In May 1930 a members' bill to give women civic rights in local government passes the lower house and is shelved by the Peers. In February 1931 the Minseitō cabinet brings in its own limited bill: women of twenty-five may vote in city, town and village elections, and may hold local office only with their husband's consent. It passes the lower house; the House of Peers rejects it. After 1933 no women's suffrage bill is even tabled. documented

In this timeline the Peers pass it. choice This is the largest single divergence in the document, so the case for it in full:

  • The real bill had the government behind it, passed the lower house, and failed in a chamber of hereditary and appointed men who were persuadable: the same chamber had killed the Article 5 revision in 1921 and passed it in 1922, after two women talked one baron round. documented
  • The pressure in this timeline is heavier. The women lobbying the Peers in March 1931 are the daughters of the Peers' own households, schooled in the same girls' schools for forty years; many of the Peers' wives had been "engaged" in a dormitory rose. inference
  • The bill's opponents had relied on the argument that Japanese women did not want the vote. In a country whose best-loved novel ended with a young woman walking out of her brother's house and through the gate on her own, that argument was harder to make with a straight face. inference

The bill passes the Peers by a narrow margin in March 1931, as the government drafted it, husband's-consent clause and all. choice The same session, riding the same majority, passes a short members' bill that repeals the wife's legal incapacity, "the Rose Bride articles" of 1898, taking its text from the outlines for reforming the family law that the government's own advisory council had drawn up in 1925 and 1927 and that, in our history, were never enacted. documented for the council's outlines and their fate; choice for the rest. Japanese wives in this timeline become legally capable adults in 1931, sixteen years before they did in ours (1947). inference

18 September 1931. Officers of the Kwantung Army blow up a stretch of railway near Mukden and begin the conquest of Manchuria. documented Nothing in this history prevents it. inference From here on, every divergence is fought against the current.

1932–1945The shell closes

1932–1933. Kawashima Yoshiko, a Manchu princess raised in Japan who had cut her hair and taken to men's clothes after a suicide attempt at seventeen, becomes a celebrity as "the beauty in men's dress": Muramatsu Shōfū's novel based on her runs in Fujin kōron and is a hit by 1933, and in February 1933 the Asahi reports her appointment to command a militia in Jehol. documented In this timeline the papers call her "the Utena of Manchuria", and the book's most dangerous image, the girl who becomes a prince, is put to work for the empire. choice She was shot as a traitor in Beijing in 1948. documented

1933. Women vote and stand in city, town and village elections for the first time since a few women household heads voted in a ward of Kōchi and a neighbouring village in 1880–84. documented for Kōchi. Some 300 are elected across Japan, most to village assemblies, a handful to city councils. choice In June the women of the Shōchiku revue strike against wage cuts and dismissals under the eighteen-year-old Mizunoe Takiko, the short-haired star of men's parts whose fan club had some 20,000 members; about 230 of them barricade themselves in an inn at the Yugawara hot springs, their Osaka colleagues occupy a temple on Mount Kōya, and the strike ends with concessions on pay and days off. documented In this timeline their banners carry the last line of the creed. choice

1935. A revue star, Saijō Eriko, and a cross-dressed heiress, Masuda Fumiko, attempt a love-suicide together; the press reports it as a lesbian elopement and casts the heiress as a woman who betrayed her class's duty to be a good wife and wise mother. documented In this timeline the panic is louder and more political, because its target is not only the revue but the most popular novel in the country, and because the women it accuses now vote. inference The Home Ministry presses the revues to cut their cross-dressed roles; the Takarazuka Utena is withdrawn in 1936. choice (In our history Mizunoe recalled that by about 1940 the authorities had forbidden her to appear in men's clothes at all. documented, from her memoir.)

1937. War with China. A reprint of the novel is permitted only if the word "revolution" is removed throughout, title included (Part XIX, document 13). choice Removed, not blanked. For two decades publishers had blanked dangerous words with circles and crosses to avoid bans, "socialism" and "anarchism" even in fiction; but the censors distrusted the blanks as an invitation to guess, and in the autumn of 1936 a national conference of the thought police decided to stamp them out. By the summer of 1937 they had almost vanished from print. documented From 1937 the book is sold, when it is sold at all, as Shōjo Utena, "Girl Utena", with nothing on the cover to show that a word is gone, and its readers, who know perfectly well which word it is, write it back in by hand. choice

1939–1940. The illustrator Nakahara Jun'ichi, whose big-eyed girls fill the girls' magazine Shōjo no tomo, is driven off its pages in 1940 by military pressure, his girls called decadent and unhealthy. documented In this timeline the 1939 printing of Utena, the last before the censor strikes "girl" from its title in 1940, has his illustrations, and his Anthy, all eyes, is the image of her the post-war decades inherit. choice In our history Nakahara's girls' illustration of the 1950s is one of the acknowledged sources of the 1997 anime's look. documented (makers' statement)

1940. The political parties dissolve into the Imperial Rule Assistance Association; the Women's Suffrage League dissolves itself on 21 September; and in October the Takarazuka Girls' Opera becomes the Takarazuka Opera, the word "girls" (shōjo) struck from its name, and every member is enrolled in the National Defence Women's Association. documented In this timeline the censor's last instruction on the novel, in December, removes its other word too, and for the rest of the war the most popular book in Japan is called simply Utena. choice Local assemblies are not abolished, but the women in them are swept into the national women's organisations and their committees for savings, rationing and send-offs to the front. inference

1942. The women's organisations are merged into the Greater Japan Women's Association, to which every woman except the unmarried under twenty must belong; by March 1944 it counts 21.49 million members. documented In this timeline a few women councillors resign rather than serve on its local boards, and their names are remembered. Most do not. choice

1944–1945. The novel goes out of print, partly for want of paper and partly because no publisher will apply. choice Takarazuka's Grand Theatre gives its last performance on 4 March 1944, to crowds that police hold back with drawn swords, and becomes a naval barracks; the Tokyo Takarazuka Theatre has closed three days earlier. documented On 15 August 1945 the emperor broadcasts the surrender. documented

Shadow play · Part IX

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-koPrinter! This word. Out. Every page, and the cover.

A-koShall I leave a little circle where it was?

B-koCircles make people guess!

A-koA little cat?

B-koCats make them guess harder! Close it up!

B-koPrinter! Me again. The other word. Now nobody will ever know!

A-koShall I put a pencil in with every copy?

B-ko…What for?

A-koDo you know? Do you know?

B-koDo you know what's missing?

(On the secondhand stall, every copy has both words pencilled back in. One has a little cat.)

X

Chronicle, 1945–1989

The Occupation, the classroom, the manga, and the mountain that moved

After 1945 Utena stopped being contested and became compulsory. The Occupation's reforms gave Japanese women in this timeline back what they had briefly held, and more; the new schools put the last chapter in their textbooks; the girls' comics that grew out of the war's ruins borrowed its princes and its roses by the cartload. By 1970 it was a classic in the full, deadening sense, and the women's movement had to rediscover it, as every movement rediscovers the classics it was taught.

1945–1952Restoration, not a gift

October–December 1945. On 10 October the Shidehara cabinet decides to give women the vote; the next day MacArthur's list of five great reforms includes it. The Public Peace Police Law is abolished on 21 November, and on 17 December the revised election law gives the vote to every man and woman of twenty. documented In our history the first women in modern Japan to vote had been a few women household heads in Kamimachi, a ward of Kōchi, and the neighbouring village of Kodakasa, from 1880 until the government took the right away in 1884. documented In this one women had voted in local elections from 1933 until the war swallowed local politics, and some hundreds had sat in assemblies. choice The difference matters less in 1945 than later. For the next eighty years conservatives in our history could describe women's suffrage, with the rest of the post-war settlement, as something the Americans had imposed. In this timeline that argument is much harder to make, because women had voted for their city, town and village assemblies under the old constitution, and lived to tell their granddaughters so. inference

10 April 1946. The first general election with women voting. In our history 79 women stand and 39 are elected, 8.4 per cent of the house; about 13.8 million women vote, 67 per cent of those eligible. documented In this timeline 112 women stand, many of them former town and village councillors with their own local organisations, and 57 are elected. choice In the 1947 election the number of women in the lower house falls in both timelines, as the novelty fades and the parties reassert themselves: to 15 in ours, to 31 in this one. documented for 15; choice for 31.

22 April 1946. Takarazuka's Grand Theatre reopens with Carmen; its Tokyo theatre stays requisitioned, as the US Eighth Army's Ernie Pyle Theatre, closed to Japanese audiences, until 1955. documented In this timeline the company's Utena, withdrawn in 1936, returns that autumn, and becomes the piece every new male-role star must play once. choice

February–October 1946. In the Government Section of MacArthur's headquarters a twenty-two-year-old civilian who had grown up in Tokyo, Beate Sirota, drafts the articles on women's rights for the new constitution; most of her text is struck out, but Article 24, which says that marriage shall rest only on the mutual consent of both sexes and that family law shall be written for "individual dignity and the essential equality of the sexes", survives from her draft. documented In this timeline the article reads the same, word for word. choice What changes is how it is received: in the Diet's debate on the constitution that summer, a woman member elected in April reads out the last page of chapter 39, the Bride walking out of the gate, and says that this is what Article 24 is for. choice She is an invented person; the article's history in our timeline is not.

1946–1948. The Occupation's censors ban 236 Japanese films as militarist on a single day in November 1945, forbid sword-fighting films as "feudal", and keep the great revenge play Chūshingura off the stage until 1947; a censor viewing a 1946 romantic comedy objects that it has no kiss and orders one added. documented In this timeline a studio's 1946 film of Utena is at first refused as a sword-fighting picture. The producers answer that it is the story of a girl who refuses an arranged engagement and wrecks a feudal institution to free another girl from it, and the censors, after some discussion, approve it, on condition that the duels be shortened. choice It is released in 1947, the first sword-fighting film made in Japan after the war. choice

March 1947. Ichikawa Fusae, the suffragist, is purged by the Occupation for her wartime place on the board of the Patriotic Press Association of Greater Japan (Dai Nippon Genron Hōkokukai), the government's body of critics and commentators, and stays purged until 1950. documented It happens in this timeline too; a movement that had won something before the war had also collaborated more, and was purged more. inference

1 January 1948. The revised Civil Code takes effect and the household system is abolished: no head of house, no single heir, marriage by the consent of the two parties alone. documented In this timeline the wife's incapacity had gone in 1931. The rest of the household goes now, as in ours. inference

1950–1969The classic

1950s. The post-war reform of the writing system, with its new kana spelling and reduced character list, makes most Meiji fiction hard going for the young, and the publishers reissue the classics they can sell in modern spelling. documented for the reform. Utena is among the first, and from 1952 the senior high school Japanese textbooks of every major publisher carry its first and last chapters, as they carry Sōseki and Ōgai. choice Every senior high school student from now on reads the gate scene in class, usually in the spring of the second year, and writes an essay on where Anthy is going; by the mid-1970s that means nine Japanese teenagers in ten. inference The textbook makes the book safe. Teachers learn to present it as a story of friendship and the triumph of individual conscience over feudal custom, which is the Occupation's reading, and to skip chapters 31 and 32. inference

January 1953 – January 1956. In our history Tezuka Osamu's Princess Knight runs in Shōjo Club: a princess born, by an angel's mischief, with both a boy's heart and a girl's, raised as a prince because only men may inherit the throne. Tezuka had grown up in Takarazuka, next door to the revue's leading male-role star of the 1930s, Amatsu Otome, and modelled Sapphire on an actress of women's roles he had seen play a man. documented In this timeline he draws an Utena in the same magazine in the same years, and the angel's mischief goes into it (Part XIV); Princess Knight and Sapphire do not exist (Part XV). choice The premise of his Utena, a girl kept from a throne because she is a girl, has an edge that our history's Princess Knight lacks, because his readers' own succession law had been written partly against their grandmothers' favourite novel. inference

24 May 1956. The Anti-Prostitution Law is enacted, its penalties taking effect in April 1958. documented As Part XVI says, nothing in this history touches it. inference

1950s–1960s. In our history women hold no more than a dozen seats in the lower house through these decades, two and a half per cent of it at most. documented In this timeline they hold between twenty-two and thirty, five or six per cent: still a parliament of men, but one in which every party has some women who have run local governments, and in which the women of the left and the right sometimes vote together on the household budget, schools and food safety. choice The Liberal Democratic Party, formed in 1955, governs in both timelines. documented for ours.

1970–1989The roses and the lilies

21 October 1970. Japan's first women-only demonstration; the group around Tanaka Mitsu hands out a hand-written leaflet called "Liberation from the Toilet", arguing that men had split women into mothers and sexual conveniences. The newspaper word for the movement, ūman ribu, had first appeared in the Asahi that month. documented In this timeline the marchers carry white roses, and the newspapers, which had spent a generation calling the book a harmless classic, rediscover that it is not. choice The ribu argument about the book is with the textbook reading: Anthy was not freed by a friend's conscience but by herself, and only after the friend had been struck down by the institution that the textbooks praised as "school life". inference

1971. Two firsts. A small group of women in Tokyo founds the Wakakusa no Kai, Japan's first lesbian circle, which meets monthly in an apartment and over five years has some five hundred members. documented In this timeline there had been such circles since the 1920s, disguised as alumnae poetry clubs with rose names; the Wakakusa no Kai is the first to say what it is. choice And in July a small Tokyo publisher, Itō Bungaku, launches Japan's first commercial magazine for gay men. In our history he called it Barazoku, "the rose tribe", and "rose" became the Japanese code word for men's love, with "lily" following in the 1970s as its counterpart for women. documented In this timeline the rose has meant love between girls for eighty years, and his magazine is called Yurizoku, "the lily tribe", instead. choice Every flower in Japanese slang is the other way round, and so are a great many shop signs. inference

1972–1976. In our history Ikeda Riyoko's The Rose of Versailles runs in Weekly Margaret from 1972 to 1973, its heroine Oscar a girl raised as a man who commands the queen's guard; Takarazuka stages it in August 1974, directed by the film star Hasegawa Kazuo, who had been trained as a kabuki player of women's roles, and well over a million people see it in its first three years. documented In this timeline Ikeda's commander is a man, because by 1972 a girl in boy's clothes was the oldest cliché in girls' fiction, and the revue's boom comes from its two-part Utena of 1974–75, under the same director (Parts XIV and XV). choice The women manga artists born around 1949, the "Year 24 Group", who remade the girls' comic in these years, had read Utena in their textbooks and their mothers' editions, and their turn to love stories between boys was, in this timeline, partly a flight from it (Part XV). documented for the group; choice for their reading.

1985–1986. Japan ratifies the UN convention on discrimination against women and passes an Equal Employment Opportunity Law that obliges employers only to "endeavour" not to discriminate in hiring and promotion. documented On 8 September 1986 Doi Takako becomes chair of the Japan Socialist Party, the first woman to lead a major Japanese party. documented In this timeline she takes the chair on the same day. choice

1987–1988. The first lesbian office in Tokyo opens, and a book of testimony from 234 women is published; in 1988 the writer Kakefuda Hiroko becomes the first woman to come out as a lesbian in the national media. documented In this timeline both are reported, as everything about women's love is reported in Japan, with a picture of a rose. inference

7 January 1989. The Shōwa emperor dies. documented On 23 July the Socialists, led by Doi, win the upper-house election on anger at the new consumption tax and a bribery scandal, the LDP loses its majority in that house, and so many new women are elected that the papers call it the "Madonna boom". Doi sums it up in four words: "The mountain has moved". She is quoting the first line of the first issue of Seitō, Yosano Akiko's "The day the mountains move is coming", seventy-eight years later. documented She says the same words in this timeline. choice It is the one place in this history where the two timelines meet in the same sentence, and it is a quotation from a poem, not from a novel.

Shadow play · Part X

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-ko(shyly) One rose, please. For a friend.

A-koWhat sort of friend?

B-koA tall one. He's very good at mahjong.

A-ko(snatching it back) Then not a rose, sir!

B-koBut it's the friendship flower. We read it at school.

A-koWhich bit did you read?

B-koThe beginning and the end. We skipped the middle.

A-koLilies for you, sir. The girls had the roses first.

A-koDo you know? Do you know?

B-koDo you know what your flower means?

(A march goes past the window. When it has gone, so have all the white roses.)

XI

Chronicle, 1989–2026

The adaptation, the succession, the certificate, a prime minister, and the house law again

The last thirty-seven years bring the two timelines closer than at any time since 1885, and one legal change pulls them apart again. The book's afterlife in this period is mostly a matter of adaptation and scholarship, and the most famous adaptation is one that exists in our timeline too, under a different description.

1989–1999The faithful adaptation

1990s. The women elected in the "Madonna boom" do not last; the Socialists collapse in the 1990s and the LDP returns. In 1996 the government's Legislative Council recommends letting married couples keep separate surnames, and the government never puts a bill for it before the Diet; in 2015 and again in 2021 the Supreme Court upholds the single-surname rule and leaves the question to the Diet. documented In this timeline both happen too. inference The first Tokyo Lesbian and Gay Parade is held in 1994. documented In this timeline its women's contingent carries roses, and its men's, lilies (Part X). choice

2 April 1997. TV Tokyo broadcasts the first of thirty-nine weekly episodes of an animated Revolutionary Girl Utena, made by J.C.Staff from an original story credited to a group calling itself Be-Papas, directed by Ikuhara Kunihiko with series composition by Enokido Yōji, original character concepts by Saitō Chiho, character designs by Hasegawa Shin'ya, and choruses for the duels by J.A. Seazer, who had written music for Terayama Shūji's underground theatre in the 1970s. It runs until 24 December. documented In our history it is an original story. In this one it is an adaptation of the Meiji classic, and the first episode goes out on the hundred and twelfth anniversary, to the day, of chapter 1. choice

Critics in this timeline call it the most faithful adaptation the book has ever had, and they are right in a way that only readers of this document can fully appreciate. After a hundred and ten years of reunions, angels, witches, jeeps and swordswomen (Part XIV), it follows the serial chapter by chapter, keeps every name and every unexplained thing and the ending, and takes a single liberty, the one every modern-dress version since 1926 had taken. It brings the furniture up to date, the customs as well as the machines. Akio's carriage becomes a red sports car; the magic lantern on the dome becomes a planetarium projector; the family register in chapter 31 becomes a chart of blood types; the phonograph becomes a tape recorder; the prize-riddle column becomes a late-night radio phone-in. choice Part IV's chapter entries, read backwards, are a list of the adaptation's changes. inference Older viewers who knew only the book complained that the car spoiled the Carriage Book, since a man who drove his own carriage in 1886 was a spectacle and a man who drives himself in 1997 is a commuter; they were reminded that Akio had been driving a car on screen since 1926. What shocked everyone else was the faithfulness: viewers who knew Utena from Takarazuka, Tezuka and the textbooks met chapter 38 for the first time. choice

What the makers said about the series in our history belongs to our history, and this document does not invent their words for the other one. choice Some of what they said reads strangely from here.
