The group's name, Be-Papas, was glossed by its makers as "let's become adults". documented (makers' statement) The director, asked in 2000 what it meant to revolutionise the world, answered that it means "to break the eggshell". documented (makers' statement) In a timeline in which those words had been printed in Tokyo in 1885, the creed of the chick and the egg would need no explanation, and the series' debts to Takarazuka and to the underground theatre of the 1960s, which its makers acknowledged, would be debts to two of the book's own descendants. inference The director has said that he dreaded the series being called a parody of Princess Knight or The Rose of Versailles, and Saitō Chiho, who drew the original character concepts, that its look derives from Versailles, which the director has called her view rather than his. documented (makers' statements) In this timeline neither of those works exists in the form he dreaded (Part XV), and the look of the 1997 Utena comes from a century of Utena pictures, from Yoshitoshi's cuts to Nakahara's Anthy to Tezuka's. inference

17–29 December 1997. A stage musical of Utena plays at the Hakuhinkan Theatre in Tokyo with an all-female cast, in the manner of Takarazuka. documented In this timeline it is the 1,000th-odd stage version since November 1885, and the first to use the anime's songs. choice In August 1999 the director's feature film, Adolescence of Utena, opens in cinemas; it retells the story differently, as the series' makers chose. documented In this timeline it is one more free version among thousands, and the end of a seventy-year-old joke: since 1926 every modern Utena had had a car in it, and in this one Utena becomes the car (Part XIV). choice

2000–2015The succession and the certificate

2004–2006. No boy has been born to the imperial family since 1965. In December 2004 Prime Minister Koizumi sets up an advisory panel on the Imperial House Law, and on 24 November 2005 it recommends opening the throne to women and to their descendants. The government prepares a bill. In February 2006 Princess Kiko's pregnancy is announced and the bill is dropped; her son Hisahito is born in September. documented In this timeline the question returns in earnest after a hundred and sixteen years with its old argument reversed. In 1886 the men who struck the female line out of the house law had not needed to say that a female succession would tell girls raised on Utena that they could be princes; the newspapers had said it for them. In 2005 columnists who support the bill point out that every girl in Japan has read Utena at school for fifty years, and that the country has survived it. choice The outcome is the same. inference A birth decided it in both timelines, and no novel could have.

5 November 2015. Shibuya ward in Tokyo issues Japan's first certificate recognising a same-sex partnership, to Higashi Koyuki and Masuhara Hiroko. Higashi had played men's roles in Takarazuka's Flower Troupe in 2005–06. documented In both timelines the first official recognition of a couple in Japan went to a woman who had been trained to play the prince. In this one, nobody thinks it a coincidence. inference

2016–2026The courts, a prime minister, and the house law

In our history, from February 2019 couples sue the state in five cities for the right to marry. District and high courts mostly find the present law unconstitutional, or in a "state of unconstitutionality"; in March 2025 the Osaka High Court becomes the fifth high court of five to say so; in November 2025 the Tokyo High Court, in a second suit, becomes the first to uphold the law. On 25 March 2026 the Supreme Court refers all six cases to its Grand Bench. As of October 2026 it has not ruled, and Japan has neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions. documented

In this timeline the courts get there sooner, and the Diet moves. The suits are filed in 2012; the Grand Bench rules in June 2023 that the Civil Code's failure to provide any form of legal union for same-sex couples violates Articles 14 and 24; and in 2024 the Diet passes a partnership law that gives registered couples most of the rights of marriage under another name. choice It is the second largest divergence in this document, and the case for it:

  • The courts of our history were already moving this way: by March 2025 every high court that had ruled had found the law unconstitutional. documented A few years' difference in when the suits are filed and how fast they climb is well within the range of real litigation. inference
  • In this timeline love between women has had a public name, a flower and a literature in Japan since the 1890s, and has been taught, at one remove, in every high school since 1952. Public opinion on same-sex unions is correspondingly ahead of ours, and a larger share of the Diet is women (below), who in both timelines support recognition at higher rates than men. inference
  • The result is a compromise of the kind the LDP makes when it must: a partnership law, not marriage. The word "marriage" stays where Article 24's drafters, and the conservative majority, left it. inference The couples who want the word keep suing.

21 October 2025. Takaichi Sanae, elected LDP president on 4 October, becomes Japan's first woman prime minister. She is a hard-line conservative who opposes letting married couples keep separate surnames, though from her marriage in 2004 until her divorce in 2017 she worked under her own name while legally bearing her husband's, and when she remarried him in 2021 he took hers. In February 2026 she wins a snap election outright. documented In this timeline the same woman takes office on the same day. choice Part XVI calls this the hardest of the convergences to defend. The defence is that Japan's prime ministers are chosen inside the governing party, by its factions and, in the end, by its members of the Diet, and that the LDP of this timeline, though it has more women in it than ours, is the same machine with the same rural base and the same internal ladder; the first woman to climb that ladder to the top was going to be the one the ladder favoured. inference A country whose best-loved novel is about a girl who wants to be a prince and is told she cannot, and whose first woman to rule it came from the party of the household and the throne, is not a contradiction. It is the novel's argument. inference

January 2026. Police in Tokyo arrest a man under the duelling law of 1889 for an arranged fight in Kabukichō the previous September, in which the other man died. documented In this timeline the headlines call it, as headlines have since 1889, an arrest under "the Utena law". choice

8 February 2026. In our history 68 women are elected to the 465-seat lower house, 14.6 per cent; in the upper-house election of July 2025 a record 42 were elected. documented In this timeline 104 women are elected to the lower house, 22.4 per cent. choice The World Economic Forum's gender-gap index for 2026 ranks our Japan 117th of 145 countries, held down above all by the share of women in politics. documented This timeline's Japan, with half as many women again in parliament and a long record of women in local government, would rank decidedly higher on the same index, though still in its lower half. inference

17 July 2026. The Diet passes the first substantive change to the body of the Imperial House Law since 1947, and it comes into force on 24 October. A princess who marries a commoner no longer has to leave the imperial family, though her husband and children do not join it. Men of the male line from the eleven branch houses that left the family in 1947 may be adopted into it, and their sons may inherit the throne. Women still may not. In the lower house the Communists are the only party to oppose it; in the upper house the Constitutional Democrats and some smaller parties oppose it, and it passes with more than three-quarters of the votes. Polls since 2005 had found most of the public in favour of letting a woman reign. documented In this timeline the same law passes in the same form, more narrowly, after weeks in which readers' letters to the newspapers quote the novel against it, and columnists who favour it answer that a house law is not a novel. choice A larger share of women in the Diet does not change the result: the bill is the government's, most of the opposition votes for it, and on the succession the governing party has set public opinion aside since 2006 in both timelines. inference What the law says, read from 1885, is the rule of 1889 with one concession: a princess may now stay in the family, and a prince must still be a man, so the state will adopt one sooner than let a princess become one. Every reader of the book recognises the argument. inference

October 2026. The serial, which began on 2 April 1885, is a hundred and forty-one years old. Its anonymous author has been out of copyright for over a century, most of its manuscripts burned in 1923, and its four volumes are on the reading list of every senior high school in the country. The schoolgirls who read it this year read it in class, in modern spelling, with notes. Some of them read it again at night, which is how it was meant to be read. inference

Shadow play · Part XI

C-koExtra! Extra! Extra!

C-koNews from our sweet shop! Big Sister is getting married!

C-koAnd she may stay at home after the wedding! Her husband may visit.

C-koBut the shop always goes to a son, and we haven't got any. So we're adopting some!

C-ko(sweetly) Welcome home, cousin! Now, where's your son?

C-ko(gruffly) I haven't got one.

C-ko(sweetly) You will have!

C-koAnd Big Sister has made every bean cake in the shop since she was six.

C-koOh, what are we going to do about the shop?

A-koGive it to your sister?

(A row of grown men in short trousers files in at the shop door, each with a name tag reading COUSIN.)

XII

The economy of the rose

A newspaper enriched, a flower bubble, a schoolgirl market, a railway's theatre, and a classic nobody owns

Novels change economies in small, specific ways: they sell newspapers, create fashions, move the prices of particular things, and give businesses a story to sell. Utena did all of these in this timeline, and none of them made its author rich. This Part follows the money, using documented prices and figures as the yardstick for the invented ones.

Money in 1885

A yen was a hundred sen, and from May 1885 the Bank of Japan's notes were convertible into silver; Japan moved to gold only in 1897. documented Some prices from the documented record, to measure the rest by:

ItemPriceWhen
A copy of a small illustrated newspaper1 sen1879 (the Osaka Asahi)documented
A month's subscription to a small paperabout 20 senc. 1875–85documented
A month's subscription to a big political paper50–70 senc. 1875–85documented
A shō (about 1.4 kg) of polished rice, retailabout 10 sen1885documented
A day labourer's daily wage16 sen1885documented
A woman silk reeler's daily wage11 sen1885documented
A maidservant's monthly wage75 sen1885documented
An issue of Jogaku zasshi5–10 sen1885–1904documented
Renting a scrapbook of a clipped newspaper serial from a lending library3 sen, half the fee for borrowing a printed bookearly 1900sdocumented
Admission to the Ryōunkaku tower8 sen1890documented
Tanabe Kaho's fee for her first novel33 yen 20 sen1888documented
Higuchi Ichiyō's first fee for a story11 yen 50 sen1892documented
The deposit a Tokyo newspaper had to lodge with the government1,000 yenfrom 1883documented
A fashionable rabbit at the height of the rabbit craze50 to 600 yen1872–73documented
A rabbit eleven days after Tokyo taxed rabbits a yen a head a month2 sen for a kit, 5 for a pregnant doeDecember 1873documented
Natsume Sōseki's salary as the Asahi's novelist200 yen a month1907documented

The paper the serial enriched

Jiyū no Tomoshibi was, by the dictionaries' account, for a time the best-selling paper in Tokyo in 1884–86; the Osaka Asahi, the country's commercial model, sold about 32,000 copies a day in 1885. documented In this timeline the Tokyo paper sells about 12,000 copies a day in March 1885, 18,000 when Part One ends in August, and about 30,000 at its peak in the summer of 1886, before the suspension. choice At a sen a copy, or a little less by subscription, the difference between 12,000 and 30,000 copies is some forty to sixty thousand yen a year in sales before costs, when the deposit the press law had demanded of a Tokyo paper since 1883 was a thousand. inference That is the measure of the serial's first economic effect: it made a Liberal paper that the deflation and the government were both trying to kill far richer for the three years it had left, and worth more when it was sold. When the Osaka Asahi's owners bought it in 1888 to make their Tokyo edition, as they did in our history, they bought a subscription list built by a novel. documented for the purchase; inference for the rest.

The serial had a second economy that the paper never saw. In the early twentieth century some lending libraries cut serials out of newspapers, pasted them into scrapbooks and rented them round the student boarding houses at three sen a time. documented In this timeline the practice begins with Utena, and the scrapbooks are the most rented item in Tokyo's lending libraries for three years, and the libraries' wear-worn clippings of chapter 31, cut from the copies of the confiscated issue that escaped the police, are what the 1886 suspension was really fighting. choice

The author was paid by postal money order, collected at Yokohama's main post office by a different payee each time (Part XVII), at about thirty yen a month while the serial ran, which is roughly what a newspaper's staff novelist could expect. Payments stopped when the paper gave up the serial in October 1886, and the author never claimed the fees for the book editions, which Shun'yōdō banked against the day someone did. Nobody ever has. choice

The rose bubble, 1886–1888

The rose was, in the 1880s, a Western curiosity with a Chinese name. Japanese gardeners had grown wild roses and a few Chinese ones for centuries, but the rose became a loved flower in Japan only after the Restoration, and a popular one only in the Taishō and Shōwa periods; until the 1900s it was not a symbol of romantic love in Japanese poetry. documented In this timeline it becomes one in the spring of 1886, all at once.

  • The boom. White roses sold as "Utena" go for a yen a plant, six days' pay for a labourer, and by 1887 for three; a deep red-violet sold as "the Bride" goes for five, then fifteen. Nurseries in Yokohama and in the old nursery villages of Somei and Komagome, where Edo's gardeners had bred the Somei-Yoshino cherry, import French and English stock by the crate. documented for the Somei nurseries; choice for the rest.
  • The fraud. By 1887 "black roses" for chapter 14 are selling at thirty yen. They are crimson roses grown in shade and treated with ink. choice
  • The crash. In the spring of 1888 a Komagome dealer who cannot pay for forty crates of French roses kills himself, the papers expose the black roses, and prices fall by nine-tenths in a month. choice It is a small crash, smaller than the rabbit crash of 1873, which a single prefectural tax brought on in less than a fortnight: a few dealers ruined, a few collectors embarrassed. inference
  • What it left. A dozen nurseries that know how to graft, grow and ship Western roses; a public that wants them; and a flower that means something. In our history the earliest nursery lists of rose varieties by name in Japanese library catalogues, single sheets issued by the Chōshun'en, the Kaikaen and Barashin, date from 1889–90, and the Yokohama nurseries built an export trade in Japanese lily bulbs that sent some twelve million bulbs abroad in 1908. documented In this timeline they also build a domestic trade in roses a generation before ours did, and by 1900 a rose bed is as standard in a girls' school garden as the chrysanthemum is in a temple's. choice

The schoolgirl market

The girls who read the serial were the first Japanese schoolgirls to be sold to as a group. inference In our history that market took shape with the girls' magazines of the 1900s, which sold to the new middle class's daughters at its own schools. documented In this timeline it starts in 1885, with three products:

  • Jackets. The tailors of Kanda and of Yokohama's Benten-dōri sell black serge "Utena jackets" cut for girls, to be worn over kimono, and from the late 1890s over hakama. By 1890 the jacket is the unofficial uniform of the Tokyo mission schools, and when the public girls' high schools set uniforms after 1899 several adopt a version of it. choice
  • Rings. Brass rings with a rose stamped on the bezel, made in Tokyo's metalworking quarters and sold for five sen at stalls near the schools, worn on a ribbon under the collar. The authorities call them a fad; the fad lasts sixty years. choice
  • Pictures. Single-sheet colour prints of scenes from the serial, then, as the print trade gave way to photography, photographs of the actresses who played Utena, and from October 1900, when private picture postcards were permitted, postcards. documented for the shift from prints to small photographs and for the postcard boom; choice for the subjects. The gidayū girl Takemoto Ayanosuke's photographs sold in great numbers around 1891; in 1921 street photographers' pictures of the Shōchiku film actress Kurishima Sumiko sold four thousand a day. documented Whoever played Utena at the Misaki-za in the 1890s sold more than Ayanosuke. choice

The stage and the railway

Most stage versions of Utena paid nothing to anyone but their casts: an author who would not give a name could hardly sue. inference The theatres made money; the money that mattered was made by a railway.

Kobayashi Ichizō's girls' opera of 1914 was a device for filling the trains of his Minoo-Arima Electric Railway on the way to his hot-spring resort; the audience saw the show free with their bath, about 1,100 of them a day in the first season, and the girls, most with only an elementary education, were paid as much as university graduates. documented In this timeline the Takarazuka Utena of 1919 is the company's first full-house run of a new piece, and the railway's Sunday traffic to Takarazuka doubles in the year it opens. choice Over the century the revue's Utena plays to more people than any other piece in its repertoire, more than the revue's Rose of Versailles has done in our history, where it reached five million spectators in 2014. documented for the Rose of Versailles; choice for Utena.

A classic nobody owns

Most of Utena never had an owner. Under the press and copyright rules of the 1880s a newspaper serial could not be collected into a book for two years without the editor's consent, and was protected after that only if someone registered it; the Copyright Act of 1899 gave nothing to works that had been published unregistered under the old law, and protected an anonymous work for thirty years, counted from the year after publication. documented Pirate editions of popular serials were common: Sakazaki Shiran's life of Sakamoto Ryōma was pirated while it was still running in 1883. documented In this timeline the newspaper text of chapters 1–33 is pirated from the late 1880s, in booklets that print the circles of 1886 as faithfully as the words, and only Shun'yōdō's registered book editions of Part Four and the collected text are protected, until the end of 1917 and 1918. Shun'yōdō shares the rights with the Tokyo Asahi after a dispute in 1900–02, and from 1 January 1919 the whole book is free. choice The economic consequence is the opposite of what the book's publishers feared. A public-domain classic is a free raw material, and everybody uses it: eleven editions in two years, the cheapest of them ten-sen booklets at railway kiosks; films from 1918, using the unprotected newspaper text; the Takarazuka operetta; the one-yen sets of 1926–27, in which Kaizōsha's first set alone drew 230,000 subscribers at a yen a volume, about two per cent of a graduate's first month's pay. documented for Kaizōsha; choice for the rest. Every company that adapts the book adds to the audience for every other adaptation, and none of them owes the author a sen.

After the war the textbook editions make it one of the steadiest sellers in Japanese publishing (Part X), and the 1997 television series, which in our history earned its makers royalties on an original work, in this timeline earns them royalties on an adaptation of a free one, which is the business model of every adapter of Dickens and Austen. inference

The ledger

WhoWhat the book did for them

Shadow play · Part XII

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-koShake the sticks! Black roses: up or down?

A-koUp! Thirty yen a plant! …Oh. They're red ones, grown in the shade with ink on.

B-koShh! …Who else gets rich?

A-koEverybody! One day, even the trains.

B-koAnd this stick? It's got no name on it.

A-koThirty yen a month, while it lasts.

B-koOne black rose a month?

A-koA fake one.

A-koDo you know? Do you know?

B-koDo you know who didn't get rich?

(A postal money order flutters down from the flies, made out to nobody, and lands in the empty cup of fortune sticks.)

XIII

The critics

A hundred and forty years of arguing about what the book is, from a Monday column of 1885 to the stylometrists

Every generation of critics in this timeline has had to decide first what kind of thing Utena is, and has decided differently: a gesaku with ideas above its station, a romance of pure love, a fairy tale for schoolgirls, a parable of capital, a hymn to sacrifice, a lesson in democracy, a feminist manifesto, a text about texts, a lesbian classic, a book about abuse. Each of those readings is still held by somebody, and each of them can quote the book.

The critics who speak in this Part are invented, with their essays and their sentences, and each is placed among the real critics, schools and magazines of their decade, whose documented ideas are the frames inside which they argue. No real critic's words are applied to the book. Where a real critic appears, it is with something they really wrote, about something else; where a real scholar is said to have written about the book, the work is described, never quoted, and labelled choice. choice throughout, except where marked.

The Monday columnist, 1885–1888

The first critic of Utena is the one who disliked it longest. Suimutei, the anonymous columnist of a rival small paper in Kyōbashi, reviewed it nearly every Monday from April 1885 to the end of the run (Part IV), and in 1888 a small Tokyo house collected seventy-four of his columns as Notes on the Rose (薔薇随筆), the first book about the book. choice It is still the most quoted. Suimutei never solved the serial and never pretended to; what he did was notice. He was the first to say in print that the faces in the cuts are erased on purpose, that the comic chapters and the others "were not written by the same pen, or not on the same day", that the creed is a riddle and not a slogan, and, on the book's last chapter, that "the author has given us a heroine who disappears and a bride who walks, and asks us which of them is the story". choice Who he was is unknown. A note in his book says that he was a former samurai of a northern domain, a claim that fits half the journalists in Tokyo. choice

The literary men of the 1880s read the serial in the terms Tsubouchi Shōyō's Essence of the Novel had just given them: the heart of the novel is human feeling, "manners and customs come next", and fiction must be rescued from being the "plaything of women and children". documented for The Essence of the Novel; choice for the reading. Utena was, embarrassingly, all three: true in its feelings, exact in its customs, and read above all by women and children. The verdict that stuck was the one Part V records, true in its people and false in its castles, and a reviewer of the 1888 collected edition put it in the form everyone repeated: "Take away the castle and you have a novel. Take away the novel and you have a castle." choice

Love and the bride, 1890–1905

In February 1892 Kitamura Tōkoku opened an essay in Jogaku zasshi with the sentence "Love is the secret key of human life", argued that "marriage makes a person worldly", and shocked a generation of young intellectuals. documented His followers, the romantic critics of the 1890s, found in Utena what Tōkoku's essay described and no other Japanese novel had shown: a love that marriage never touches. The fullest statement was Love Without a Husband (1894), by Kōno Seiu, a young poet who published it in a coterie magazine of his own: the love between Utena and Anthy, he argued, is the purest in Japanese literature because it has no future, no household and no name, and the book is right to end it at a coffin. choice It is a beautiful essay and, as later critics pointed out, it needed the girls to be apart.

The women's answer came four years later, from Nagase Fusa, a graduate of a Yokohama mission school who taught in one. Her essay On the Bride (花嫁論, 1898), printed in a Christian women's monthly in the month the Civil Code's books on the family took effect, read Anthy as the wife the new code had just created: legally incapable, transferred from owner to owner, addressing each in the form the household required, and smiling. choice It was Nagase who called the code's articles on wives "the Rose Bride articles" (Part VII), and Nagase who first argued that the book's ending is not a love story but a legal one: in a world where a wife can do nothing on her own account, the one thing Anthy can do is leave. choice She also took on the shinpa stage, whose Witch of the Rose (Part XIV) had made Anthy a "poison woman": "They have made her a witch," she wrote, "because they could not bear to make her a wife." choice Nagase married in 1902 and published nothing more. Her essay was reprinted in 1971 by the women's liberation movement and is now in every anthology. choice

The naturalists' fairy tale, 1906–1920

Naturalism, as Shimamura Hōgetsu and Hasegawa Tenkei preached it from 1906 and Tayama Katai's Futon practised it in 1907, wanted literature to lay reality bare, and came to mean the frank confession of the author's own life. documented To the naturalists Utena was everything they were against: anonymous, allegorical, crowded with marvels, and popular. The most quoted dismissal is the critic Sakaki Tōsen's, in 1909: "a fairy tale for schoolgirls, which schoolgirls are right to love and men are wrong to discuss". choice Sakaki made one exception, and it became famous: the only chapter of the book that a naturalist could respect, he said, was chapter 8, in which a cooking class goes wrong and two girls wake up in each other's bodies, "because it is the only one in which the author admits that nothing is happening". choice The joke was on him. By 1920 the comic chapters had their own defenders, who argued that they were the book's realism and the duels its dream, and the naturalist verdict survived mainly as the thing every later critic began by refuting. inference

The commodity and the gate, 1920–1945

It took a Marxist method to invert the Meiji verdict. choice When Aono Suekichi argued in 1926 that the spontaneous expression of the oppressed must be raised to purposive class consciousness, and Kurahara Korehito in 1928 called for a proletarian realism with the party's point of view at its centre, they gave younger critics a method for reading anything. documented Its best application to Utena is Oda Rintarō's The Rose Bride as Commodity (1929), in a proletarian monthly: Anthy is a thing exchanged among owners; the duel is the market; End of the World, who issues orders unseen until the last chapters, is capital; the castle he projects from his tower, which everyone works for, is ideology; and Utena, the girl who tries to win the commodity's freedom by beating its owners at their own game, is the petty bourgeoisie, heroic and doomed. choice Oda's conclusion, that the castle is the truth of the book and the feelings of its people the projection, was the one Part V mentions, and it lasted. choice So did his last line, which read Anthy's walk out of the gate as "the first strike in Japanese literature", and annoyed historians of the real one at Kōfu ever after. choice Oda was arrested in 1933 and recanted in 1934, and wrote nothing about the book again.

The most dangerous reading came next. Yasuda Yojūrō and the Japan Romantic School, from 1935, sang what the dictionaries call an "aesthetics of defeat", and drew young readers away from both Marxism and the realist novel toward a lofty, ironic love of beautiful failure and the neglected classics. documented In that air the critic Hasebe Sōun, who never joined the school and is always counted with it, published The Gate (門, 1938): Utena's fall at the Rose Gate is the most beautiful death in modern Japanese literature, because it is useless; the coffin is a lotus seat; the hand that reaches for her is the nation's; and Anthy's walk out of the gate, which spoils all this, is either cut from his account or, in one notorious footnote, called "a desertion". choice The essay was read by students who went to the war, and some of them wrote about it in letters home. choice It is the reading that the national-policy film of 1939 (Part XIV) bent to the state's use, sending Utena to the front instead of the gate and marrying Anthy off instead of letting her desert, and the reason the book's post-war critics have always been nervous about its coffin. inference Hasebe served on the criticism section of the Patriotic Association for Japanese Literature, which existed from 1942, and was purged from public life after the war, as Yasuda was in 1948. documented for the association and Yasuda's purge; choice for Hasebe.

Two other things happened to the book's criticism in these years. The Home Ministry's instruction to publishers of children's books in October 1938, which told them to avoid depictions of romantic love, tightened a squeeze on open writing about the girls' culture that had grown from the book (Part XV), and by 1940, when the illustrator Nakahara Jun'ichi was driven off the pages of Shōjo no tomo (Part IX), there was none. documented for the instruction and for Nakahara; choice for the rest. And the women who had read it as girls in the 1890s were now writing their memoirs, and the memoirs, more than any critic's essay, recorded what the book had been to them. choice

Whose castle? 1945–1970

In 1946 Maruyama Masao described Japanese ultranationalism as a "system of irresponsibility": every value and every order flowed down from the emperor, each person's authority came from nearness to him, the emperor's own came from his ancestors, and so nobody along the chain acted as a free subject or answered finally for what was done. documented Three years later Nozaki Hiroshi, a young political scientist, applied the idea to the book in an essay whose title became a classroom question, Whose Castle? (1949): the letters signed End of the World, which everyone obeys and nobody admits to sending, are the system of irresponsibility exactly, and Akio, who turns out to be End of the World and says he only shows people what they want to see, is the man at its centre. choice Nozaki's reading and the textbooks' (Part X), which taught the book from 1952 as the triumph of individual conscience over feudal custom, were the two halves of the post-war Utena: one said what the castle was, the other who had fought it. inference

The 1960s added doubts. When Etō Jun argued in 1967 that maturity in Japanese fiction requires the collapse of the mother, the critic Miura Ryō answered, in an essay on the book called A School Without Mothers (1968), that Utena had been there first: it has almost no mothers, only a letter from the twins' mother that goes into the waste-paper basket, a stepmother without a face, and a fiancée's mother who calls a young man her prince, and its children are therefore never allowed to grow up, which is the point. documented for Etō; choice for Miura. And when Yoshimoto Takaaki called the state a "communal illusion" in 1968, the students who read him read the castle as one, and painted it on the barricades at two universities. documented for Yoshimoto; choice for the rest.

Anthy left, 1970–1989

The women's liberation movement found the textbook Utena intolerable (Part X), and its answer was a pamphlet. Anthy Left (アンシーは出て行った, 1972), by Saeki Kazue, a high-school teacher who had taught the book for ten years, mimeographed and sold at the movement's meetings, argues that the textbooks had the wrong heroine. Utena, the girl who wants to be a prince and save a princess, is the fantasy; Anthy, who is saved by nobody and leaves, is the woman; and the book's whole action is the destruction of the fantasy so that the woman can walk out. choice Saeki's last page, which asks every girl who has written the essay on where Anthy is going to write instead about where she herself is going, was read aloud at the movement's meetings for a decade. choice

The scholars came next. Maeda Ai's The Formation of the Modern Reader (1973) taught Japanese literary studies to ask who read a book and how, and argued that the readers of the 1880s were still reading aloud, in company. documented His student generation took the method to the serial's letters columns. Tachibana Mie's The Readers of 1885 (1979) reconstructed, installment by installment, what the paper's readers wrote, who they were and what they argued about, from the letters column, Suimutei's book, the editor's memoir and the private letters and diaries of readers printed in the 1930s; Part IV's notes on how the serial's chapters were received rest chiefly on it. choice Its most quoted finding is that from chapter 7 onward more of the letters came from women than from men, and that the women wrote longer. choice The same year a word-frequency study found at least three hands in the text (Part XVII). choice

Two real works of these years, a book and an essay, have in this timeline the same titles and the same subjects as in ours, and readers of Utena claim both. Komashaku Kimi's The Logic of the Witch (1978), which re-read Sōseki and Genji as a feminist and was called a bible of women's liberation, never mentions Utena, and every reader assumes the witch is Anthy. documented for the book; choice for the readers. And when Sata Ineko challenged, in 1985, the long-standing reading that the change in Midori at the end of Takekurabe was her first menstruation, and Maeda Ai and others answered, the quarrel over what had happened to a girl offstage in a classic was one that readers of Utena had been having about chapter 31 for a century. documented for the Takekurabe debate. The "sofa debate" (ソファ論争) of 1986, between a novelist who said that every reader knows what Nanami saw and a scholar who said that the whole force of the chapter is that no reader does, ended, like the Takekurabe one, with both sides keeping their supporters. choice The book has not settled it either.

Then theory. In 1983 Asada Akira's Structure and Power, inviting the young to "a gradual sideways slide into knowledge", started the boom a newspaper named the New Academism. documented Kuga Shin's The Projected Castle (1984) is the book's contribution to it: the castle is an image with no original, the lantern the first postmodern machine in Japanese fiction, and the book a text that knows it is projected; Anthy's walk out of the academy is the sideways slide, out of a story that had no outside. choice Kuga's book sold surprisingly well, and is now mostly remembered for its cover, which is blank. choice

Roses and lilies, 1990–2026

The criticism of the last thirty-five years has mostly been about what earlier critics would not name. inference Mizuhara Aki's The Rose Was Ours (1995) is the history of a century of reading Utena as a story of love between women: the dormitory roses of the 1890s, the alumnae poetry clubs, the flower that means women here and men in our history (Part X), and the critics who looked away. Its argument, that the book's love between girls was always the open secret its readers kept for one another, is now the common reading. choice The magazines of love stories between girls that began in the 2000s in our history, where they are called yuri, began in this one too, under the rose's name, and their critics argue about whether Utena is the first rose story or the thing the genre was invented to escape. documented for the magazines in our history; choice for the name and the argument.

After 2004, when the law first let people in Japan change their registered sex, critics began to ask what Utena's jacket is. documented for the law. The question is old (Meiji readers called her henjō nanshi, Part V), but the answers are new: a girl who wants to be a prince, a prince the world calls a girl, or someone the book's own language has no word for. The book says she is a girl and says she wants to be a prince, and critics have built on both statements. choice

Since about 2010 the most-read criticism has been about Akio. Read in an age that has learned the word grooming, the chapters the textbooks skipped (Part X) are a precise account of how a charming adult isolates and uses two girls, and of how a whole institution helps him; several critics have argued that the book is the first in Japanese to show it from inside, without either excusing it or making it lurid. choice The most read of their books, The Carriage at Night (夜の馬車, 2019), by Kagamida Sumi, a school counsellor, follows the Carriage Book chapter by chapter and argues that the adults of Ōtori Academy, from the woman teacher and the vice-principal Akio charms away in chapter 30 to his fiancée's mother, all see enough to stop him and none of them does. choice Others have written about Anthy's skin, which the colour prints of the 1880s made a deep red-brown (Part III), and about what it meant for the most frightening woman in Japanese fiction to be drawn darker than everyone else. choice

The tools changed too. The 2002 critical edition (Part XVIII), a digitised run of the newspaper with its letters columns, and the stylometric studies of 1998 and 2017 (Part XVII) have made Utena one of the most studied texts in Japanese digital humanities. choice In our history the method was tried on Genji's Uji chapters in 1957, and in 2018 it found Kawabata's girls' novel Hana nikki to be a co-authorship with Nakazato Tsuneko. documented In this timeline those studies were done too, and the Utena study of 1979 took the Uji study of 1957 as its model. choice

Abroad

After the settlement notices of 1885–91 and the Paris reviews of 1900 (Part VIII), foreign criticism began in earnest with the French, who read Judith Gautier's abridged Fiancée des roses of 1902 as Japonisme and a little as a book for women. The first complete English translation was Ruth Penhallow's, in 1962 (the English version of 1911 had been abridged, like Gautier's French), by an American who had taught English at a Tokyo girls' school before the war; her introduction, which compared the book to Alice, Jane Eyre and Revelation in that order, sent a generation of American students of Japanese to it. choice The English-language scholarship that in our history wrote about Takarazuka, the "S" relationships of girls' schools and the girls' magazines (Jennifer Robertson in 1998, Deborah Shamoon in 2012, Hiromi Dollase in 2019) writes in this timeline about the same subjects, and in each case about the book behind them. documented for the books; choice for their subject.

The standing arguments

Six questions have divided the book's critics in every decade, and none is closed. choice

Who failed at the gate?
Utena, because she tried to be a prince (Hasebe, admiringly; Saeki, gladly); the prince, because there was none (Kuga); the reader, who wanted one (Mizuhara).
Victim or witch?
The shinpa stage and the play inside chapter 34 say witch; Nagase, Saeki and most critics since say a woman made into one; a minority, citing the blade in chapter 38, says the book refuses to choose, and that is the point.
Is the book in love with Akio?
The readers of 1886 were, and said so (Part IV). Critics since have asked whether the book's charm is his, and whether a reader who enjoys the carriage chapters is being groomed with Utena.
What are the comic chapters for?
Filler (Sakaki), relief, the book's realism (its defenders by 1920), or its other argument: that Nanami, who loses both her duels and gains nothing from the game, is the only character who changes without anyone's help.
Does the castle exist?
Yes, as a slide (chapter 38); no, as anything else (Kuga); yes, as everything the characters do for it (Oda); and in the essays of a great many schoolchildren, yes, and Utena is in it.
Where is Anthy going?
The question every senior high school student in this timeline has written on since 1952 (Part X). The book says she is looking for Utena. Saeki's answer, "out", is the most quoted.

Shadow play · Part XIII

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-koStep right up, step right up! The castle in the sky! Upside down at no extra charge!

A-koAha! There it is! The truth of the whole book!

B-koYour dad sat in that very seat, mister. Said it was a fairy tale for schoolgirls.

A-koMy father was a fool! That's money up there! Everybody's wages, hanging in the sky!

B-koIt's a lamp. And a bit of painted glass.

A-koA lamp… A lamp! Then the castle is… the castle is…

B-koWant me to blow it out?

A-ko(in the dark) There never was a castle! Even better!

B-koDo you know? Do you know?

A-koHave you heard what it is this year?

(The lamp comes back on, the castle still upside down, and in the critic's seat sits a smaller hat with a notebook.)

XIV

Versions and riffs

Continuations, parodies, plays, films and games: a hundred and forty years of other people's Utenas

Nobody in this timeline has read the same Utena twice, and most people have read only its first and last chapters, in class. They have seen it, heard it, sung it, played it as a board game at New Year and argued about the ending of a version the author never wrote. The book was rewritten from its first autumn, and in a hundred and forty years almost every part of it has been changed by somebody, the duel least of all.

How Meiji treated a hit

The yardstick is what happened to the hits of our own history. When Takahashi Oden, the papers' "poison woman", was beheaded on 31 January 1879, the small papers ran her story the next day, two rival picture-books raced each other into print, and Kawatake Mokuami's kabuki of her opened at the Shintomi-za four months after the execution, with two more illustrated books of the play on sale the same month. Ozaki Kōyō's Konjiki yasha reached the stage fifteen months after its serial began, with four years of the novel still to come; its most famous line, the vow to cloud next year's moon with tears, is the stage's tidy version of a speech Kōyō wrote as a stammer, and the frontispiece's leather shoes became, in a statue of 1985, the geta of the popular memory. Tokutomi Roka's Hototogisu collected an entire shelf of what its scholars call "Hototogisu things": a prequel of the lovers before their marriage, side-stories about each of them, "true story" exposés of the family behind it, knock-off sequels and a sequel to one of the knock-offs, songbooks, a naniwabushi text with the singing marks printed, biwa ballads, children's versions and a comic-strip version of 1928. Konjiki yasha was filmed twenty-two times by 1937, and its heroine was played on screen in 1918 by a man, the onnagata Kinugasa Teinosuke, who played Hototogisu's heroine the next year. documented (Part XXI)

The law did nothing to stop it. Under the ordinance of 1887 a novel had no performance right at all: only a script or score carried one, if its author had published it marked "performance rights reserved" or had not published it at all; and the Copyright Act of 1899 gave the author of a novel the right to translate it but still no express right to dramatise or adapt it; its drafter thought an adaptation earned no copyright of its own. When the kamishibai men of the 1930s told Ōgon Bat, each teller's was different, because the scripts were never written down and nobody in the trade thought of copyright. documented A serial larger than any of these, whose author would not give a name and so could not object, and which was entirely out of copyright from 1919 (Part IX), was going to be remade by everyone who could hold a brush, a sword or a camera. inference The "Utena things" (ウテナ物) of this timeline fill a bibliography of more than four thousand entries, compiled since 1951 by a society of collectors in Yokohama and still growing. choice

Before the ending, 1885–1887

Continuations. In the eight weeks between Parts One and Two, three rival small papers printed continuations, unsigned, in which the sleeping prince of chapter 13 woke and came down to claim Utena; one ran for three weeks (Part IV). In the six months before Part Four they were sold as books, and by the spring of 1887 there were at least nine endings on sale, among them a marriage of Utena and Akio, a death of Anthy, a convent and a steamer to France. choice

The first parody. In the spring of 1886 a new comic paper, started that season to live off the serial and gone by the autumn, ran Revolutionary Boy Tenjō, in which a schoolboy dresses as a princess to win back his bride from a council of girls, who settle everything by sewing contests. choice The comic papers already ran parody serials of other people's genres: Kibi dango, the sister magazine of the satirical weekly Marumaru chinbun, had serialised a mock life of a "poison woman" in 1879. documented It is the first of the turned-around Utenas, of which there are now hundreds, and its central joke, that a boy in a dress was funnier than a girl in a jacket, told 1886 something it did not want to know about itself. inference

Games and pictures. For the New Year of 1886 a Tokyo print publisher issued an Utena sugoroku, a race game printed on one sheet, which starts at the academy gate and ends, for the winner, in the castle; a throw of six on the square of the lift sends a player straight to the top, and the square for chapter 11 sends everyone back to the beginning. A set of karuta cards with the creed split across the reading cards followed the next year. choice Picture sugoroku tied to a novel were an Edo habit (one for a version of Hakkenden survives from 1852), and in 1890 a boys' magazine gave away a sugoroku of student types as its year-end supplement. documented The Utena sugoroku has been reprinted, redrawn or reinvented nearly every New Year since. choice

The first stage. The Rose Bride of the Bluff, by a women's company at a Yokohama theatre in November 1885 (Part XIX, document 4), invented a scene the book does not have: Anthy, alone on the stage after the duel, takes off her spectacles and looks at the audience. Every stage version for the next twenty years kept it. choice

The Meiji stage and the storytellers, 1887–1912

Kabuki, 1887. The Shintomi-za's Utena (Part VI), staged with the publisher's leave, gave the book's published ending its first rewrite: Anthy, walking out of the gate, finds Utena asleep in the forest beyond it, and the curtain falls on the two of them under a rain of paper roses. choice The kabuki stage had always preferred a reunion to an absence, and audiences who had read the book cried at both. inference The reunion has been the commonest ending of Utena ever since. More people in this timeline have seen Utena and Anthy reunited at the gate than have read the whole book in which they are not. choice

The first sequel, 1888. Utena, the Later Tale (後のウテナ), anonymous, in three paper-covered volumes, sends Anthy and Chu-Chu across Japan in search of Utena and ends with them finding her in a mission hospital in Nagasaki, without her memory, being nursed by Juri. choice It was a great success and was followed by a sequel to itself, The Later Tale Continued (1889), in which the memory comes back. choice The pattern is the one Hototogisu's knock-offs followed twenty years later in our history: a sequel to a knock-off. documented for the Hototogisu titles.

A ghost story, 1889. San'yūtei Enchō, the greatest storyteller of the age, had spent the mid-1880s turning French and English novels, recited to him by educated friends, into Japanese tales for the yose, and his ghost stories were best-sellers in shorthand transcript. documented In this timeline, in the winter of 1888–89, he tells a ghost story of his own about a burned seminar hall: no duellists, no Utena, only a young professor who trades a hundred boys for a teacup with a woman's rouge on it, and a sister who keeps roses in sugar because she cannot bear to watch them die. Enchō's version answers the question the book will not: the professor lights the fire with his own hands, and his ghost walks the ruins every year on the night of the fire, counting to a hundred. choice That is Enchō's answer, not the book's, and it is the one most Japanese children know, because the kamishibai men of the 1930s borrowed it. choice

Gidayū, 1889. The duel in the forest garden, newly written for the chanters, was the girl chanter Takemoto Ayanosuke's most requested piece (Part VII). choice

A villain's life, 1891. A kōdan storyteller's True Record of Ōtori Akio, taken down in shorthand and sold in eight parts, gives Akio the childhood the book never does: a gifted boy, a prince to every child who saw him, adopted into the Ōtori house, and ruined by a sister's sacrifice he could not forgive. choice It was the first version to make Akio the hero of his own story, and the first to be accused of excusing him. Both kinds of version have been written ever since. inference

Shinpa, 1896. The new-school theatre staged Utena more often than any other novel of the 1880s (Part VI), and in its own way. Its most successful version, The Witch of the Rose (1896), makes Anthy a "poison woman" in the tradition of Oden, who has bewitched her brother and destroys the innocent Utena, and ends with Anthy's death by her own hand in the gateway. choice Shinpa audiences, who in our history would weep a few years later for the faithful Namiko of Hototogisu, wept for Utena and hissed Anthy every night for a decade. choice Women readers of the book hated it, and said so in letters to the women's magazines; it is the version against which the "Anthy story" of the 1900s was written (Part XV). choice

Women on stage, 1893–1908. The Misaki-za's all-woman Utena of 1893, with Ichikawa Kumehachi as Akio (Part VII), kept the book's ending, as no other stage version of the Meiji years did; Kawakami Sadayakko's Paris fragment of 1900 (Part VIII) ended on the duel; the Imperial Actresses' Training Institute played the ball (Part VII). choice

Small change. In 1907, as the last volume of Natsume Sōseki's I Am a Cat appeared and its imitators began (I Am a Mouse that year, I Am a Silkworm the next, I Am a Frock Coat in 1910), a hack in Tokyo published I Am Chu-Chu, in which Anthy's small animal narrates the whole book with comments on the food. documented for the cat and its imitators; choice for the small beast of the southern seas. By 1912 there were also a prequel, The Prince in His Youth; a side-story for every member of the council; an exposé, The Truth of Ōtori Academy, which claimed to name the real school and named three; a New Utena set in a Kyoto girls' high school; songbooks of new-style verse; and an English crib for students. choice

Free for all, 1912–1945

Film. After the two-reel duel of 1918 (Part IX) came a full-length Utena from Nikkatsu in 1920, with the onnagata Kinugasa Teinosuke, who had played Konjiki yasha's heroine in 1918 and Hototogisu's in 1919, as Anthy. documented for Kinugasa's earlier roles; choice for the third. It was the last time a man played her on screen; the reform that the Utena of 1918 had begun finished with her. choice By 1940 there had been at least twenty-six Utena films: fewer than the sixty Chūshingura films made by 1926, the story the studios reached for whenever they were short of a hit, and more than the twenty-two Konjiki yasha films of our history by 1937. documented for Chūshingura and Konjiki yasha; choice for the count. A few kept close to the book as far as they went, none filmed it whole, and three of them changed the book for good:

  • The car, 1926. A silent remake from Shōchiku's Kamata studio set the story in the present and gave Akio a motorcar in place of the carriage. It ends with Utena killed when the car goes off the coast road and Anthy walking away from the wreck. Critics hated the car; audiences came to see it. choice Every later modern-dress version has a car in it, and so, in 1997, did the anime (Part XI). inference
  • The sword-fighting Utena, 1930. In the year an independent producer turned Konjiki yasha into a sword-fighting film, another made Utena a wandering swordswoman of the Edo period who fights her way into a castle to free a captive princess. documented for the Konjiki yasha film; choice for the Utena. It has no Akio, no council and no school, and its heroine wins. It was the most profitable Utena film before the war. choice
  • The talkie, 1932. The first sound Utena used the book's dialogue, and audiences heard the creed spoken from the screen, in the actors' own voices, for the first time. Its Anthy, whose low, polite voice was the first thing every review mentioned, is the voice most Japanese still hear when they read the book. choice

Rensageki. In 1915 the chain-drama houses, where live actors alternated with filmed scenes on a screen lowered in front of the stage, played an Utena in which the duels were filmed in a real forest and everything else was played live. The form lasted only until the police regulations of 1916–17 ended it. documented for rensageki; choice for the play.

The revue. The Takarazuka operetta of 1919 (Part IX) gave the reunion ending its music: the two girls meet beyond the gate and sing. In 1927, the year the company staged its first revue, the last scene became a descent of the whole company in white down a great staircase, with Utena and Anthy at the bottom, and it has stayed so. choice In Asakusa, in the same years, the light-opera houses played a parody, Utena of Asakusa, in which the council are rival opera troupes and the Rose Bride a soprano everyone is trying to hire; the opera fans who sang mocking words to the Carmen prelude had new words for the creed. documented for the Asakusa parodies and fans; choice for this one.

Records and radio. A naniwabushi Utena was recorded in 1912, and benshi narrations of the films were sold on disc through the 1920s, as they were for Hototogisu and Konjiki yasha. documented for those records; choice for Utena's. Radio broadcasting began in 1925 documented, and in 1934 the broadcaster read the book aloud in weekly parts, without chapters 31 and 32, without the night drives of the Carriage Book and without the creed's last line, the first of the cuts the censors would make in print three years later. choice

The Rose Knight, 1933. Street kamishibai, which in 1930–31 had invented Ōgon Bat, a golden-skulled hero born in the last episode of a villain's serial, made the most changed Utena of all. The Rose Knight (薔薇の騎士) has a girl in a black jacket who fights the Demon King of the Night Carriage, a cloaked figure with no face, with a sword that comes out of a rose; Anthy is a princess in a cage who is rescued in every episode and captured again in the next. documented for Ōgon Bat; choice for the Rose Knight. Each teller's was different (Part XIX, document 12, imitates a patter sheet). A generation of Tokyo children knew Utena as a superhero before they knew she was a girl in a book. inference

The national-policy Utena, 1939. The last pre-war film, released under the censored title Shōjo Utena (Part IX), turned the duels into kendō matches at a girls' school, made Akio a foreign agent posing as a benefactor, and ended with Utena, the swordswoman of her school, leaving for the front in China as an army nurse while Anthy, freed, marries a naval officer. choice It is the only version in which every character ends where the state wanted them, and it is the version critics have in mind when they say that Utena can be made to say anything (Part XIII). inference

The classic and its children, 1945–1989

The Occupation film, 1947. The first post-war film (Part X) ends with Utena and Anthy leaving the academy together, through the gate, while the police take Akio away in the back of a jeep. choice It is the most cheerful ending the book has ever had, and the one the textbooks quietly assumed for the next twenty years. inference

Tezuka's Utena, 1953–1956. Tezuka Osamu, who adapted Faust in 1950 and Crime and Punishment in 1953, ending the second with the Russian Revolution breaking out, and who had grown up in Takarazuka next door to a star of its male roles, drew an Utena for the girls' magazine Shōjo Club from January 1953 to January 1956, in the slot where in our history he drew Princess Knight. documented for Tezuka's adaptations, his childhood and the slot; choice for the manga. It is Tezuka's own book: a mischievous angel gives the infant Utena a boy's heart as well as a girl's, which gives her wish to be a prince a cause in her nature, where the book gives it one in a memory; the castle is a real castle; Akio is a usurping regent; the duels are fought by a girl with two hearts against a court of boys; and it ends at the gate, with both girls riding out on the white horse. choice That is Tezuka's answer to the book's question, not the book's. Princess Knight was never drawn in this timeline. Its premise, a girl raised as a prince because only a man may inherit, went into the Tezuka Utena as the angel's mischief, and its heroine Sapphire does not exist. choice Mushi Production animated Tezuka's version for television in 1967–68, the years in which it animated Princess Knight in ours. choice

The underground, 1968–1971. The comics for grown-ups of the late 1960s produced a hard-boiled Akio (1968), told from inside the carriage, and the theatre produced the most important stage Utena since 1893. choice Terayama Shūji, whose troupe Tenjō Sajiki had staged Kegawa no Marī (Marie in Furs) in 1967, with Maruyama Akihiro in the title role, a male prostitute who lives as a woman, and whose composer through the 1970s was J.A. Seazer, who had joined the troupe in 1969, staged Utena, or the Bride in the Coffin in Tokyo in 1970: the council as masked chorus, the audience seated in the duelling garden, and the duels sung by a rock chorus with Seazer's music. documented for Terayama, the troupe and Seazer; choice for the production. Its ending, in which the actress playing Utena walks out through the audience into the street and does not come back, was the one the student movement remembered. choice

Takarazuka, 1974–1975. In our history the revue's great boom of the 1970s came from The Rose of Versailles, staged in August 1974 under the direction of the film star Hasegawa Kazuo and seen by well over a million people in three years. documented In this timeline the boom comes from a new two-part Utena, directed by Hasegawa in 1974 and 1975, which for the first time brings the Carriage Book to the revue's stage, carriage and all, with Akio made Anthy's guardian, as the kabuki had made him her cousin, the tower scenes told in dance, and the staircase at the end. choice Why there is no Rose of Versailles on that stage is a question for Part XV.

The fans, 1975 onward. At the first Comic Market, in December 1975, among a few dozen circles selling their own magazines, several sold Utena parodies, and Utena circles have been a fixture of every one since. documented for the first Comic Market; choice for the circles (Part XIX, document 15, imitates a flyer). The fan parodies did what no publisher would: they paired Utena with Anthy in plain words, paired Tōga with Saionji, paired Juri with everyone, and made Akio a joke. choice

Play. A home video game of 1987, Utena: Gate of the Rose, made the player Utena and the duels into a fencing game; its bad ending, in which Utena becomes the Rose Bride, was found by nearly every player first. choice

The faithful one, and after, 1989–2026

The 1997 television series (Part XI) was faithful in a way no screen version had ever been: it kept Parts Three and Four whole, the carriage (as a car), the inn, the siblings and the ending, and dropped every reunion, angel and jeep that adapters had added since 1887. choice That was its shock. Viewers who had known Utena from Takarazuka, Tezuka and the textbooks discovered in December 1997 what the book actually does to Utena in chapter 38, and the broadcaster took complaints about the last six episodes every week until the series ended. choice

The director's film of 1999, Adolescence of Utena, is in this timeline one more free version, and one of the oldest kind: it begins again from Utena's arrival, redraws everyone, and at its climax turns Utena into a car, which Anthy drives out of the academy. documented for the film. Since 1926 every modern Utena had had a car in it; the 1999 film is the first in which Utena is the car, and critics who knew the history called it the end of a seventy-year-old joke. choice

Since 2000: a light-novel sequel series in which Anthy, grown up, runs a tea shop on the coast road and waits; two "2.5-dimensional" stage musicals, after the manner of the ones our history staged in 2018 and 2019; a picture book for small children, with no Akio in it; three novels told by Akio, each attacked as an apology; a retelling by Anthy, which won a literary prize in 2011 and is taught beside the book in some schools; an isekai parody in which an office worker wakes up as Nanami's cowbell; and, in 2025, a streamed live-action series in twelve parts. documented for our history's musicals; choice for the rest.

What changes, and what hardly ever does

Lay the versions side by side and three things change in almost all of them, and three hardly at all. inference

VersionYearHow it ends
The book1887Utena vanishes; Anthy walks out of the gate alone to look for her
Kabuki, Shintomi-za1887Anthy finds Utena asleep beyond the gate; paper roses
Utena, the Later Tale1888Anthy finds Utena in a Nagasaki hospital, nursed by Juri
Enchō's ghost story1889No Utena; the professor's ghost counts to a hundred
The Witch of the Rose, shinpa1896Anthy dies in the gateway by her own hand
Takarazuka1919Reunion beyond the gate, sung; from 1927 a staircase
Shōchiku, silent1926The car goes off the coast road; Anthy walks away
Sword-fighting film1930Utena storms the castle and wins
The Rose Knight, kamishibai1933Never ends: "come back tomorrow"
Shōjo Utena, national policy1939Utena leaves for the front; Anthy marries

Every row but the book's, the 1997 series' and the 1999 film's is choice; the 1999 film is documented.

What changes. The ending, first: most versions bring the two girls together or kill one of them, and very few leave them, as the book does, apart and looking. Akio, second: he has been a demon, a spy, a usurper, a tragic hero, a guardian and a joke, and in many of the modern-dress films from 1926 on hardly more than the car he drives, until the film of 1999 made Utena the car; only the book and its few faithful versions let him be what he is, a charming man nobody stops. The brother and sister, third: stage, screen and textbook have cut, softened or explained Akio and Anthy more often than any other thing in the book, from the kabuki of 1887, which made them cousins, to the national-policy film, which made them strangers. choice

What hardly ever changes. The duel: almost every version keeps a contest for the Bride, and most keep the sword drawn from a girl; the exceptions are remembered for it, from the sewing contests of 1886 and the kendō of 1939 to Enchō's ghost story, which has no duellists at all. Nanami: nearly every version that keeps the school has her, and every one that has her makes her funny. And Chu-Chu, who has been a monkey, a mouse, a kitten, a kangaroo, a dragon and a car's mascot, and is missing from hardly anything but the ghost stories. choice

Shadow play · Part XIV

C-koExtra! Extra! Extra!

C-koGrandma and Grandpa haven't spoken in forty years! All over the end of a bedtime story!

C-koAnd tonight it's my turn to tell it!

C-ko(as Grandma) The two girls find each other at the end, or I'm not speaking to you either!

C-ko(as Grandpa) One of them dies at the end, or I'm not speaking to you either!

C-ko(as little brother) And the bad guy's a car!

C-koAnd I'm stuck being the silly sister. Again.

C-koOh, what am I supposed to do?

A-koSkip to the sword fight?

(At the foot of the bed, a small animal is eating the last page.)

XV

The culture it made

Words, genres and stock figures that exist only here, and the famous things that, because of it, came out differently or not at all

A classic does not only inspire. It takes up room. Once a story is in every classroom, its shapes become clichés, its words become slang, and the young artists who might have invented its kind of thing for themselves either rework it or run from it. This Part follows both: what Utena added to Japanese culture, and what it displaced.

Two rules govern what follows. A real work made after 1885 still exists in this timeline unless the serial gives its maker a strong reason to make something else (Part XVI); and where the reason is strong, the work changes, and is described here and labelled, never quoted. choice

Words

The serial's vocabulary has been in this timeline's dictionaries since the 1890s. Some of its words are given in earlier Parts: 学園 for a school (Part III), the Duellist and the Utena law (Part VI), Bride and Prince in the dormitory (Part VII), "Let's just go home" (Part IV). The rest:

アンシーする, to "do an Anthy"
To walk out, with nowhere in particular to go: of a marriage first, from about 1905, then of a job, a family or a political party. In the 1920s the papers' divorce reports used it of wives who left without a settlement; in the 1980s it was what a woman did when she left, with no wedding to go to, a company that expected her to resign on marriage. choice
To "graduate" (卒業)
From Akio's order in chapter 23 (Part IV): to be dropped by someone who has used you. Schools still graduate their pupils, but the word has an edge: in our history a Japanese pop group says a departing member has "graduated", and in this one no agency would dare. documented for our history's usage; choice for the rest.
An Akio
A charming older man who preys on girls and is protected by the institution he runs. Women's magazines warned against "the Akio type" from the 1920s; since the 2010s the word has been used in reporting on abuse in schools and sports clubs. choice
A Nanami
A vain, absurd, devoted younger sister; by extension, anyone who is the comic relief in her own tragedy and survives it. Usually affectionate. choice
From the End of the World (世界の果てから)
Of an order that nobody admits to giving. Office slang since the 1950s, helped by Nozaki's essay (Part XIII): a memo "from the End of the World" is one whose author cannot be found. choice
Ten-years tea (十年後の茶会)
From chapter 37: a class's reunion ten years after leaving school, held by girls' schools from 1897 and now by schools of every kind. The tea is mandatory; the laughing is the point. choice
Rose (薔薇)
Love between women, since the 1890s (Part VII). Lily, in consequence, is love between men (Part X). choice

Genres that exist only here

The Anthy story (アンシー物), 1902–1930s. A girl leaves home with a trunk and a small animal to look for someone she has lost (Part VII). It is the first plot of the Japanese girls' novel, printed by the hundred in the girls' magazines, and its greatest writer is Yoshiya Nobuko, whose Flower Tales (1916–24) exist in this timeline too, as stories of girls who look for each other and, increasingly, find each other (Part IX). choice The convention it set lasted into the girls' comics of the 1970s. choice In our history the love stories between girls drawn in those years almost all ended in separation or death, which their critics have blamed on everything from patriarchy to the end of the girls'-school culture. documented In this timeline they end, as often as not, with one girl walking out of a gate to look for the other, and the genre's critics call these "gate endings". choice

The duellist novel (決闘小説), 1888–1904. The boys' answer to the girls' book: middle-school boys who fight secret duels for honour, a friend or a girl, in boarding houses and on riverbanks, under rules taken from the serial's. It boomed with the real duelling craze of 1888 (Part VI), was banned from school libraries after the Duel Act of 1889, sold all the better for it, and died when the war with Russia gave boys' fiction real battles to write about. choice Its last trace is in the school stories of the 1910s, in which a challenge is always issued by letter, sealed with a rose. choice

The carriage melodrama, 1890s–1920s. In the domestic novels that filled the newspapers from the late 1890s, whose heroines suffered for husbands, mothers-in-law and money, and which shinpa staged as fast as they appeared, this timeline adds one stock villain: the charming man with a carriage, later a car, who drives a girl out at night to show her something. documented for the domestic novel; choice for the villain. Readers called him "an Akio" before the novels did.

The Black Rose mystery, 1920s–. When Japanese detective fiction came into its own in the 1920s, with Edogawa Ranpo's first stories in 1923, it found a setting waiting for it: the school with a secret society beneath it. documented for Ranpo's debut. Stories of a seminar, a hall, a fire long ago and a lift that goes down are a recognised sub-genre in this timeline, called after Part Two, and they are still written. choice

The shadow-girl duo, 1930s–. When comic double acts in the new manzai style filled the variety halls of the 1930s, women's duos in schoolgirl costume, one sharp and one slow, performed in silhouette behind a lit screen and called themselves "shadow girls" after the serial's. documented for 1930s manzai; choice for the duos. The form passed to radio, then to television, and every Japanese comedian of this timeline knows the opening formula. choice

The prince play, 1890s–. Girls' schools have staged a play with a girl as the prince every year since the 1890s: at first in secret, in the dormitories, then at the leavers' farewell parties, and since the war at the school festival; at many schools the part is chosen by the outgoing seniors and is the highest honour the school has. choice

Stock figures

By the 1950s the book's people had become types, and editors used their names as shorthand. choice The girl in boy's clothes who wants to be a prince is "an Utena", and by 1960 an Utena was the most familiar figure in Japanese girls' fiction, more a cliché than a heroine. The silent, smiling girl who belongs to somebody is "a Bride". The comic rival-sister is "a Nanami", the predator "an Akio". Every girls' story has a small animal that understands everything and eats too much, and the trade calls it "the Chu-Chu". In our history the long-running television series of children's classics that began in 1975 gave almost every story a pet mascot to sell; in this one the custom had a name before television existed. documented for our history; choice for the name. And every school story has a letter from someone the characters never see. choice

What came out differently

This is where the book's weight shows, because a classic changes what the next generation can do with the same materials. inference

The revue's princes. Takarazuka's male-role players had their signature part from 1919 and their Western men's dress from the first Utena, five years before our history's (Part IX). choice In our history the revue's audience changed from mostly male to mostly female in the late 1930s, with the cropped-haired male-role star. documented In this timeline women were the audience from the first Utena, and the revue never had to be discovered by them. choice

No Princess Knight. Tezuka Osamu's Princess Knight (1953–56), one of the first story comics for girls in our history, is not drawn in this timeline. Tezuka, who in our history called the strip the sum of his Takarazuka experience, draws an Utena instead, and its premise, a girl raised as a prince because only a man may inherit, goes into his Utena as a mischievous angel's gift (Part XIV). documented for our history; choice for this one. The difference is that Tezuka's girl in armour, in this timeline, is somebody else's heroine, adapted, and Japanese girls' comics begin with a classic, not with an original. inference

No Oscar. In our history Ikeda Riyoko's The Rose of Versailles (1972–73) began as the story of Marie Antoinette, and its guards' commander became a woman raised as a man because, Ikeda has said, she thought a woman would be easier to draw freely; the character, at first a supporting one, took over the series, and the Takarazuka stage version of 1974 began the revue's greatest boom. documented In this timeline a girl in boy's clothes who means to be a prince was, by 1972, the most familiar figure in girls' fiction: the book had made her an Utena, and Tezuka's Utena of the 1950s had already given her a prince's upbringing. Drawing one was the opposite of drawing freely. Ikeda keeps the commander a man, as he was in history, and her Rose of Versailles is the story of Antoinette and Fersen and the Revolution: a solid success and a long seller, but not a phenomenon, and Takarazuka does not stage it. choice The revue's boom of 1974 comes instead from its two-part Utena (Part XIV). choice Of all the changes in this Part, this is the one most open to argument, and the one that takes the most away: the most famous girl in a uniform in our history does not exist in this one.

The flight to the boys. The women artists born around 1949, the "Year 24 Group", remade girls' comics in the 1970s, and their great innovation in our history was the love story between boys, from Takemiya Keiko's In the Sunroom (1970) to Hagio Moto's The Heart of Thomas (1974) and Takemiya's Song of the Wind and the Trees (1976). Takemiya has said that drawing a man and a woman in bed could get an artist called in by the police, so she moved the subject to two boys; the friend who urged her on gave her Hesse's Demian among other books. documented In this timeline the same artists make the same move for one more reason. A love story between two girls was not new in 1970; it was in the textbooks, and their mothers had read it. Yamagishi Ryōko's Two in the White Room (1971), the story of two girls at a French boarding school that our history counts the archetype of the yuri story, is in this timeline the same story, with the same death at the end. Yamagishi chose girls, she later explained, because teenage readers would accept a love story between girls more easily documented; in this timeline they had been accepting it since the 1880s, and her ending, with one girl dead and no gate, is read as a deliberate refusal of the gate ending. choice The one love story the classroom had not got to first was between boys, and the young artists went there. inference The works themselves are the same. choice What changes is what they meant: in our history a rebellion against the girls' comic; in this one a rebellion against the classic behind it, and against a teacher's reading of it. inference

Girls' schools in fiction. Kawabata Yasunari's Otome no minato (1937–38), a story of a love triangle between girls at a mission school in Yokohama, drafted by Nakazato Tsuneko and revised by Kawabata, exists in this timeline as in ours. documented Every reader in this one takes its school for Ōtori Academy, and the booksellers sold it as an Anthy story. choice

The uniform. The sailor suit came to girls' schools in 1920–21 and conquered them in both timelines. documented In this one it competed with the black jacket with gold buttons that several girls' high schools had adopted from the Utena jacket after 1899 (Part XII), and lost everywhere except a few dozen schools, whose girls still wear the jacket and are told every April which book it comes from. choice

Things nobody could have predicted

  • Chu-Chu. A tin toy in 1886, a celluloid doll in the 1920s, a mascot on everything from savings-bank money boxes to a railway's commuter pass in the 1980s. Its species is still argued about. choice
  • The New Year sugoroku. Printed, redrawn or reinvented almost every year since 1886 (Part XIV). Throwing a six on the lift square is, in some families, a reason to pour the first sake. choice
  • White roses at graduation. Girls' schools gave each leaver a white rose from the 1890s, a real one while they graduated in summer and one of silk once graduation moved to March, before any rose is out in Tokyo, and the custom spread to every school after the war; a red rose given to one particular friend is a different matter. choice
  • Girls named Utena. The name, a Buddhist word with no history as a girl's name (Part V), had two spikes: 1886–90, when registrars objected and parents insisted, and 1997–98, after the television series. choice
  • No red gowns at weddings. Japanese brides of this timeline, who began to wear Western white in numbers after the war, will change into a red kimono for the reception but never into a red Western gown, the Rose Bride's, and dressmakers know not to suggest one. choice
  • Nemuro. The real city at the eastern tip of Hokkaido, which has no memorial hall, has received letters every year since 1886 asking for directions to it. choice
  • The rose tribe's room. In our history the gay magazine Barazoku opened a column for women readers in the 1970s called "The Lily Tribe's Room", and the word yuri followed. documented In this timeline the magazine is Yurizoku (Part X), and its women readers' column is "The Rose Tribe's Room". choice

The two timelines, culture only

The Rose of Versailles, with Oscar, 1972–73The Rose of Versailles, without her

Barazoku, 1971: the rose is men's loveYurizoku, 1971: the lily is men's love

Shadow play · Part XV

A-koDo you know? Do you know? Have you heard the news?

B-koPlaces, everybody! New show, new faces! The girl in a boy's jacket who wants to be a prince!

A-koHere! Here! Here! Forty of her, Boss. They're sharing one jacket.

B-koThe princess raised as a prince!

A-koNever showed up.

B-koThe lady commander of the royal guard!

A-koHere. He's a man.

A-koDo you know? Do you know?
